text:
A Boston University study found that NFL players with advanced CTE did not qualify for compensation under the NFL Concussion Settlement.

Researchers linked cognitive testing performance during life with CTE confirmed after death in 33 former NFL players.

Despite showing measurable cognitive impairment, players with advanced CTE received the lowest impairment rating in the settlement's assessment program.

The study suggests the settlement's diagnostic criteria may miss cases of cognitive impairment associated with confirmed CTE.

NFL players diagnosed with advanced CTE after death who also demonstrated cognitive impairment in testing during their life still did not meet the requirements for financial compensation under the NFL Concussion Settlement, according to a Boston University study published Wednesday.

Researchers examined 33 NFL players diagnosed with CTE after an autopsy who had completed the baseline assessment program (BAP) stipulated by the 2014 settlement – that ended a years-long class-action lawsuit – in what researchers called the largest study to date linking cognitive testing performance during life with CTE confirmed posthumously.

The results, published in JAMA Network Open, found that seven participants had advanced (Stage 3 or 4) CTE. Six of those seven showed measurable cognitive impairment on testing, yet all seven received the lowest impairment rating (Level 0) on the BAP's system, according to documentation provided to researchers by players' families.

"The BAP's diagnostic criteria might miss cases of cognitive impairment that are objectively measurable and associated with confirmed CTE pathology," Michael Alosco, PhD, co-director of clinical research at the BU CTE Center said in a statement. "This has important implications for former players seeking diagnosis and potential compensation through the NFL Concussion Settlement."

USA TODAY Sports has reached out to the NFL for comment.

The participants' average age at the time of testing was 63, and their average age of death was 65. The most-common problem was memory, particularly short-term, with 63% of the participants affected. Executive function (52%) and language (41%) were other common impairments.

"This is the largest study of its kind to directly link the amount of CTE pathology found at autopsy with objective cognitive testing during life," Anna Aaronson, lead author and a PhD student at the Boston University CTE Center said in a statement. "These findings provide an important roadmap for recognizing CTE in living patients."

text:
photo by: AP Photo/Gareth Patterson

The biggest news of the NFL preseason from a University of Kansas perspective was undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels’ ascension to the No. 2 spot for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Daniels, who started portions of six seasons at KU, including the entirety of 2024 and 2025, beat out veteran Jake Browning and second-year quarterback Connor Bazelak in order to back up Baker Mayfield. That’s a promising start to his career that suggests Daniels could stick around in the professional ranks for longer than most former KU quarterbacks.

Several past Jayhawks also survived Sunday’s roster cutdown deadline, while others have caught on with practice squads in the days since. Quite a few more were not so lucky and will be looking for new homes.

Dorance Armstrong, now an outside linebacker for the Washington Commanders, is the longest-tenured Jayhawk in the NFL. The veteran missed much of the 2025 season after suffering a torn ACL. He has been working his way back into action at practice but will not technically be on the Commanders’ 53-man roster due to a one-game suspension for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. The Athletic reported that Armstrong “kicked a police officer while being arrested during an incident in May 2025 in Frisco, Texas.”

Also technically absent from his team’s initial roster this season is running back Devin Neal of the New Orleans Saints. Neal received a fair bit of playing time and scored two touchdowns as a rookie but will miss the 2026 season due to a hamstring injury after being placed on season-ending injured reserve.

Austin Booker, now entering his third year, seems poised for a big role with the Chicago Bears after playing just nine snaps in one preseason game, according to Pro Football Focus. However, he is currently battling a groin injury.

Two former KU linemen, both recent NFL Draft selections, made the San Francisco 49ers’ 53-man roster. Dominick Puni has long been firmly ensconced as a starter at guard. Enrique Cruz Jr., a rookie fifth-rounder, saw extensive action with 156 snaps across three preseason contests.

The Seattle Seahawks had entered camp with three Jayhawks on the roster. Second-year guard Bryce Cabeldue earned a spot on the final 53, while second-year tackle Logan Brown returned to the practice squad; both received Super Bowl rings with the team last season. Sixth-round rookie wideout Emmanuel Henderson Jr., who caught four passes for 65 yards, returned four kicks and made a pair of tackles in the preseason, will join Brown on the practice squad.

Bangally Kamara, who initially made the Minnesota Vikings in the spring via a minicamp tryout, found his way onto their practice squad. Tommy Dunn and D.J. Withers had been reunited on the interior defensive line for the Dallas Cowboys, but now they’ve been split up as Dunn made the practice squad, while Withers was waived on Sunday.

Cobee Bryant, who was thrust into action as an undrafted rookie for the Atlanta Falcons as a rookie last year and recorded eight tackles with a pass breakup for the team this preseason, initially appeared to have made the Falcons’ practice squad but was released on Wednesday morning.

Other current free agents include wide receiver Luke Grimm (waived by Los Angeles Chargers with an injury settlement on Aug. 25), kicker Laith Marjan (cut by Pittsburgh Steelers on Aug. 23) and wideouts Quentin Skinner (released by Buffalo Bills on Saturday) and Levi Wentz (waived by Steelers on Saturday).

Offensive lineman Hakeem Adeniji retired during training camp shortly after signing with the Baltimore Ravens.

title: Moorehead explains how Eagles didn't let Lemon fall behind - NBC Sports Philadelphia
description:
It’s not ideal when any player misses significant time in training camp.
The Eagles’ first-round receiver from USC suffered a hamstring injury on Day 4 of training camp and missed the next nine practices and the first two preseason games.
And it took a group effort to make sure he didn’t fall too far behind.
What was the biggest challenge with Lemon missing that much time in training camp?
There’s an intensity to Lemon that the Eagles seem to like.
text:
It’s not ideal when any player misses significant time in training camp. But it can be a big hurdle when it’s a first-round pick the team is relying on this season.

That happened with Makai Lemon this summer.

The Eagles’ first-round receiver from USC suffered a hamstring injury on Day 4 of training camp and missed the next nine practices and the first two preseason games.

And it took a group effort to make sure he didn’t fall too far behind.

“With Makai, we had to come up with creative ways to get him walkthroughs and to get him different things that he could do while he was out,” Eagles receivers coach Aaron Moorehead said on Tuesday. “He couldn’t physically run but we could walk through things or we could talk through things and we could have him break the huddle and go where he needed to go just to catch him up that way.

“It wasn’t the most fun thing in the world. I know he wanted to be out there and I know we all wanted him to be out there but that’s what you do. You sacrifice your time and you sacrifice your energy to get where you want to go. For the short term, it’s, ‘Hey, let’s get to Washington.’ But long-term, it’s like, ‘Where are we going to be at the end of the year?’ He took it really well and I thought that it was a collaborative effort.”

Moorehead gave credit to Howie Roseman, Nick Sirianni, Parks Frazier, the entire coaching staff and players for helping to make sure Lemon would be able to be quickly reintegrated when he returned from the injury.

That has since happened.

Even though Lemon’s first preseason game didn’t go particularly well, the Eagles wasted no time getting him back with the first-team offense in practice when he returned from injury. And it seems like their plan is for him to be the team’s starting slot receiver when they host the Commanders in the season opener on Sept. 13.

What was the biggest challenge with Lemon missing that much time in training camp?

“It’s just really timing,” Moorehead explained. “That’s really the big thing. Timing and getting on the same page with everybody and making sure that they’re pressing forward.”

Even though Lemon couldn’t practice for nine days because of that hamstring injury, the Eagles kept him involved in walkthroughs. Basically, Lemon would join the huddle to hear the call from Jalen Hurts and would then back off and let the other players run the rep.

Moorehead stressed the importance of Lemon hearing Hurts in the huddle.

“Jalen is the guy that you have to be in the huddle with in a game and it’s not going to be this quiet,” Moorehead said. “You’ve got to get in there, you’ve got to hear it and you back off and you go to your spot after the huddle and let the other guys run the play. But to me, it’s how many times can you get with Jalen and hear him say exactly the word that he’s going to say in the huddle and you go into your spot and kind of getting that mental rep.”

Even when Lemon was out for most of training camp, Hurts seemed impressed by the way the rookie from USC was attacking walkthroughs. There’s an intensity to Lemon that the Eagles seem to like.

And Moorehead sees it too.

“It matters,” Moorehead said. “He focuses. He doesn’t want to mess up. He wants to get in there and make sure. There’s 10 other guys that are counting on him and he understands that. I think that, that’s a good thing for him to understand that, that’s the reality of the NFL.

“You came in as a first-round pick, of course, but there’s a lot of first-round picks in this offense and we’re all counting on you to do your 1/11. If he can do his 1/11 every play on the plays that he’s in, he’s going to have a chance to have a really good year.”

When Lemon finally returned from injury, he talked about the need to be more professional, but never really got into the specifics of what he meant by that. Moorehead explained that he thinks Lemon meant that he needed to take care of his body with stretching, prehab and rehab.

Moorehead’s directive: “Whatever Smitty does, you do.”

“No one wants to be hurt,” Moorehead said. “It’s the worst feeing in the world when you’re any player, you’re a 10th year guy or you’re a rookie, that’s the worst thing. But when you’re trying to prove yourself to your teammates or even to yourself what kind of player you can be in this league, being hurt you can’t do it. I think the big thing he meant was just like, ‘I got to make sure every day I’m taking care of my body like it’s my job.’ There are no days off with that.”

text:
Miller is entering his fourth season as a pro and his second season in head coach Kellen Moore’s offense. He’s been slowed by injuries ever since entering the league as a third-round pick in 2023, and he rushed 47 times for 193 yards and one touchdown last season, while adding another 5-30-0 through the air on five targets. Kamara is expected to be out for about a month, so it’s possible he avoids IR to start the season. If Kamara were to land on IR and miss at least the first four games, Miller could be worth a stash in deeper leagues while we wait to see how his usage plays out alongside Travis Etienne, but he is unlikely to have any real standalone value.

The Saints’ backup running back statuses continue to change. Veteran No. 2 RB Alvin Kamara (knee) is expected to be sidelined for at least one month, and RB Audric Estime is now sidelined with an undisclosed injury. Miller and RB Devin Neal (hamstring) both returned this week, though. Beat reporter Jeff Nowak notes that Miller, Neal and RB Ty Chandler were all allowed to rotate in for first-team reps today, as coach Kellen Moore presumably seeks out a viable primary backup for starting RB Travis Etienne. Per Nowak, Miller “looks sharp despite the time missed.” This is worth tracking for short-term bench stash purposes.

As of Thursday, Neal was taking advantage of RB Kendre Miller’s back injury by playing well at practice. Miller is still sidelined, but now Neal is too. The two backs, along with RBs Audric Estime, Ty Chandler and CJ Donaldson, are all competing for the RB3 job. The fact that Neal is working with the training staff out in the open is a good sign, but this is worth keeping an eye on because a hamstring injury ended his rookie season prematurely.

The good news is that Miller was not listed with a knee injury after suffering a season-ending ACL tear in Week 7 last year. The bad news is that he evidently has a new injury, and the Saints have a fairly deep running back room right now. RBs Devin Neal, Audric Estime, Ty Chandler and CJ Donaldson are all vying for roster spots. Per Underhill, Neal is taking advantage of the extra reps. He could have the inside track to the RB3 role right now.

Triplett and his colleague, Nick Underhill, joked about how RB Kendre Miller (knee) will likely once again dazzle at organized team activities, before things fizzle for him. It’s a brutal take on the 23-year-old Miller, who has dealt with ankle, hamstring and knee injuries, plus one concussion, in his short career. Miller is currently rehabbing a torn ACL suffered in October 2025, but it sounds like he is expected to participate next week. If Kamara is released, Miller should at least get a chance to compete for the No. 2 role. Triplett believes the team has one A-back in RB Travis Etienne, and two B-backs in Miller and, presumably, RB Devin Neal.

Miller’s season ends with a 47-193-1 rushing line to go with five receptions for 30 additional yards. The third-year back was carving out a small role in Kellen Moore’s offense, earning 6.3 touches per game while averaging a career best 4.1 YPC. Miller, who was drafted by the Saints in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft, will enter next season on the final year of his rookie contract in what will be a prove-it season.

Miller injured his knee in the second quarter but was able to walk into the locker room under his own power. He will not return to the game, but the Saints will hope that the injury isn’t serious. Miller finished the day with one carry for seven yards. Expect some more work for Devin Neal and also Taysom Hill.

Jarrett, who has been battling a knee injury, was said to be likely to suit up on Sunday, but that will not be the case. With the weather making this likely to be a run-heavy game, Jarrett being out is a slight bump for Alvin Kamara and Kendre Miller.

Miller added one grab for 11 yards on his lone target. The third-year back continued to cut into Alvin Kamara’s workload, but a 1B role between the tackles isn’t worth much on a team like the Saints. Miller has at least nine touches in each of his past four games but has posted just one usable fantasy week over that stretch. He is more of a thorn in the side of Kamara managers than a standalone fantasy bet heading into Week 7 against the Bears.

Brooks and Zach Sieler are expected to provide veteran leadership for the NFL's youngest team.

Brooks will be paired with rookie Jacob Rodriguez in the upcoming season.

MIAMI GARDENS — Linebacker Jordyn Brooks has missed two games in the past five years.

In his six-year NFL career, he has averaged 140 tackles per season.

Put them together and you have a player who doesn’t miss games and doesn’t miss tackles.

At 28 years old, Brooks and defensive lineman Zach Sieler will be counted on to provide veteran leadership on the NFL’s youngest team, a role both players embrace.

Buy Miami Dolphins tickets on StubHub

“It's a lot of young guys, a lot of inexperienced guys, and so as older vets on the team, that's a responsibility that we have to be responsible for,” Brooks said. “It's going to be a gauntlet of a season. We got such young guys, it's easy for young guys to kind of ride the wave, highs and lows in the season. So our job is to be somewhere in the middle and help those guys in the best way that we can. We're up for the challenge and excited for this upcoming season.”

Brooks, like Sieler, welcome new coach Jeff Hafley’s edict that the Dolphins will shed their “soft” label and become a physical team.

“To me, physicality is a choice that takes no talent,” Brooks said. “It's just a decision that one man's got to make, whether he wants to be physical or not. And so that's a mindset that we're trying to bleed into this team on a consistent basis.”

Ask Brooks a question, he’ll answer it, whether the answer is one you hoped for or not.

“There’s been some times where we had very physical practices,” he said. “There’s been times that we haven't, right? That's what practice is for, is try to build that consistency, so when we get to the games, that's what shows up on tape. That's where we're in the process of doing, being the most physical and toughest team we can be.”

There were times during training camp when as much as Brooks wanted to go, a leg injury forced him not to. Taking the smart approach seems to have paid off with the season still 1½ weeks away. It makes no sense to gamble with a player coming off an All-Pro season, which Brooks is.

“I knew it wasn't long term,” he said of the injury. “It was just something I had to get taken care of. A couple days, couple weeks, it's all good to go now.”

When he does line up in the opener against the Las Vegas Raiders, Brooks will have a new partner at his side. The Dolphins are going with second-round pick Jacob Rodriguez after releasing veteran Tyrel Dodson.

“Jacob is, I like to say, like a rookie vet,” Brooks said “He's already seasoned. Whatever he was doing at Texas Tech, he was doing the right things. Came in very knowledgeable of the game, very mature and just ready to go. He's just gotten better and better since OTAs, honestly. I'm excited to see his growth and what he does this year.”

title: NFL execs rank NFC teams: Rams, Seahawks clear favorites. Can the Bears keep rising?
description:
We start with the NFC, where the Seattle Seahawks are reigning champs, but the Los Angeles Rams are the strong betting favorite.
One of the execs had the Chicago Bears atop his ballot, on the thinking that seasons rarely play out as expected.
"It is hard for me to go against Seattle being the top team in the NFC," the voter putting the Seahawks atop the conference said.

text:
With the NFL preseason finished, it’s time to check in with team executives to set expectations for the coming 2026 season one final time.

The six executives polled this week ranked teams 1-16 in each conference, under the condition of anonymity to allow them to speak freely. I also asked them to place each team into four buckets: Super Bowl contenders, division contenders, sub-.500 teams and likely top-10 pickers in the 2027 draft.

We start with the NFC, where the Seattle Seahawks are reigning champs, but the Los Angeles Rams are the strong betting favorite. One of the execs had the Chicago Bears atop his ballot, on the thinking that seasons rarely play out as expected. Teams are ranked below in median order, with average as a tiebreaker.

1. Los Angeles Rams

Votes: 2-1-1-1-1-2 | Avg: 1.3 | Median: 1 | Vegas wins: 11.5 (1st-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 6

All but two voters moved the Rams to the top of the NFC after an offseason that saw Los Angeles overhaul its defense with Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and two cornerbacks from Kansas City.

"I think they are the best team in the NFC by far," a former GM said. "Beyond all the defensive additions, Matthew Stafford is just surgical. So impressive."

The Rams went 1-2 against Seattle last season largely because they finished those games with a -26.7 EPA differential on special teams.

"It is hard for me to go against Seattle being the top team in the NFC," the voter putting the Seahawks atop the conference said. "Talent-wise, it is going to be really close."

One other voter had the Bears first, partly on the theory that things tend to play out unexpectedly.

"I would say there is a clear gap (between the Rams and the rest of the NFC) with the return of Aaron Donald," another voter said.

The Rams are the strongest preseason Super Bowl favorite since 2002, per covers.com.

"I think Myles Garrett puts them over the top," another exec said.

2. Seattle Seahawks

Votes: 1-2-3-2-2-6 | Avg: 2.7 | Median: 2 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 5 | Division contender: 1

The Seahawks have an unproven offensive coordinator (Brian Fleury) after Klint Kubiak's departure to become the Raiders' coach. They spent their offseason extending key players (Leonard Williams, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Devon Witherspoon) while the Rams were adding big names from the outside. The cornerback situation remains a worry, and it's unclear whether their top defensive chess piece, Nick Emmanwori, will be at his best physically following ankle surgery.

"It's hard for me to see them continuing to get better now that they are a marked man," one exec said. "A lot of people got paid. Is the hunger still there?"

The transition from hunter to hunted affects every Super Bowl winner.

"I don't know about Super Bowl, but they are going to go deep in the playoffs," another exec said. "I think them and the Packers are probably the next (NFC) teams after L.A."

Voters trust Seattle's defense while taking a wait-and-see approach with the offense.

"It is hard for me to think you're not going to have some kind of dropoff going from Kubiak to Fleury, even if it is in the same schematic realm," one voter said. "You lost Kubiak, you lost the Super Bowl MVP (Kenneth Walker III). I know you're excited about Jadarian Price, but …"

3. Philadelphia Eagles

Votes: 3-4-5-3-3-4 | Avg: 3.7 | Median: 3.5 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 4 | Division contender: 2

With Seattle on "Hard Knocks" and the Rams making splash after splash this offseason, the Eagles are about as under the radar as can be. Reminder: Philly leads the league in regular-season victories over the past four seasons (50) while ranking second to Kansas City in postseason wins (six).

"They could go either way, to be quite honest," one exec said of the Eagles, who finished 11-6 last season. "I think they will be better. The thing that was really good for them is a potential concern, and that is the receiver position and running back. Saquon (Barkley) did not have a great year. The offensive line health and age is a concern. They will still be formidable."

Will A.J. Brown's departure be addition by subtraction? One voter said the pressure's on quarterback Jalen Hurts, whose relationship with Brown had grown cold and who will be playing in an overhauled offensive system under new coordinator Sean Mannion.

"It was hard for me to ding Philly even if the offense is unknown, even if they are taking a step back without A.J. Brown," another exec said. "Vic Fangio and that defense is going to be top five. That O-line is going to be pretty good. It is still Saquon Barkley. Could they win 16-13 every week? Probably."

4. Dallas Cowboys

Votes: 5-8-2-4-4-3 | Avg: 4.3 | Median: 4 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 3 | Division contender: 3

All agree the Cowboys' offense appears formidable. How much can the defense improve?

"Anything is better than what they did last year on defense," the voter placing Dallas second in the NFC said. "They shocked the system by trading Micah Parsons, and I just think generally speaking, new coordinators on defense create variance."

No team is seeking greater variance on defense from last season than the Cowboys, who ranked 32nd in EPA per play by a wide margin, per TruMedia. They replaced Matt Eberflus with first-time coordinator Christian Parker.

"Quinnen Williams is good, and they have a little more girth up front, so it should be better, but they've got some unknowns there too with coaches and philosophy," the voter ranking Dallas eighth said.

The voter ranking Dallas fifth thought the Cowboys' defense might outrank the Packers' defense, notable in light of the Parsons trade last year.

"I like the coordinator," this voter said of Parker. "He is going to help maximize what they have. The secondary is still not a strength, but they have an impressive front seven."

Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown's health is a key variable multiple voters highlighted.

"I have defensive concerns, for sure," one said. "Do they have enough pass rush? How healthy is Overshown? How good are the corners? But they did address the interior with Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, and I like Caleb Downs. They will be better up the middle."

5. Chicago Bears

Votes: 4-7-6-7-5-1 | Avg: 5.0 | Median: 5.5 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 2 | Division contender: 4

The one voter ranking Chicago atop the NFC said the Bears have an elite coach in Ben Johnson, a rising, super-talented quarterback in Caleb Williams and enough talent to take another step.

"I know all the regression stuff," this voter said, alluding to the Bears' ability to win seven games last season after trailing in the final two minutes. "The coach is really good, they have a really good ascending quarterback, the roster is super talented. They did all the right things in the offseason to fight the regression."

The top three teams in the NFC North are tightly bunched in these rankings.

"I love the whole NFC North," one voter said, "but the top three all have defensive concerns."

New safety Coby Bryant's season-ending knee injury hurts Chicago. The Bears still have uncertainty at left tackle.

"Can they win a playoff game again?" an exec asked. "Sure, but I guess that's where I cap the Super Bowl contender of like, do I see them coming out of the NFC over the Rams? I can't see it. Kyle (Shanahan), (Brock) Purdy and the Niners, they have been there, done that. Even Detroit, I trust."

Another voter thought the Bears' rise under Johnson last season painted a target on their backs heading into 2026.

"I'm going to double down on them," the exec placing the Bears fourth in the NFC said. "They are not going to catch people by surprise this year, and the NFC North will be tough. I still think they'll be OK."

6. San Francisco 49ers

Votes: 7-6-4-5-8-5 | Avg: 5.8 | Median: 5.5 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 3 | Division contender: 3

There's a gap between the 49ers' Vegas win total (tied for second in the NFC) and where voters see them headed this season. Should there be?

"I think they are going to be just fine," the voter ranking the 49ers fourth in the conference said. "Veteran team, not concerned. The quarterback (Brock Purdy) is really good. We forget, because he's not this in-37-commercials guy."

So much of the noise around the 49ers should be separate from what happens on the field, unless the injuries coach Kyle Shanahan suffered in a car accident limit him in any way. The science doesn't support concerns over the electrical substation near their practice fields. Owner Jed York's arrest shouldn't be more than something to discuss in the locker room. The situation with Brandon Aiyuk is largely a social media fixation, while the 49ers imposter receiver has nothing to do with the product on the field.

This is still a team banking on some aging players with injury concerns.

"There is something missing with that group," the voter ranking San Francisco sixth in the NFC said. "You can break down their personnel and come out with average in a lot of places. I would probably take Philly's history over San Francisco. They are very similar to Detroit, but I think Detroit is probably first."

7. Green Bay Packers

Votes: 6-3-9-8-6-8 | Avg: 6.7 | Median: 7 | Vegas wins: 9.5 (T-6th-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 1 | Division contender: 5

The Packers' best players on both sides of the ball — tight end Tucker Kraft and pass rusher Micah Parsons — are rehabbing season-ending injuries. Kraft could see his snaps limited early in the season, while Parsons will miss at least the first four games. Throw in Josh Jacobs' arrest on domestic-violence charges, and the buzz is subdued.

"Figuring out how to sort through the contenders came down to: Who do I trust?" one exec said. "I didn't trust Green Bay's O-line and Parsons' injury and the run game with Josh Jacobs' situation."

The Packers finished 9-7-1 despite their injury situation last season.

"Jordan Love's quietly become a really good Tier 2 quarterback, and he can do some top-level stuff," one of the voters ranking the Packers sixth said. "And then I think you're going to see the maturation of previous draft classes. They'll get something out of (Matthew) Golden. I think they've had some good drafts."

Much depends on Kraft and Parsons returning to health.

"I have concerns about their O-line, concerns about what they are doing at some of the skill positions, and we'll see," another exec said. "I'm not super high on them. It's a tough division, tough schedule."

The voter ranking Green Bay third did so because he thought Love was improving and could help the Packers take another step. This voter also didn't like how the Packers' defense finished and thought new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon could provide a boost.

8. Detroit Lions

Votes: 8-5-7-6-10-7 | Avg: 7.2 | Median: 7 | Vegas wins: 10.5 (T-2nd-NFC)

Tier votes: SB contender: 1 | Division contender: 4 | Sub-.500: 1

The voter projecting Detroit to finish 11th in the NFC last year was an outlier. He also came closer than anyone else in the rankings (the Lions finished ninth).

Others have come around entering 2026.

"They are teetering on the seesaw of whether they're going to go into one of those two-year dips to restock the roster with draft picks," said the voter ranking Detroit lowest.

Detroit's Vegas win total ranks far higher than voters' expectations here.

"Detroit, I just don't know if they have all they need on defense to hold up," another exec said. "Offensive line is still a concern for me with those guys, but I like what they have in place on that side of the ball. Defensively, I think it's going to be a struggle to produce the style of play they need."

Another voter drew parallels between the 49ers and Lions as teams that remain strong but have peaked.

"I questioned whether I could really have Dallas over San Francisco and Detroit, but I know what I'm getting with that (Cowboys) offense," another exec said. "That is a top-five offense with continuity, while the Lions are breaking in a new OC, and the Niners are coming off all the injury woes."

9. New Orleans Saints

Votes: 10-9-11-12-13-9 | Avg: 10.7 | Median: 10.5 | Vegas wins: 7.5 (T-11th-NFC)

Tier votes: Division contender: 3 | Sub-.500: 2 | Top-10 pick: 1

The Saints haven't won the NFC South since 2020, Drew Brees' final season. Three of the six voters projected New Orleans to end that streak this season.

"The way they ended last year with the quarterback (Tyler Shough) and the head coach (Kellen Moore) was promising and checks some boxes for me as a potential team on the rise," one of these voters said.

This voter forecast Washington's rise in the NFC entering Jayden Daniels' first season. Last year, he had the Lions falling to 11th in the NFC, while everyone else had Detroit contending (the Lions finished ninth in the conference).

"If there were better teams in the NFC South, I think that would be more of a wow," this voter added. "I think New Orleans wins the division, and Carolina misses the playoffs."

That's a bet on Shough.

"Yeah, he's going to be OK," another exec said. "He's a good quarterback. With (Jordyn) Tyson being hurt early, that is a little alarming. They need production from that (receiver) group. But they should be a good team in Year 2 of their system."

10. Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Votes: 9-10-14-11-11-10 | Avg: 10.8 | Median: 10.5 | Vegas wins: 8.5 (T-9th-NFC)

Tier votes: Division contender: 3 | Sub-.500: 3

The Buccaneers' streak of four consecutive NFC South titles ended last season.

Only one of six voters has Tampa on top this year.

"The big question is, what will the run game look like?" one voter said. "The new coordinator (Zac Robinson) was in Atlanta when they struggled to marry the run and the pass. But they get a motivated Baker (Mayfield) in a contract year, and they have arguably one of the best offensive players in the division with Emeka (Egbuka), plus a ton of draft capital in the defense."

With Mayfield entering his fourth season in Tampa, his unsettled contract situation remains a leading storyline. One voter suggested Mayfield could be the type of quarterback everyone loves when things are going well, but not as much during tougher times. Whatever the case, a good season would put pressure on the Bucs to step up.

"Defensively, they should be more physical up front, adding A'Shawn (Robinson), Rueben Bain, (Josiah) Trotter in the front seven," another voter said. "(Keionte) Scott is a physical nickel built for (Todd) Bowles' blitzes. They'll need that rush to get home with questions in the secondary outside (Antoine) Winfield (Jr.)."

The Bucs won the division in 2022 with an 8-9 record, same as Carolina did last season.

"I think all four of those teams are gonna be under .500 again," one exec said. "So, great, you're the best of the bad teams in your division."

11. Carolina Panthers

Votes: 11-13-12-9-7-11 | Avg: 10.5 | Median: 11 | Vegas wins: 7.5 (T-11th-NFC)

Tier votes: Division contender: 3 | Sub-.500: 3

The top three teams in the NFC South — everyone but Atlanta — averaged between 10.4 and 11 in their average votes. Not much separation, in other words.

"It's going to be a dogfight in that NFC South," the voter slotting Carolina 11th said.

Two voters were quite a bit higher on Carolina than the rest, citing personnel upgrades on defense.

"Carolina is ready to take a step if the quarterback (Bryce Young) does what he did at the end of last year, because they have improved greatly on defense," the voter ranking the Panthers seventh said.

Another exec thought all four NFC South teams might have losing records for a second consecutive season.

"New Orleans beat Carolina twice last season," the exec slotting the Panthers 13th said. "I think the quarterback (Young) holds them back ultimately. I would put them behind Tampa."

Tampa carries the highest Vegas win total (8.5) in the division.

12. Minnesota Vikings

Votes: 12-11-8-10-12-12 | Avg: 10.8 | Median: 11.5 | Vegas wins: 8.5 (T-9th-NFC)

Tier votes: Division contender: 2 | Sub-.500: 4

There's a big drop from the first eight teams to the next six. The fault line runs between the Packers and Vikings, even though Minnesota has had the best defense in the division statistically.

"I think they will get a bump from Kyler Murray, and they have the skill on offense," the voter ranking Minnesota highest said.

The Vikings finished 9-8 last season despite ranking 30th in EPA per pass play. Murray ranked 15th last season among 45 quarterbacks with at least 100 pass attempts. He was 14th in his last full season (2024). That was two spots higher than then-Vikings quarterback Sam Darnold, who had a 14-3 record as a starter.

"With Dallas, Tampa, Minnesota and New Orleans, you can line them up any way you want," another exec said.

The other voters disagreed on Dallas, but less so on the other three.

"Kyler may be better than what they had last year, but he's the fourth quarterback in the division," one of the execs slotting Minnesota 12th said. "And when you look at those divisions where it's clumped together, the quarterback usually is a determining factor."

13. Washington Commanders

Votes: 13-12-13-14-9-13 | Avg: 12.3 | Median: 13 | Vegas wins: 7.5 (T-11th-NFC)

Tier votes: Division contender: 1 | Sub-.500: 4 | Top-10 pick: 1

The voter highest on Washington thought Jayden Daniels' return to health was enough to lift a Commanders team that has question marks entering coach Dan Quinn's third season, including first-time coordinators on offense (David Blough) and defense (Daronte Jones).

"They get Jayden back, and Terry McLaurin will be healthy," this exec said. "They've added some really good parts defensively in free agency. They have to get the offensive line solidified."

Left tackle Laremy Tunsil's season-ending injury will not help.

"I think they are going to be bad," another exec said. "The quarterback is talented, but his style of play, unless he changes it, is a concern. The weapons around him are OK, but I don't think it's a dynamic team offensively. Defensively, they plateaued."

14. New York Giants

Votes: 14-14-10-13-15-14 | Avg: 13.3 | Median: 14 | Vegas wins: 7.5 (T-11th-NFC)

Tier votes: Division contender: 1 | Sub-.500: 3 | Top-10 pick: 2

The voter highest on the Giants pointed to their defense.

"They have a lot of pieces on defense, and I really liked their draft," this exec said. "(John) Harbaugh will play everything close, and they'll be in a ton of one-score games, and we'll see what happens in the moment of truth. They're a candidate for those games to play out really well."

Questions at quarterback, running back and receiver persist.

"I like the Giants' potential on defense," another exec said. "Abdul Carter, Arvell Reese, Brian Burns. But then I don't know how good that secondary is at corner. They lost Dexter Lawrence in the middle. On offense, Jaxson Dart's health, Cam Skattebo's health and Malik Nabers' health are all concerns. There's a lot of unknown."

15. Atlanta Falcons

Votes: 16-15-16-15-14-16 | Avg: 15.3 | Median: 15.5 | Vegas wins: 6.5 (15th-NFC)

Tier votes: Sub-.500: 1 | Top-10 pick: 5

The Falcons won their final four games last season to finish 8-9. It feels like they've lost four straight entering 2026, mostly because the quarterback situation remains a big concern.

"It might be the (Jack) Strand kid who winds up with that job," one exec said, referring to the undrafted rookie out of Minnesota State-Moorhead.

Strand is fourth on the depth chart behind Michael Penix Jr., Tua Tagovailoa and Cooper Rush.

"I'm confused as to where the new coach's identity is with the team," another exec said.

Kevin Stefanski's NFL background is mostly on offense, but coordinator Tommy Rees will call the plays. Rees debuted as a play caller in Week 10 last season, also under Stefanski, when both were with the Browns. Cleveland ranked 31st in offensive EPA per play before Rees took over and 30th thereafter, with a quarterback situation even less appealing than the one in Atlanta.

Execs from other teams did not like the moves Atlanta made in free agency or in the draft, so the lack of excitement entering the season is no surprise. If the Falcons produce a solid season, they can accurately say very few gave them much of a chance.

16. Arizona Cardinals

Votes: 15-16-15-16-16-15 | Avg: 15.5 | Median: 15.5 | Vegas wins: 4.5 (16th-NFC)

Tier votes: Top-10 pick: 6

First-round rookie running back Jeremiyah Love was the most exciting thing the Cardinals had going for them entering this season. But with an ankle injury calling into question his availability for Week 1, the excitement level is subdued.

"Mike LaFleur is at least an offense-oriented head coach out of the McVay system, so there is going to be something there," one exec said.

Would you rather have Jacoby Brissett or the Falcons' quarterbacks?

"Atlanta would at least be solidified if they had Jacoby, and you'd know how to play with him," another exec said. "I love Jacoby as a guy, but if you're going into the season with him as your starter, that's kind of where your season's going to be."

title: Fantasy football predictions that can happen, from a Loveland breakout to a Skattebo bust
description:
Colston Loveland is the TE1 Loveland averaged 12 targets and 20 fantasy points over the final four games (including the playoffs) as a rookie.
Swift has been an underrated fantasy back perennially, and he’s in a Ben Johnson system that churns out fantasy points.
Brock Purdy is a top-five QB Purdy has finished as a top-10 fantasy QB for three straight seasons and was the QB1 in expected fantasy points per game last year.
He still finished as the RB18 in fantasy points per game despite playing hurt and not seeing one carry inside the 5-yard line.
Murray is the QB4 in fantasy points per game since 2020, yet he’s the QB17 in ADP.
text:
Predicting the NFL is a fool’s errand, but I’ll be the sucker for 2026. It’s a tricky exercise finding the middle ground between irrationally wild calls and not bold enough; the following predictions are unquestionably underdogs yet scenarios within reasonable range of outcomes. Here are 20 fantasy predictions for 2026.

Predictions that could actually happen …

Jahmyr Gibbs has a top-10 all-time PPR season

Gibbs has produced the most running back fantasy points over the past two seasons despite David Montgomery seeing the fourth-most carries (31) inside the 5-yard line. Detroit now has arguably the thinnest backup RB group in the NFL. Gibbs will benefit from the league’s easiest schedule — the Lions are favored in 14 games. Gibbs has averaged 27.4 fantasy points during games without Montgomery, which would be a top-10 running back season of all time.

Lamar Jackson is the QB1

Jackson was easily fantasy’s QB1 last season before suffering a hamstring injury that prevented him from running over the rest of 2025. Offensive line is a concern in Baltimore, but the move from John Harbaugh to Declan Doyle’s new play-action system could bring dramatic improvements (albeit a slower start could ensue). This isn’t extremely bold, but Jackson is available rounds after Josh Allen. Jackson also wins another MVP, and the Ravens win the Super Bowl.

Colston Loveland is the TE1

Loveland averaged 12 targets and 20 fantasy points over the final four games (including the playoffs) as a rookie. He owned a team-high 33% target share when he was on the field with DJ Moore, Luther Burden and Rome Odunze (94 routes). Loveland averaged more expected fantasy points (19.1) over his final five games than Arizona TE Trey McBride (18.6) during his historical season. Moore is gone, and head coach Ben Johnson is a true cheat code. Brock Bowers still has PCL and QB concerns, while McBride regresses; Loveland has the path to a top TE finish.

KC Concepcion is fantasy’s highest-scoring rookie WR

Saints’ WR Jordyn Tyson could be sidelined for at least half the season, and Eagles rookie Makai Lemon missed a lot of time with a recurring hamstring injury. Meanwhile, Carnell Tate could get out-targeted by Wan’Dale Robinson in Tennessee, where there are major questions at quarterback. De’Zhaun Stribling is another candidate, but he’ll likely require injuries in San Francisco to see enough targets.

The Browns’ QB situation undoubtedly isn’t ideal, but Concepcion is set for a valuable role in fantasy as Cleveland’s underneath and intermediate WR. He was highly productive in college and has a first-round pedigree. Concepcion (WR47) is available rounds after Tate (WR31).

Nico Collins is a top-three WR

Collins saw a 29% target share (WR4) last season when he didn’t share the field with Jayden Higgins, who’s out for 2026. Tank Dell may not contribute at all this year, and elite defenses often regress. It’s wheels up even more if we get starts from QB Davis Mills. Collins has legit competition and is drafted as the WR9, but he’ll finish top three.

D’Andre Swift is a top-10 RB

Swift enters the season as Chicago’s clear lead back, and he’ll see increased touches with Kyle Monangai sidelined indefinitely with a bone bruise in his knee. Swift has been an underrated fantasy back perennially, and he’s in a Ben Johnson system that churns out fantasy points. Swift is drafted as the RB20, but he was fantasy’s RB1 after Chicago’s Week 5 bye last year.

Bonus: Luther Burden is a top-15 WR, as the Bears’ offense feeds families for fantasy managers.

Brock Purdy is a top-five QB

Purdy has finished as a top-10 fantasy QB for three straight seasons and was the QB1 in expected fantasy points per game last year. He has underrated rushing equity that could increase should injuries strike RB Christian McCaffrey coming off 450 touches. Purdy now gets WRs Mike Evans and emerging rookie Stribling in a Kyle Shanahan offense. Purdy undeniably benefits from his system, but he’s also underrated — both can be true. Purdy isn’t even drafted as a fantasy starter (QB13).

Bucky Irving is a top-12 RB

Irving was fantasy’s RB9 over the first four weeks last season before suffering significant foot and shoulder injuries (the latter requiring offseason surgery). He still finished as the RB18 in fantasy points per game despite playing hurt and not seeing one carry inside the 5-yard line. Kenneth Gainwell is now in Tampa Bay, but Rachaad White left. Meanwhile, Sean Tucker was forced to take a pay cut to avoid being released. Irving will lose some catches to Gainwell (who was an Aaron Rodgers merchant last year), but Irving looked like a star when healthy as a rookie. He will benefit from Tampa Bay’s elite offensive line, a healthier Baker Mayfield and a new play caller.

Malik Willis is a top-10 QB

Willis owns a 14.5% scramble rate, has averaged 58 rushing yards during games started and is the all-time leader in fantasy points per dropback by a wide margin. There have been 34 QBs with 100+ rush attempts in a season since 2014, and 31 of them (91%) finished as a top-12 QB in fantasy points per game. Willis is in a tough situation in Miami, but intriguing rookie Chris Bell will emerge as an alpha as the year progresses (Bell will be drafted as a top-25 WR in 2027). It’s a small sample, and Willis (QB21 ADP) is a heightened injury risk given his style, but the rushing propels him to a top-10 QB fantasy season in 2026.

Dalton Kincaid is a top-five TE

Kincaid led all tight ends in yards, targets, first downs and fantasy points per route run last season despite playing all year on a torn PCL. Kincaid is another year removed from the injury and says it’s the best he’s felt in his career at this point in the year. Kincaid had by far the highest percentage (39%!) among TEs in team receiving yards while on the field last year and was third among all pass-catchers in YPRR.

Kyler Murray is a top-10 QB

Murray was a QB1 during each of his previous six seasons in the league before last year and gets a big upgrade joining Minnesota. Murray has limitations as a passer, but he’ll be motivated to run more than ever while searching for a new contract. He’ll benefit from playing under center more in Kevin O’Connell’s system and throwing to Justin Jefferson. O’Connell has made every QB (including non-running) a QB1 other than J.J. McCarthy, who’s fallen behind Carson Wentz on Minnesota’s depth chart. Murray is the QB4 in fantasy points per game since 2020, yet he’s the QB17 in ADP.

Cam Skattebo is a fantasy bust

Skattebo has real fantasy upside should he see last season’s role again, but he’s coming off major surgery and has a new coaching staff planning to make Najee Harris a “significant contributor.” Skattebo is returning from an ankle dislocation, a fibular fracture and a ruptured deltoid that required the dreaded “TightRope” surgery. Further injuries, new OC Matt Nagy and the veteran Harris all contribute to Skattebo massively disappointing as a Round 4 pick (ADP = 42).

Garrett Wilson is a top-10 WR

Wilson was fantasy’s WR6 over the first five games last year before suffering a knee injury that ultimately ended his 2025 season. He finished with the third-highest air yards share (46.4%) among wide receivers. Wilson produced despite dealing with arguably the worst quarterback play in the league. He remains in a bad situation in New York with Frank Reich as OC, but QB Geno Smith will be an upgrade; Smith’s 2025 should be thrown out thanks to coaching malpractice in Las Vegas. Wilson’s discouraging environment is baked into his ADP (WR20), but he’ll overcome it.

Marvin Harrison is a top-15 WR

Harrison dominated Michael Wilson when they were on the field together last season in all metrics, including seeing more targets during every full game together (10). The Cardinals led the league in passing yards per game (282.7) with QB Jacoby Brissett as a starter in Weeks 6-18, and MHJ will benefit from improved usage. Now healthy, Harrison will make the leap in Year 3.

Juwan Johnson is a top-10 TE

Johnson quietly finished third in receiving yards among tight ends last year, and he’ll catch more touchdowns in 2026; the Saints are due for regression after scoring a TD on an NFL-low 44% of red-zone drives last season, and Taysom Hill is gone. Johnson benefits from a Kellen Moore system that put him in the slot 40% of the time (TE3) and ranked first in plays per minute last season. Johnson will be a big part of the Saints’ offense with Tyson possibly not returning until Week 9, helping him post TE1 numbers in 2026.

Chris Godwin outscores Emeka Egbuka

Godwin was fantasy’s WR2 (ppg) in 2024 before suffering a season-ending injury. He struggled after returning from an ankle dislocation and fibula fracture, but he was fantasy’s WR24 with strong underlying peripherals to close last season (Weeks 13-17). New OC Zac Robinson implements a ton of pre-snap motion, and Godwin has produced the league’s third-highest yards per route run rate over the last two years in such plays.

With Mike Evans gone, Egbuka is being drafted (WR21) rounds before Godwin (WR35), but he struggled mightily over the second half of his rookie campaign. Injuries were to blame, but Egbuka enters 2026 with a turf toe injury that could linger. Godwin is the favorite to play the slot and will post more fantasy points than Egbuka this season.

Jaylen Warren is a top-15 RB

Late-career Rodgers produced the second-most RB targets last season, and Gainwell left Pittsburgh. Newcomer Rico Dowdle will share the Steelers’ backfield and is a threat at the goal line, but Warren is the superior back who should handle most of the passing-down work. The Steelers’ backfield quietly produced the fifth-most fantasy points last season, yet Warren is drafted as the RB27.

Jayden Reed is a top-25 WR

Green Bay will pass far more with Josh Jacobs possibly not playing a snap in 2026. The Packers already planned to increase tempo and condense WR routes this season, evidenced by the departures of WRs Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks. Reed’s season was ruined last year after suffering a broken collarbone and a Jones fracture in his left foot, but he’s the WR1 in fantasy points per target and passer rating when targeted from 2023-2025.

Christian Watson and Matthew Golden will also benefit, but the former has an extensive injury history and has never reached 625 receiving yards in a season, while the latter was the WR62 in YPRR during a highly disappointing rookie campaign. Reed is drafted as the WR43 but will end the season as a top-25 fantasy wideout.

Mike Evans is a top-10 WR in FPPG

Evans just turned 33 years old and is coming off an injury-ruined season, but he has a ton of fantasy upside as Shanahan’s new X receiver. Evans had 11 straight 1,000-yard seasons to open his career and scored 24 touchdowns over 2023-2024 before a broken collarbone/concussion ended his year abruptly in 2025. He was playing through a hamstring injury before that, yet Evans still posted elite separation metrics while dealing with an injured and shaky quarterback.

Evans is the WR3 in first downs per route run and fantasy’s WR11 in points per game over the past two seasons. He’s now the clear WR1 in a productive 49ers offense that vacated 38% of last year’s red-zone targets. Wide receiver Ricky Pearsall is out for the season, and TE George Kittle is coming off Achilles surgery. Purdy might be the NFL’s most accurate downfield passer. Evans (WR29 in ADP) has continuously battled different leg injuries throughout camp and will likely miss time in 2026, but he’ll be a top-10 fantasy WR when active.

Tank Bigsby and/or Emmett Johnson win fantasy leagues

Bigsby and Johnson are drafted as purely bench stashes, but at least one will emerge as a fantasy difference-maker. Bigsby is an explosive runner who would immediately become a fantasy RB1 should Saquon Barkley suffer an injury, while the rookie Johnson has quickly emerged as Kansas City’s RB2 (Brashard Smith is a Round 7 pick who contributes on special teams). Kenneth Walker has battled health issues throughout his career despite never reaching 225 carries in a season, and he’s now expected to see the biggest workload of his career. Johnson has three-down capability and obvious juice. Bigsby (RB51) goes after the top-150 picks, while Johnson (RB61) is available even later

description:
Here's what to know about Guardian Caps entering the 2026 NFL season: What are Guardian Caps?
Guardian Caps are soft shell covers on top of helmets that provide extra cushioning and enhanced safety for head-to-head contact.
For 2026, the NFL has approved use of a new Guardian Cap — teams can choose between the Guardian Cap NXT and the Guardian Cap NXT 2.0.

text:
New helmet protection is sweeping the National Football League.

The NFL announced before the 2024 season that Guardian Caps could be worn by players during regular-season games, a first for the league.

Ahead of Week 8 that season, Miami Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa made headlines for saying he will not wear the protective gear after returning from another concussion. But a number of other players have started wearing them, and the Guardian Caps have a new, sleeker design for this season.

Here's what to know about Guardian Caps entering the 2026 NFL season:

What are Guardian Caps?

Guardian Caps are soft shell covers on top of helmets that provide extra cushioning and enhanced safety for head-to-head contact.

For 2026, the NFL has approved use of a new Guardian Cap — teams can choose between the Guardian Cap NXT and the Guardian Cap NXT 2.0. The new caps have an "external energy-absorbing layer designed to help reduce impact forces, no interference with helmet fit, vision or mobility and a new sleek surface for customization and team branding."

See the comparison here:

When did the NFL start using Guardian Caps?

The NFL started allowing Guardian Cap usage during the 2022 training camp before making it mandated for some position groups in 2023. That then rolled over to regular-season and postseason practices, and more positions have since been added to the mandate.

For 2026, Guardian Caps are mandatory for all contact practices for all positions except quarterbacks, kickers and punters. They are still optional for games, but at least 25 players wore them in 2025.

Are Guardian Caps required for NFL players?

Guardian Caps are required for all positional groups during practices, except for quarterbacks, kickers and punters. Wide receivers and defensive backs were the last position group added to the mandatory list for 2026 after other groups were required to wear it in prior years.

Guardian Caps remain optional for all players in the regular season.

The Daily Slop - 2 September 2026

It feels like Washington may be a sneaky contender for “worst team in the league” this year. We all know the Browns and Dolphins stink; why will Washington be worse? – Kevin Langstaff

Reader Brutus Rugburn chimed in:

Kevin, I agree completely. Looking at their schedule, 3 wins should be the over/under mark. The miracle of 2024 completely screwed up any reasonable, orderly rebuild.

Mike, to add to Kevin’s query, how, if at all, could Washington have responded differently to their winning 2024 season with the clearly deficient roster they had?

The Commanders are projected to win 7.7 games by DVOA. I think they have had a miserable offseason, despite adding Stefon Diggs. The cavalcade of 32-year old acquisitions I have been dunking on all summer leaves me with little faith about the quality of the front office and the lower tiers of the roster. Dire tales from joint practices make me wonder about the reconfigured coaching staff.

So I think the Commanders could be the worst team in the NFL. It’s hard to project them with the worst record, because the Browns quarterback situation is so dire that the team could surrender at the trade deadline, while the Cardinals schedule is so brutal.

Relitigating what the Commanders did after reaching the NFC Championship Game in 2024 is tricky. It’s easy to condemn the Laremy Tunsil and Deebo Samuel trades, but those moves made sense at the time. The Commanders got so little besides Jayden Daniels from the 2024 draft that the seeds of decline may have already been sewn.

The Commanders needed to do a better job self-scouting the bottom half of their roster and creating competition among younger players in 2025 and this offseason. They should have stockpiled late-round picks and UDFAs and given the ones they did have better opportunities to win roster spots and roles. One or two come-from-nowhere contributors would make their roster look a lot less like the result of an end-of-free-agency shopping spree.

What I’m hearing: This isn’t about Daniels himself. He’s an absolutely awesome player, and assuming he can get through the season healthy, I expect him to perform at a high level. It’s what’s around him that has me concerned. He has a thin and aging group of wide receivers. He has question marks at running back. And the offensive line issues, especially with left tackle Laremy Tunsil going down with a training camp injury, are too significant to overlook.

Earlier in the offseason, I was high on the Commanders’ chances to rebound and contend in the NFC East. But the concerns that arose during camp are giving me pause. The fact that they have a young, first-time offensive coordinator in David Blough adds to the mystery (as, to be fair, it does with the first-time OC in Philadelphia and the first-time defensive coordinator in Dallas). There could be significant growing pains early in the season, if not longer. The Athletic (paywall)

Last season the median NFL offense huddled about 82 percent of the time. When Daniels was on the field, the Commanders huddled about 32 percent of the time. If you remove the first play of the drive (when almost every team huddles), that number plummets to 20 percent. Taking away huddles after timeouts or penalties would drop it even more. For all intents and purposes, Daniels has never huddled play-to-play in his pro career.

Kliff Kingsbury’s offense the last two seasons didn’t require it, but Daniels also didn’t do it in college. Without a huddle, there is less information a quarterback can communicate to the other 10 players.

That lends itself to a less complex offense, one that’s easier for defenses to decipher. Tempo typically offsets some of that. Even if you have a simpler offense, going quickly can create an edge. Instead, the Commanders self-neutralized their inherent advantage. Last year, on average, there were 9.6 seconds remaining on the playclock when the Commanders snapped the ball, eighth-highest in the NFL and much closer to the league average (9 seconds) than the Dallas Cowboys’ league-leading 12 seconds.

Commanders coaches know Daniels is going to run — they just don’t have to call it. Quinn estimates Daniels will have four or five rushing attempts off scrambles alone each game. Adding designed runs to that “is how you end up with 10,” Quinn says.

The league’s average quarterback scramble rate the past two seasons is 5.5 percent. Daniels sits atop the NFL at 13.8 percent, multiple percentage points ahead of runners-up like Justin Fields, Tyler Huntley and Drake Maye.

So Washington has to set up some guardrails. And this is the biggest reason why Daniels will be under center more often this year. Getting under center should, in theory, make defenses respect the play-action game more than shotgun, where sometimes defenders can see the entire exchange (or lack thereof). That will help Daniels as a passer, as defenses have to play the run more honestly, and help the run game be more explosive.

Just like the huddle, no team the last two seasons has been under center less often than the Commanders. Last year Washington was under center just 13.1 percent of the time, and that dropped to 5.8 percent when Daniels was on the field. The Cincinnati Bengals had the second-lowest percentage of plays under center (18.4).

With one training camp and three preseason snaps in the books, Daniels hasn’t decided on whether to stand up, hunch over or take a knee [in the huddle].

“It might depend,” Daniels tells The Athletic. “I might get down on a knee. I tried it a little bit. I kind of like it. It’s easier for guys to hear me if I project up, so it’s still a process.”

Ben Sinnott’s welcome-to-college football moment came with a rather blunt message: You’re not a tight end yet.

He arrived at Kansas State as a roughly 200-pound walk-on. The Wildcats wouldn’t even let him play tight end on the scout team. Sinnott then saw the visual evidence. Ball don’t lie. “I have a clip of me getting completely laid out by one of our starting linebackers,” Sinnott said. “I thought I was never going to play football ever.”

The solution? Eat. A lot.

Sinnott estimates he gained roughly 50 pounds in six months. Sonic Blasts. M&M’s. Reese’s. Snickers. Whatever could help move the scale. “It was amazing,” he said. “I love to eat in general, so it was awesome to just go put on as much weight as possible.” Things worked out.

text:
Kenyon Sadiq was back participating in position drills for the first time in nearly a month on Monday afternoon after head coach Aaron Glenn provided a promising update about the rookie TE and CB D'Angelo Ponds.

"The plan is to get them out there as much as we can, but we have to make sure we do the right thing and make sure we don't mess up anything as far as our plan to be ready for Week 1," Glenn said.

Ponds missed all of training camp with a calf strain and has yet to practice. Sadiq participated in the first three practices of camp before suffering a setback in his recovery from offseason hernia surgery.

With the regular season rapidly approaching, what is realistic to expect from the rookies? Well, Glenn said it's no different than any player coming back from injury.

"We cannot say, 'OK, these guys are going to get 60 plays out there.' We don't want to do that," Glenn said. "We want to make sure that we understand how many plays they can get, if those are 20, 25, whatever it is, to make sure that we manage them the right way to where they can build up to play a number of plays in the game."

It's about building stamina, and returning to practice is the first step for Sadiq and Ponds to eventually make their professional debuts.

The Standard

Aaron Glenn doesn't need to clarify his standards for the Jets – the players are well aware.

"The expectations have been set by AG, by the coaches, by the leadership, is that we're going to go out there, play physical football, we're going to execute at a high level and we're going to play our standard of football," S Minkah Fitzpatrick said. "And I have confidence in knowing that we're going to do that because that's what we did during camp."

And if anyone isn't meeting those demands, they'll be called out.

"It could be a coach, teammate, trainer," Fitzpatrick said. "Everybody knows the standard that we're trying to live up to."

Deserving Opportunity for Jelani Woods

TE Jelani Woods took full advantage of training camp, practiced well and earned a spot on the active roster.

"I think we all saw that from the games and in practice, he deserves an opportunity to be a part of this team," Glenn said.

At 6-7, 253, Woods is the biggest tight end in the room. Jeremy Ruckert and Mason Taylor are listed at 6-5, and rookie Kenyon Sadiq is 6-3.

"His ability to block at the point of attack has been really, really good," Glenn said. "Then his ability to make plays in the red zone has been good, too."

Against the Steelers in the preseason, the Jets drove down the field into the red zone and from the 13-yard line, Woods moved off his block and into space on the left side where QB Geno Smith threw him the ball. Woods ran into the end zone to score on that opening drive.

"He deserves the opportunity, I'm glad he took advantage of it," Glenn said.

Keep on Kicking

The Jets claimed K Blake Grupe off waivers on Monday as the kicking competition continues – Jason Sanders was waived and signed to the practice squad.

Grupe was on the Colts' practice squad last season but was signed to the active roster for the final five games of the season. He made all 11 of his field-goal attempts, including a franchise-long 60-yarder in the elements at the Seahawks. Grupe spent the summer in Indianapolis but was released on Sunday.

At 5-7, 157, Grupe's size drew a laugh from HC Aaron Glenn during his press conference.

"He's a small guy, but he's a good player," Glenn said with a grin. "I'm looking forward to getting him out here with us and kicking. To me, when you look at that position, you always want to have competition and to me, we always try to get competition at the positions and we're always looking at it that way."

text:
The Arizona Cardinals came into the 2026 NFL Draft with many needs. They opted not to address the holes they had at premium positions in the first round and decided to take arguably the most talented football player in the draft class, who plays a non-premium position: RB Jeremiyah Love from Notre Dame.

In his first preseason game, Love looked all the part of an elite NFL RB. He made defenders miss, broke tackles, and made an impact both on the ground and through the air. Against the Las Vegas Raiders in that preseason bout, he had 11 carries for 58 yards and three receptions for 14 yards.

While his time on the field certainly bolstered his high ADP in fantasy, which is currently at RB13 in ESPN PPR formats, he picked up an injury that could hold him out for Week 1 of the NFL season.

Jeremiyah Love Injury Update

Against the Raiders, Jeremiyah Love suffered a high ankle sprain. Since his injury, he has not yet practiced at full capacity. He has started to do some light individual work at practice, which should indicate that this injury will not hold him out for a significant amount of time. So fantasy managers with Love should not be too worried about his 2026 season outlook and should make no drastic decisions with him.

Insider and reporter for the NFL Network, Mike Garafolo, said the following regarding Love and his injury.

“Jeremiyah Love, the Cardinals running back, is progressing in his return from a high ankle sprain, according to head coach Mike LaFleur. Trending towards a Week 1 return? Maybe. I talked to a source yesterday who said I’ll put it at about 50/50. Nobody really knows right now. They need to see how he progresses over the next week plus. We will continue to monitor that one for the highly drafted running back.”

If Love is out in Week 1, Cardinals 2026 free agent signing RB Tyler Allgeier immediately becomes a starting option in fantasy football.

Tyler Allgeier

Allgeier, for the bulk of his career, played the RB2 role behind the Atlanta Falcons' current star RB Bijan Robinson. In that role, he was able to carve out some big fantasy performances, including a game back in 2024.

Against the Carolina Panthers in Week 6, he had 18 carries for 106 rushing yards and a TD. That is one of three games in his NFL career where he had over 100 rushing yards. The other two came back in rookie season in 2022, when Robinson was not on Atlanta's roster. He had 139 rushing yards against the New Orleans Saints and 135 yards against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

That season, Allgeier showcased what he could do if he got the opportunity to be a team’s starting RB. He logged his most starts in 2022, that he has had in a single season in his career: seven.

Allgeier’s fantasy ceiling is lower than it could be as a starter because he is limited in the passing game. He has yet to have a single season where he has had 20 or more receptions. Those opportunities, if Love missed time, would likely go to the current RB3 for Arizona, Bam Knight. In 2025, in 12 games, Knight had 22 receptions for 160 receiving yards. In four of his last five games, he had three or more receptions.
