text:
The Raiders placed Dont'e Thornton on injured reserve, knocking him out for at least the first four games of the season.

Thornton suffered an undisclosed injury during training camp and missed the final two games of the preseason. Now he will be out to start the regular season as well.

Advertisement

The second-year wideout needed a big season to prove he belongs in the NFL. Last season, Thornton caught just 10 passes for 135 yards. It was a disappointing season for Thornton, who was selected in the fourth round, but never made a serious impact.

Despite his lack of success in the NFL, his injury leaves the Raiders shorthanded at wide receiver.

Raiders' Wide Receiver Depth

With Thornton's injury, Las Vegas only has five wide receivers on the active roster. Just 2 of those 5 have ever had a 300-yard season in the NFL.

Advertisement

Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor are set as the top two wide receivers on the team. Jack Bech and rookie Malik Benson are battling for the third spot, but Bech has the edge. Rounding out the position is special teamer Dareke Young, who has played 499 more snaps on special teams than offense in his career.

It is a position group devoid of talent and now lacks any semblance of depth, which will lead to the Raiders relying heavily on their tight ends.

As the offensive coordinator in Seattle last year Kubiak called 12 (one running back, two tight ends) personnel at the eighth highest rate in the NFL, according to Sumer Sports. The Raiders will line Brock Bowers up as a wide receiver and allow Michael Mayer to play on the end of the line of scrimmage as a traditional tight end.

Advertisement

Those two will see the field frequently, which will allow the Raiders to avoid using their wide receiver depth.

Injury Setback

The Raiders have not disclosed any information on Thornton's injury. But it is clear Thornton suffered some sort of setback.

He last practiced on Aug. 7. A week later, head coach Klint Kubiak said he expected Thornton to return and play in the preseason.

The Raiders' final preseason game was Aug. 27. Now Thornton won't be able to play until Oct. 11 when the Raiders play at New England. That puts Thornton at least six weeks behind Kubiak's initial expectation.

Advertisement

Whenever Thornton returns, the Raiders will need to evaluate if he can be part of the future in Las Vegas.

title: 2026 NFL season: Top 10 contenders for Comeback Player of the Year 2.0
description:
If the magician returns for another awe-inspiring act, Comeback Player of the Year might not be the only accomplishment he’s celebrating.
He looked every bit like a franchise signal-caller and just as much like a potential Comeback Player of the Year.
CPOTY history: Last season, Christian McCaffrey snapped a seven-year streak of QBs winning Comeback Player of the Year.
CPOTY history: No Vikings player -- or Cardinals player, for that matter -- has ever won Comeback Player of the Year.
CPOTY history: The only Washington player to win Comeback Player of the Year was Alex Smith in 2020.
text:
Coming back from: Torn ACL/LCL.

The three-time Super Bowl winner seems next door to certain to return from December knee surgery for the Chiefs' season opener. It's been his goal (or obsession) all along. That alone is astounding. However, there’s more -- much more. Mahomes’ passing numbers in 2025 (3,587 yards, 22 touchdowns, 62.7 completion percentage, 89.6 rating) were each career lows as a starter. So too were his six wins as a starting QB, with the Chiefs failing to make the playoffs for the first time since 2014. It’s not hyperbole to opine that NFL history resides on Mahomes’ comeback. The magnificent Mahomes is one of the greatest talents the football world has ever seen, a certain Hall of Famer after less than a decade in the game. He has captained the league’s most recent dynasty. Is that dynasty dead? Or was 2025 merely the turning point to set the stage for another brilliant saga? Mahomes has claimed six Pro Bowl selections, a pair of first-team All-Pro nods, three Super Bowl MVPs and two AP NFL MVPs. He is no stranger to awards. If the magician returns for another awe-inspiring act, Comeback Player of the Year might not be the only accomplishment he’s celebrating.

CPOTY history: Seventeen of the last 25 Comeback Player of the Year winners have been quarterbacks.

Coming back from: Retirement in March 2024

It’s fitting that Los Angeles keeps producing blockbusters. Trading for Trent McDuffie and signing him to a record contract wasn’t big enough. The Rams then shook up the NFL world with their trade for Myles Garrett. And now, Donald has postponed surefire first-ballot Hall of Fame entry to return to L.A. If he performs anywhere close to his previous level of pure unbridled dominance, he might just author one of the finest comebacks in sports lore. Too much? Donald played 10 years. He was a Pro Bowler in every single season and an eight-time first-team All-Pro. He won three Defensive Player of the Year awards, averaging 11.1 sacks per season playing primarily as an interior defensive lineman. Regardless of what does or doesn’t happen in 2026, take a moment to reflect on just what a prince of defensive darkness Donald was during his career. Donald, 35-years-young, wouldn’t have returned had he not believed he could play at a sky-high level. He’s a bad, bad man, but a prideful one, too. Hence, he was methodical in his decision-making. The amount of snaps and games Donald will play should be an ongoing storyline, but he dominated the game for a decade. It’s an arduous endeavor to bet against No. 99.

CPOTY history: Tommy Maddox, with the Pittsburgh Steelers, won AP Comeback Player of the Year in 2002. He played sparingly in 2001 after three years away from the game.

Coming back from: Torn Achilles.

Often times, the best stories take time to build. An often-maligned figure with the New York Giants, who picked him sixth overall in 2019, Jones was released in 2024. He joined the Minnesota Vikings that season but was never active, and in 2025 was signed by the Colts to compete with Anthony Richardson. Not only did he win the starting job, but he was scintillating from the start of the season. The Colts were darlings of the league. Then the wheels came off, and Jones was hobbled. First, it came out that he was playing through a broken fibula. Then, he tore his Achilles in Week 14. Amazing comebacks are prevalent in 2026, but Jones apparently will be ready to play in Week 1, which is next door to shocking. Indy got off to a 7-1 start last year with Jones at the reins. He looked every bit like a franchise signal-caller and just as much like a potential Comeback Player of the Year. The Colts didn’t win a game without Jones last season. This could be the year that Jones completes his comeback arc.

CPOTY history: Last season, Christian McCaffrey snapped a seven-year streak of QBs winning Comeback Player of the Year. The run began with the last Colt to garner the accolade: Andrew Luck.

Coming back from: Foot injury/release from Cardinals.

Once viewed as the savior of the Cardinals franchise, Murray’s seven seasons with Arizona came to an unceremonious end when he was released in March. He played just five games in 2025, hobbled by a foot injury and sullied by play that was hardly stellar. He quickly signed with the Vikings this offseason, aiming to resurrect his career under head coach Kevin O’Connell, who has previously coaxed Pro Bowl-caliber play from Kirk Cousins and a stunning career rally from Sam Darnold. The No. 1 overall pick of the 2019 NFL Draft is still just 29, has a pair of Pro Bowls on his résumé, an array of receiving talent around him and a potential kingmaker at coach. If Murray ushers the Vikings back into the postseason after a disappointing 2025, it might be time for Comeback Kyler at NFL Honors.

CPOTY history: No Vikings player -- or Cardinals player, for that matter -- has ever won Comeback Player of the Year. Three of the last six winners (Joe Burrow in 2021, 2024; Alex Smith in 2020) were former No. 1 overall picks, like Murray.

Coming back from: Knee/hamstring/elbow injuries.

The 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year cleared the injury hurdle this offseason, but his ability to stay healthy and reclaim the phenomenal form of his first year will likely tell the story of the 2026 Commanders. After rocky performances from the Commanders in joint practices and during the preseason, the odds are getting steeper. Still, Daniels led the resurrection of the Washington franchise as a rookie, quarterbacking the team to its first NFC Championship Game appearance since 1991. Then came 2025, a season marred by injuries for Daniels and a free fall back to earth for the Commanders, who went 5-12 -- the exact opposite of their record in the feel-good 2024 campaign. After ailments limited Daniels to just seven games and only two wins as a starter, the player who seemed like an instant D.C. savior must put his cape back on. As a passer and runner, Daniels had 4,459 yards of offense and 31 offensive TDs in 2024. Will that Daniels be back?

CPOTY history: The only Washington player to win Comeback Player of the Year was Alex Smith in 2020.

Coming back from: Torn ACL/meniscus procedure.

Sent to the Packers in a 2025 offseason blockbuster, Parsons didn’t disappoint in Year 1 with Green Bay. He posted 12.5 sacks in 14 games and was a first-team All-Pro, continuing the narrative that he’s one of the game’s greatest defenders, nay, players overall. However, Parsons not only tore his ACL in Week 15, but also had to undergo a procedure to repair his meniscus. So, it appears the best-case scenario is that he returns in 2026 just in time for a showdown with his former team -- the Dallas Cowboys -- in Week 6. The football gods do love their drama, after all. While all the histrionics last year that preceded his Dallas exit were plenty to deal with, this is another type of adversity for Parsons to overcome. The odds might be against him returning to elite form in his first year back from an ACL tear, but Parsons is set on coming back and leading the Pack into the playoffs.

CPOTY history: The last defensive player to win CPOTY was Chiefs safety Eric Berry in 2015 -- one year before wide receiver Jordy Nelson earned the honor and became the only Packers winner in history.

Coming back from: Torn ACL.

Atlanta had no first-round pick in 2026. The team made two first-round selections in 2025: Jalon Walker, who is out for the season with a torn ACL, and James Pearce Jr., who is suspended for the first eight games of the season. In 2024, the Falcons drafted Penix eighth overall, despite having signed Kirk Cousins to a massive contract that same offseason. With their recent roster gambles not paying off like they hoped, the franchise’s trajectory might well ride on the left shoulder of Penix. He has just 14 NFL games under his belt, but he’s 26 and his play (2,757 passing yards, 12 touchdown passes, six interceptions in those 14 games) hasn’t come close to securing his spot as the future of the franchise at QB. Penix was recently cleared for 11-on-11 work -- yet didn't play in preseason action -- and must convince head coach Kevin Stefanski to give him the starting nod over Tua Tagovailoa. The Falcons have locked up RB Bijan Robinson, WR Drake London and TE Kyle Pitts this offseason, so there's a strong foundation of talent on offense. If Penix emerges from his injury and fulfills the potential that convinced the Falcons to shock the NFL world with their draft day decision, an amazing turn of events could unfold. Expectations are relatively low for the team in 2026 because of the muddied waters at QB. Penix can change everything in Atlanta with a successful comeback.

CPOTY history: No Falcons player has ever won CPOTY. However, 2001 Falcons first-round pick Michael Vick won the award with the Eagles in 2010 and remains the only left-handed QB to garner the recognition.

Coming back from: Being traded by the Raiders.

Gotham’s prodigal son has returned. Eleven years ago, a Jets teammate broke Smith’s jaw in a locker room donnybrook. He played his last game for the team that selected him in the second round of the 2013 draft a season later. He was written off, but, as he memorably quipped years later, he didn’t write back. Smith resurrected his career with the Seahawks, going to a pair of Pro Bowls and winning 2022 Comeback Player of the Year. Smith’s winding road led him to the Raiders, but 2025 was a calamity. Vegas won three games. Pete Carroll, Smith’s career-saving grace, was fired after the season and Smith was traded. In theatre that only the Jets -- and New York -- can produce, Smith was sent back to his original squad, with Aaron Glenn quickly proclaiming him the starter. Is there another comeback in Geno? If there is, oh, what a story it will make.

CPOTY history: Should Smith win CPOTY, he would become the third player to ever win the award twice, joining the Bengals' Joe Burrow and Chad Pennington, who won it with the Miami Dolphins in 2008 and the Jets in 2006.

OBJ was absent from the NFL for the 2025 season. He hasn’t played in a game since Dec. 8, 2024, when he caught one pass for one yard on one target from Tua Tagovailoa in a Miami Dolphins loss to Aaron Rodgers and the New York Jets. Times have changed.

Beckham making the Giants’ initial 53-man roster was already a feel-good accomplishment on its own. Once one of the elite wide receivers in the game, Beckham’s best days were long ago. But he’s found himself back where he made that catch, put up monster numbers and became a bona fide superstar. Should he play in Week 1 against the Cowboys in a Sunday night showdown with the world watching, it’ll mark his first game in a Giants uniform since Dec. 2, 2018. Eight years later, if he’s got anything left in the tank, OBJ can empty it here and he can make it … all the way to NFL Honors.

CPOTY history: No Giants player has ever won the award.

Coming back from: Dislocated kneecap/multiple ligament tears suffered in December 2024.

It's been the longest of roads traveled for Dell and the finish line is still unknown. Placed on injured reserve to begin the season, Dell is still poised to be back on the field this year, aiming to play his first game since Dec. 21, 2024. On that December day, Dell suffered a gruesome knee injury. Prior to his IR designation, he was checking off all the mile markers this offseason. Should he sprint back into the fold and become a contributor to a Houston squad with high aspirations, it will be a phenomenal tale of perseverance. His chemistry with quarterback C.J. Stroud, who’s looking for a rebound season of his own, should also be a major boon for the Super Bowl hopefuls. A 2023 third-rounder, Dell had seven touchdowns in 11 games in his and Stroud’s rookie season. The Texans' success, particularly over the past two campaigns, has centered on a dastardly defense. Such a dreadful injury seems bound to slow the speedy wideout, but if he can breathe life into the offense and bounce back, perhaps the 2026 finish line will be NFL Honors.

CPOTY history: A wide receiver hasn't won CPOTY since Keenan Allen with the Chargers in 2017. No Texans player has ever won the award.

text:
While we know Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty avoided a significant injury at practice last week, we still don't know his status for Week 1.

At first, we feared the worst, as Jeanty needed to be helped off the field during the Aug. 23 practice, and his teammates took a knee as he exited with trainers.

Advertisement

Thankfully, ESPN's Adam Schefter has since reported that it's just a sprained ankle, and Jeanty has avoided the worst.

While there hasn't been a word one way or the other about Jeanty's Week 1 status, we've seen a few positive updates recently, one of which came on Tuesday, Sept. 1.

Ashton Jeanty in attendance at practice

Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty (2) holds a banana on the sideline after catching a touchdown pass against the Houston Texans during the third quarter at NRG Stadium. Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

While Jeanty did not practice, he was spotted on a side field, according to The Athletic's Sam Warren.

Advertisement

This is the first time we've seen him since his injury, a sign he's moving in the right direction.

"Ashton Jeanty is now out at Raiders practice working off to the side with trainers," Warren said. "First time we've seen him in the field since his injury last week."

MORE: Ashton Jeanty's insane hops leaves fans in disbelief

This update comes after head coach Klint Kubiak said the team is counting on Jeanty for Week 1.

"Still on the mend. Still working to get him back," he said, per ESPN's Ryan McFadden. "We got another week to assess how he's going to look going into this first game, but we're counting on him."

Advertisement

Of course, none of this confirms that Jeanty will be ready to roll in Week 1, but it definitely brings more optimism.

Who is Ashton Jeanty's handcuff?

title: 5 things learned from GM Brian Gutekunst about Packers' roster
description:

text:
GREEN BAY – Packers General Manager Brian Gutekunst addressed the media Tuesday after all the roster decisions made over the previous several days.

Here are five things learned from his comments:

1. Keeping a ton of big guys was no accident.

The Packers have 10 offensive linemen and seven defensive tackles on their 53-man roster, plus three more O-linemen and one DT on the practice squad as of Tuesday morning. While the players had to earn those spots, the large contingents are also partly by design, for multiple reasons.

On the offensive side, Gutekunst always wants to guard against injuries and getting caught short. The Packers began training camp with 17 offensive linemen, and 13 of them are still here.

"That's always, for me, being heavy, particularly early in the year with big guys is important," he said. "Because when we get to October and November and injuries pile up, finding big guys is almost impossible, right? There's just not very many of them out there."

On the defensive side, Gutekunst anticipates new coordinator Jonathan Gannon needing more interior linemen active on game day to have a deep rotation of players available for snaps. Their overall workload is expected to be greater than it was the last two years with Jeff Hafley as defensive coordinator.

Even with keeping seven, that position group was strong enough that second-year pro Nazir Stackhouse was claimed by Tennessee upon hitting waivers.

"It was just a deep group for us, and you want to try to keep as many of those guys as you can," Gutekunst said.

2. Trading QB Kyle McCord wasn't easy, but there's already another QB3 on the way.

As the third-string quarterback, McCord shined in the preseason, which prompted a call from Miami (where former Packers personnel executive Jon-Eric Sullivan is the GM) about a possible trade. At that point, Gutekunst had to decide whether to keep three quarterbacks on the 53-man roster, or likely lose McCord to waivers for nothing.

"We were obviously contemplating do we keep three? Do we try to get him to the practice squad? What's the likelihood of that?" Gutekunst said. "When somebody calls you up and starts offering you, talking about a trade, I think the likelihood of you getting him to the practice squad's probably not strong."

Gutekunst acknowledged when a player like McCord shows so much progress, "it's hard to just move on." But the fluidity of the overall roster as the season unfolds was going to make it difficult to keep three QBs all the way through the year, even if they could've found a way to keep McCord initially.

"It's our job to find the next guy and develop the next guy," he said. "That's kind of what we do, and that's what we'll do as we go forward."

That next guy appears to be Kedon Slovis, who was just in Green Bay last week with Arizona for the joint practice and preseason finale. The transaction presumably will be official later in the day, but Slovis will be signed to the practice squad.

Slovis, who went undrafted out of BYU in 2024, threw for 223 yards on 21-of-35 passing with one TD and two interceptions last Friday night at Lambeau Field. The Packers are his fourth NFL team.

3. The Packers hope RB Josh Jacobs will be playing for them at some point in 2026.

Placed on the commissioner's exempt list over the weekend while his case involving two misdemeanor charges continues to be investigated by the league, Jacobs' status for the upcoming season is in limbo.

The Packers believe Jacobs will be an active player for them at some point, and both Gutekunst and Head Coach Matt LaFleur voiced their support for that outcome.

"I think that's to be seen," Gutekunst said regarding Jacobs playing for the Packers in 2026. "But I'm certainly hopeful that he will, and certainly would expect that. But we're going to let this process play out, and we'll be prepared either way."

The Packers are heading into Week 1 with MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks and newly acquired Kaleb Johnson (via trade with Pittsburgh) as running backs on the active roster, with Pierre Strong Jr. on the practice squad after a solid training camp and preseason.

LaFleur confirmed that Jacobs will remain around the team during his time on the exempt list, but according to league rules he can't practice or play in games.

4. The tight end position has undergone considerable change, but the Packers like where they landed.

Signing veteran Jonnu Smith and trading for the Rams' Mark Redman to join Tucker Kraft and Josh Whyle on the initial 53 gives TE coach John Dunn and the offensive staff a lot of work to do to get the whole group ready to play. Drake Dabney also was retained on the practice squad.

Smith's versatility and ability to line up anywhere and perform any duty asked of a tight end made him an attractive acquisition. Redman is more of an in-line blocking tight end, a role Gutekunst has talked about filling ever since the draft.

"It's going to be a process to get them up to speed and then we'll see how much they can handle and where it goes from there," LaFleur said of the new additions. "But yeah, definitely feel much, much better about the depth in that room."

As for Kraft and whether he will be without any restrictions for the start of the regular season, coming off his ACL injury from last November, LaFleur said: "I hope so but we'll take it one day at a time and see where he's at."

5. There's some good news on the injury front.

DT Warren Brinson, who missed the latter portion of training camp due to a calf injury, has "a good chance" to be ready for Week 1, Gutekunst said.

Meanwhile, WR Savion Williams (high ankle sprain) and edge rusher Collin Oliver (Achilles), who were placed on injured reserve with the designation to return, aren't expected to be out longer than the mandated four-game IR absence.

Also, TE Luke Musgrave, who is remaining on the physically unable to perform list (PUP) due to a neck injury, is projected to return to action eventually, but there is no timeline.

"We're really hopeful and I expect that to happen," Gutekunst said of Musgrave's availability. "(Neck injuries) are obviously sensitive. I would expect him to play. One of those unknown things, so we'll see."

Last but certainly not least, edge rusher Micah Parsons is also on PUP, which requires him to miss a minimum of four games, but a new rule this year allows players to come off PUP and begin practicing after two games. Gutekunst left the door open to that possibility with Parsons.

"I imagine when that time comes, there's going to be some conversations about … what he can and can't do, because he's going to be really eager to get out there," he said. "It doesn't shock me at all, obviously, but these guys, they want to play. They're unhappy when they're not playing. They want to be out there with their teammates, they want to be competing. He's definitely in that category."

text:
In this week’s Injury Report, the Red Sox lose Willson Contreras to a hamstring strain. The Nationals could be getting James Wood back on Tuesday. And Aaron Judge could be returning to the Yankees lineup sometime next week. All that and more as we highlight the most relevant injury news around the league this week.

⚾️ Baseball is back! MLB returns to NBC and Peacock in 2026! In addition to becoming the exclusive home of Sunday Night Baseball, NBC Sports will broadcast MLB Sunday Leadoff, “Opening Day” and Labor Day primetime games, the first round of the MLB Draft, the entire Wild Card round of the postseason, and much more.

Willson Contreras (hamstring)

Contreras was pulled from Sunday’s blowout loss to the Yankees with hamstring tightness. The Red Sox then placed him on the 10-day injured list on Monday with a left hamstring strain, an issue that Contreras has reportedly been dealing with for about a month. The 34-year-old first baseman will now get at least the next week and a half to rest. The hamstring issue can explain his August struggles, as he’s hit .217 in the month. Mickey Gasper was recalled to take his place on the active roster and fill in at first base.

James Wood (oblique)

CJ Abrams (back)

Wood could be back in the Nationals lineup on Tuesday or Wednesday during a two-game set against the Braves. The 23-year-old star has been out since August 4 with a left oblique strain and took batting practice on Friday before playing seven innings and hitting a home run in a rehab game with Double-A Harrisburg on Sunday. Manager Blake Butera stated Wood would get Monday off before deciding when he’d be activated. There was some thought that Wood wouldn’t need a rehab assignment, but he wanted to see some live pitching before returning. Meanwhile, keep an eye on Abram’s status on Tuesday. He was scratched from Monday’s lineup against Miami with back tightness, though it’s thought to be precautionary.

Aaron Judge (rib)

Yankees manager Aaron Boone said Monday that Judge could be ready to return to the Yankees lineup during the team’s next homestand, starting on Tuesday, September 8 against the Rockies. The 34-year-old star has been out of action since early June with a rib fracture. Despite the extended absence, it seems as though he’ll bypass a minor league rehab assignment and join New York as soon as he’s ready to return to game action.

Konnor Griffin (finger)

Griffin may be ready to return from the injured list when first eligible on Friday for the team’s series opener against the Angels. The 20-year-old shortstop started a minor league rehab assignment with Double-A Altoona on Sunday and went 1-for-3 while playing seven innings. He’s been out of action since early July with a torn ligament in his left ring finger.

JJ Wetherholt (wrist)

Masyn Winn (thumb)

The Cardinals lost both starting middle infielders over the last week. Winn had sat out a handful of games with a thumb issue before he was diagnosed with a fracture that landed him on the 10-day injured list, retroactive to August 22. The 24-year-old shortstop has already been swinging a bat with significant improvement and could return as soon as Tuesday when first eligible. Meanwhile, Wetherholt was placed on the 10-day injured list on Sunday with right wrist tendinitis. There’s no word on how much time he’s expected to miss. The 23-year-old second baseman has enjoyed an excellent rookie campaign, slashing .242/.343/.370 with 17 homers, 88 runs scored, and 14 steals across 586 plate appearances.

Xavier Edwards (thumb)

Edwards was removed from Sunday’s game against the Nationals after colliding with Jorbit Vivas on a slide into second base, leaving with thumb and elbow discomfort. He was diagnosed with a left thumb sprain and placed on the 10-day injured list on Friday. There’s no timetable for a return, but the Marlins will certainly want to get him back quickly as long as they remain in the playoff hunt. The 27-year-old second baseman is having a strong season in Miami, hitting .282/.361/.376 with six homers and 20 steals over 137 games.

Emerson Hancock (groin)

A groin issue for Hancock surfaced while making a diving play at first base against the Blue Jays on Friday, though he remained in the game, allowing five runs over five innings. The team then placed him on the 15-day injured list on Sunday with a left adductor strain, sidelining Hancock for at least the next two weeks. The Mariners had been operating with a six-man rotation, but could revert to a five-man while Hancock is unavailable. While he hasn’t been quite as successful in the second half, he’s still enjoyed a strong breakout season, posting a 3.57 ERA, 1.14 WHIP, and 126 strikeouts over 138 2/3 innings.

Byron Buxton (hip)

Buxton initially left last Tuesday’s game against the Athletics with a re-aggravation of his hip injury. After sitting out three games, the team placed him on the 10-day injured list with a right hip impingement. Twins general manager Jeremy Zoll told reporters last week that the 32-year-old outfielder could be looking at offseason hip surgery, so there’s a chance Buxton could be shut down if the Twins fall out of contention. Top prospect Walker Jenkins was recalled to take Buxton’s place on the roster after hitting .308 with 12 homers and 17 steals across 69 games with Triple-A St. Paul.

Joe Ryan (glute)

Ryan is getting closer to a return to the Twins rotation. The 30-year-old right-hander is set to make a rehab start with Triple-A St. Paul on Tuesday and is aiming to get to around 50 pitches. He’s been out of action since early August with a glute strain. Assuming he comes out of his rehab start feeling well, he could be in line to make the following start with the Twins.

text:
In discussing the unfortunate circumstances that landed DeShon Elliott on injured reserve to open the season, Pittsburgh Steelers general manager Omar Khan on Monday motioned to an open spot on the floor in front of him in a room at UPMC Rooney Sports Complex.

“He’s a warrior,” Khan said of Elliott. “I mean, if he walked in here and I said, ‘Hey, give me 1,000 push-ups,’ he’s going to give us 2,000 right there.”

Elliott could probably offer up those 2,000 push-ups right now — but he is not, by rule, allowed to participate in a Steelers practice.

At least for a few weeks.

Elliott was placed on the injured reserve list to open the season, the Steelers announced Sunday in conjunction with final cuts that set the 53-man active roster. Elliott suffered a significant knee injury during a game early last season that necessitated surgery and prevented him from practicing fully until the third week of training camp at Saint Vincent.

Elliott returned to full practice participation and appeared in the Steelers’ second preseason game Aug. 21 against the New York Jets. But he had been missing practices since.

“He had a significant injury last year,” Khan said, “and it’s been less than a year so we just said, ‘Hey, let’s be smart about it.’

“There’s been nothing to tell us that things have regressed or there was any type of setback, but … we were able to see how he came out of (the Jets game) and just felt like the right thing to do was to be smart and have him ready to go. But excited to have him on the roster, and when he’s ready to go, we’ll have him back up.”

Elliott was projected as a starting safety, leaving veteran Rayshawn Jenkins as the player most likely to pick up the slack and play alongside Jaquan Brisker and Jalen Ramsey. Rookie Robert Spears-Jennings also impressed during camp.

Jenkins joined the Steelers a week into camp.

When asked if the Steelers might add a veteran safety, Khan said that was possible — to the practice squad — but re-directed his answer to praise seventh-round pick Spears-Jennings.

“He’s done a really good job,” Khan said, “and I expect him to contribute this year.”

‘Positive’ injury news

Brisker was among a host of players who have been afflicted by injury in recent weeks whom Khan gave a positive diagnosis for Monday.

“All these guys are trending positively,” Khan said, “and expect them to be available to us for Atlanta.”

Backup quarterback Will Howard and receiver/special-teamer Ben Skowronek suffered concussions during last week’s preseason finale at the Buffalo Bills, Khan said.

“They’re in the protocol,” Khan said, “but I see them clearing in the next couple days here.”

Khan said rookie fullback Riley Nowakowski (ankle) is “good to go.” Starting receivers DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. (undisclosed) will be “eased in” to practice this week. “But, don’t foresee any issues there,” Khan said.

Brisker was grouped with defensive tackle Sebastian Joseph-Day (undisclosed) in what Khan termed “trending positively.”

Are There Any Answers On Jonathan Greenard's Injury?

The fact that the Eagles did not keep Greenard on the PUP through final cuts is a positive. When the Eagles released the 53-man roster after training camp concluded, Greenard took up one of the spots.

Philadelphia Eagles general manager Howie Roseman noted that the decision to include Greenard on the actual roster is a sign that they anticipate him playing "sooner rather than later."

As for actual answers regarding an update of some sort—or a status for Week 1 against the Washington Commanders—that's going to be kept "close to the vest," the GM said.

During the 2026 NFL Draft, the Eagles acquired Greenard and a seventh-round pick in exchange for a 2026 third-round pick (which became Jakobe Thomas), and a 2027 third-round pick. Therefore, the trade's package will be officially finalized next spring.

Meanwhile, the Eagles banked on Greenard with further investment. As he arrived, they offered a four-year, $100 million extension, with half of that money already guaranteed. It was a major show of confidence in the veteran edge rusher.

Jonathan Greenard's NFL Career

Coming out of the University of Florida in 2020, Greenard was a third-round pick for the Houston Texans.

As a rookie, he appeared in just 13 games, totaling 19 tackles and 1.0 sack. By year two, Greenard was a full-time starter for the 12 games he played. He racked up 33 tackles and completed 8.0 sacks.

His fourth and final season with the Texans in 2023 put him on the map. Over 15 games, Greenard produced 52 tackles and 12.5 sacks. text:
With the initial 53-man roster out, the San Francisco 49ers are turning their attention to Week 1 of the 2026 season.

President of football operations and general manager John Lynch and head coach Kyle Shanahan spoke with the media on Monday as the team prepares for three practices before departing for Australia on Wednesday.

The two provided updates on several players working their way back from injury, discussed the decisions behind the initial roster, and detailed the unique preparation for the season opener against the Los Angeles Rams.

Here are five takeaways from Monday's press conference:

1. Nick Bosa and George Kittle Set to Return to Practice

Defensive lineman Nick Bosa and tight end George Kittle are expected to participate in practice over the next three days as they continue working toward Week 1.

"We're going to get them out there in these three days and hope it goes well," Shanahan said.

The 49ers will manage both their workloads rather than have them practice for three consecutive days. Kittle is expected to take another step in his return by working with the team after previously participating in individual and non-competitive periods.

Bosa experienced soreness earlier in Training Camp, but has continued working on the side. Shanahan said the team is now focused on being smart with his workload, while Lynch said he has confidence in the plan they put together.

"We put together a really good plan that we believe will have him ready for Australia," Lynch said.

The next three practices will provide another test for both players before the team departs Wednesday.

2. 49ers Take Long-Term Approach With Mykel Williams

Defensive lineman Mykel Williams will start his season on the Reserve/Physically Unable to Perform List as he continues his recovery.

Lynch said Williams is just over nine months removed from an ACL injury that also involved cartilage damage, with the recovery timeline being closer to 10 months.

Lynch said the team considered activating Williams with the possibility that he could return within the opening weeks of the season but ultimately opted to give him additional recovery time. Beginning the season on the PUP list means Williams will miss at least the first four games of the regular season.

"It's going to stink not having him for the first four weeks, but we'll have him the rest of the year in really good fashion, we believe, if we allow him the necessary time," Lynch said.

Even with a big divisional matchup ahead in Week 1 against the Rams, Lynch emphasized the importance of keeping the long-term outlook in mind when evaluating injured players.

"Yes, division games count double. Yes, it's the Rams. They're all so important, but we're also always very conscious of a long-term play," Lynch said.

3. Australia Trip Accelerates Week 1 Preparation

Opening the season internationally has added another layer to an already busy ramp-up period.

The 49ers will hold three practices before departing for Australia on Wednesday, which accelerates a schedule that would usually have additional time before the team dives into regular-season Week 1 routine.

The unusual timeline has impacted everything from injury and roster decisions, to forming the practice squad. Lynch noted the team has even had to ask potential practice squad players whether they have passports readily available.

"There's a lot of little logistics like that that are complicated by this," Lynch said. "We're embracing it. We're having a plan for everything and we're getting it done."

Lynch also credited the staff working behind the scenes on visas, travel, nutrition, health, and performance to prepare the team for the international trip.

Once the 49ers arrive in Australia, Shanahan said Saturday will function as the team's typical game-week Monday.

4. Competition Continues at Left Guard and Running Back

The initial 53-man roster is set, but the competition for several roles continues.

When asked who would start at left guard and serve as the backup to running back Christian McCaffrey, Shanahan had the same answer for both.

"Don't know yet," Shanahan said. "It's truly fluid."

The offensive line competition added another piece with offensive lineman Jarrett Patterson, who has experience at both center and guard. Shanahan said the team plans to immediately work Patterson into the group during the next three practices to determine where he fits.

At running back, Lynch highlighted the depth of the room behind McCaffrey, including Kaelon Black and Jordan James. James returned from an early Training Camp injury and closed out the preseason with a strong performance. Lynch also noted wide receiver Deebo Samuel Sr. provides additional versatility out of the backfield.

The upcoming three practices will give San Francisco another opportunity to evaluate both groups before settling on its Week 1 lineup.

5. Reinforcements Return as 49ers Shift Focus to Week 1

Safety Malik Mustapha is expected to return to practice during the three-day stretch after injuring his hamstring in early July. Mustapha will rejoin a safety group that includes Ashtyn Davis, who Shanahan highlighted for his experience and contributions on special teams.

With the initial roster in place, the final three practices in The Bay will give the 49ers an opportunity to get several players back into the mix before shifting fully into preparation for Week 1 against the Rams.

text:
After years of the NFL being run by its top offenses and quarterbacks, 2025 saw the top defenses control the flow of the sport. We head into the 2026 season with the offensive hierarchy as jumbled as it has been in years. No longer can you simply pencil in the teams quarterbacked by Patrick Mahomes, Josh Allen, and Lamar Jackson at the top.

These rankings are based on three primary components: the quarterback and play caller combination, the offensive line, and the skill-position group. Last year’s efficiency and PFF grades matter, but this is not simply a list of last season’s DVOA or EPA standings. Personnel changes, coaching transitions, and the sustainability of last year’s production are all somewhat baked into the projections.

Several of the league’s best offenses are aging or replacing key pieces, and more than half of these teams enter the new season with a different offensive play caller from last year.

The result is a league with a handful of trustworthy offenses and a large middle class whose success will ultimately be determined by health, coaching, and play caller volatility. Here is how all 32 offenses stack up entering the 2026 season.

text:
After cutting the roster down to the 53-man regular-season limit, the Jets added 16 players to their practice squad on Monday. They are able to sign 17 players since Paschal Ekeji meets the international pathway guidelines.

CB Mory Bamba

Bamba was a standout defender against the Buccaneers in the preseason opener when he recorded 4 PDs and 4 tackles. However, a knee injury, which he suffered in that game, sidelined him for the rest of the preseason. Bamba signed with a Jets as an undrafted free agent out of BYU. Before playing football in college, he competed in Division III track and field as a hurdler and triple jumper.

WR Cam Camper

Over three summer games, Camper (6-2, 198) had four receptions for 63 yards (15.8 per) and saw time on special teams. He was a college teammate of Jets rookie WR Omar Cooper Jr at Indiana in 2022-23. Camper most recently played for former Jets TE Anthony Becht's Orlando Storm in the UFL, hauling in 25 receptions (17 resulted in first downs) for 366 yards and 3 TDs.

DB Jordan Clark

Clark (5-9, 184) appeared in 6 games in 2025 after being called up from practice squad in late November. He signed with the Jets as an undrafted free agent after a six-year college career at Arizona State and Notre Dame. This preseason, Clark totaled 14 tackles and defended one pass.

DL Paschal Ekeji

Ekeji was one of 13 players from 12 counties selected to the NFL's IPP Program class. He was born in southern Africa and played rugby for the Sharks, a southern African professional team before playing football. Ekeji appeared in all three of the Jets' preseason games, seeing snaps on defense and special teams – he assisted on 3 tackles.

OL Marquis Hayes

Hayes played over 20 snaps in each of the three preseason contests for the Jets. He was on the Green & White's practice squad last season. Hayes played collegiately at Oklahoma where he was the team's starting left guard.

DT Jack Heflin

Heflin (6-3, 304) spent the past two seasons on the Rams' practice squad and played in the 2025 regular-season finale where he registered two tackles. He played collegiately at Northern Illinois and one at Iowa and signed with the Packers as an undrafted free agent in 2021. Heflin saw action in all the Jets' preseason games, and he recorded 14 total tackles (7 solo) and 2 TFL.

RB Al-Jay Henderson

Henderson is an Irvington, NJ native who played collegiately at the University of Buffalo. After primarily playing special teams in 2023, Henderson made 21 starts in 25 games for the Bulls over the next two seasons. In 2024, Henderson led Buffalo with 1,078 rushing yards and 9 TDs, becoming the 11th different player in program history to rush for 1,000 yards. Last season, he had 755 rushing yards with 6 TDs and added 25 receptions for 181 yards and a TD. Henderson was a tryout player at rookie minicamp with the Jets in May.

LB Jaden Keller

Keller (6-3, 235) signed with the Jets in May after rookie tryouts during minicamp. He played collegiately at Virginia Tech, and last season played in 11 games and ranked third on the team with 50 tackles. During the preseason, Keller had 10 total tackles (5 solo) and a PD.

Edge Nate Lynn

Lynn (6-3, 252) signed with the Jets on Aug. 18, played in the preseason games against the Steelers and Giants and recorded 3 sacks. He played collegiately at William & Mary and finished his career ranked second in school history in sacks (28) and third in TFL (40). Lynn started his NFL journey in Detroit but spent the 2024 season on IR with a torn ligament in his shoulder. Last November, Lynn joined the Titans' practice squad.

WR Malik McClain

McClain (6-5, 205) transferred three times in college and had to learn five different playbooks before signing with the Jets as an undrafted free agent. He was targeted six times in the preseason and made 3 catches for 33 yards. When he played at Arizona State (2024-2025), McClain was coached by Hines Ward, the former Pittsburgh Steeler, Super Bowl XL MVP and former Jets offensive assistant (2019).

OL Xavier Newman

Newman (6-2, 297) saw 77 snaps across the preseason. He has been on the Jets since the Titans waived him in Oct. 2023. In his career, Newman has appeared in 25 games and played 338 snaps. He spent his entire collegiate career at Baylor (2017-2021) and made starts at center, left guard and right guard.

DL Payton Page

Page signed with the Jets as an undrafted free agent out of Clemson in 2025. He was on the practice squad last season and appeared in four games (at Cincinnati, home against Cleveland and New England and at Buffalo for the season finale). Page played in all three preseason games and combined for 3 tackles.

WR Jamaal Pritchett

Pritchett signed with the Jets as an undrafted free agent in May 2025 and spent the season on the practice squad. He did not appear in a regular season game. Pritchett saw action against the Buccaneers in the first preseason contest and made three receptions for 24 yards.

LB Troy Reeder

Reeder played collegiately at Penn State and Delaware before signing with the Rams as an undrafted free agent in 2019. His rookie season, he had 58 tackles and two forced fumbles. In 2022, Reeder recorded two tackles in the Rams' Super Bowl LVI victory over the Bengals. In total, Reeder has played in 106 games over seven seasons and was most recently with Detroit before joining the Jets' practice squad.

K Jason Sanders

Sanders signed with the Jets in March after missing the 2025 season due to a hip injury. He previously played for Miami where he ranks No. 3 in Dolphins' franchise history with 826 points. In preseason play, Sanders connected on his first two field goal attempts. Against the Giants, however, he missed an extra point and was short on a 54-yard field goal try.

CB Samuel Womack III

Womack played against the Steelers, where he recorded an interception, and the Giants during the preseason. Womack was signed to the Jets' practice squad on Dec. 2 and was elevated for Week 18 – he defended one pass and registered 7 tackles. Womack, who played collegiately at Toledo, was originally drafted in the first round of the 2022 NFL Draft by the San Franscico 49ers.

title: Reds Make Baffling Decision With Elly De La Cruz After Latest Injury - Sports Illustrated
description:
The Cincinnati Reds received relatively good news on star shortstop Elly De La Cruz on Monday, but their plan for handling him moving forward is questionable at best.
De La Cruz left Sunday night's game against the Chicago Cubs with tightness in his left quad, the same quad that bothered him throughout the second half of last season.
“He has a small strain but it’s a strain," Reds manager Terry Francona told Charlie Goldsmith.
De La Cruz is in the lineup as the DH and batting second in Monday night's series opener against the San Diego Padres.
De La Cruz played all 162 games in 2025 despite dealing with a left quad injury during the second half.
text:
The Cincinnati Reds received relatively good news on star shortstop Elly De La Cruz on Monday, but their plan for handling him moving forward is questionable at best.

De La Cruz left Sunday night's game against the Chicago Cubs with tightness in his left quad, the same quad that bothered him throughout the second half of last season. After being evaluated Monday, De La Cruz was diagnosed with a small strain.

“He has a small strain but it’s a strain," Reds manager Terry Francona told Charlie Goldsmith. "The doctor thinks Elly can play through this with the caveat that if it gets worse, he’s got to let us know. He has promised he’ll do that.”

The Reds are listening to that advice. De La Cruz is in the lineup as the DH and batting second in Monday night's series opener against the San Diego Padres.

Did the Reds Not Learn From 2025?

While it's certainly encouraging that the injury isn't considered serious, it's hard to understand why the Reds would take any risk at all with De La Cruz at this point in the season.

Cincinnati isn't going to the postseason. There is simply no good reason for De La Cruz to play through a quad strain during the final month of the season, especially considering what happened just one year ago.

De La Cruz played all 162 games in 2025 despite dealing with a left quad injury during the second half. His production declined considerably down the stretch, and Francona admitted during the offseason that he should have done a better job of protecting his star player.

“There were a lot of things going on. I think I need to take responsibility -- and I have, and I will,” Francona told MLB.com's Mark Sheldon in the offseason. “I need to find ways to get him off his feet from time to time, and I didn't do a very good job of that, and I own up to that.”

Francona went even further when discussing how he planned to handle De La Cruz in 2026.

“I don’t think there’s a number. But I also think if you wait to a certain point, like I did last year, you wait too long,” Francona said. “I’m not sure a day is going to do a whole lot of good in September. I think you have to be proactive and I just need to explain it to him better to make him understand. … I just need to do a better job of managing that and I will.”

That's what makes Francona's decision to put De La Cruz right back in the lineup on Monday so difficult to understand.

Someone in the organization needs to wake up and tell Francona that it's not worth the risk.

title: Dillon Gabriel remains stuck between Browns' present and his future - The Athletic
description:
Dillon Gabriel has finally found his place in the Browns’ quarterback room.
Gabriel reportedly hurt his back during the game, and there is no evidence the Browns fabricated anything.
Then the Browns drafted Sanders two rounds later, and Gabriel became the answer to an entirely different question: Why did the Browns take him before Shedeur?
The Curious Case of Dillon Gabriel is fascinating because selecting him in the third round was an organizational decision aimed at developing a backup quarterback.
As a cheap backup, Gabriel is serviceable in small doses.
text:
Dillon Gabriel has finally found his place in the Browns’ quarterback room.

Injured reserve.

It’s almost perfect. The Browns can keep him without committing to him. Gabriel remains under contract and eligible to return, but he doesn’t occupy one of the 53 active roster spots. Cleveland begins the season with Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders and Taylen Green, while delaying another decision on the quarterback who has spent his entire career in organizational limbo.

Good enough to keep. Rarely good enough to choose.

The timing of Gabriel’s back injury certainly is convenient. Gabriel entered Thursday’s preseason finale against New England seemingly competing with Green for the third quarterback job. Then he completed 12 of 15 passes for 186 yards and three touchdowns, which perhaps made releasing him more difficult.

The Browns had four quarterbacks and room for three. By Sunday, the Browns placed him on injured reserve with a designation to return. He must miss at least four games, but he does not count against the active roster.

Problem solved.

The injury may be completely legitimate. Gabriel reportedly hurt his back during the game, and there is no evidence the Browns fabricated anything. But injuries can also create opportunistic roster solutions. Both can be true.

The Browns no longer had to choose between Gabriel, the former third-round pick who performed well in the finale, and Green, the rookie with the size, speed and physical upside this coaching staff clearly values. They retained both without sacrificing a roster spot at another position or exposing either quarterback to waivers.

The NFL is filled with coincidences around cutdown weekend. This one worked perfectly for the Browns.

It’s the latest unusual turn for Gabriel, who has spent the past 16 months trapped in everyone else’s story.

The Browns drafted him with the No. 94 pick last year after one of the most productive careers in college football history. Gabriel tied the FBS record with 155 touchdown passes, finished second in career passing yards and started more games than any quarterback in major college history.

Under normal circumstances, a third-round quarterback with that resume would have arrived as an intriguing developmental prospect.

Gabriel received about 24 hours.

Then the Browns drafted Sanders two rounds later, and Gabriel became the answer to an entirely different question: Why did the Browns take him before Shedeur?

The Curious Case of Dillon Gabriel is fascinating because selecting him in the third round was an organizational decision aimed at developing a backup quarterback. The front office and coaching staff were aligned in believing he could be a long-term backup, which raises a multitude of questions about a bad team with plenty of holes spending valuable draft capital on a quarterback unanimously believed to have the ceiling of being a career backup.

Nevertheless, the Browns have struggled for generations to develop any sort of quarterback, and they loved the way Gabriel saw and thought the game. He wasn’t supposed to play last year because the Browns had two veterans in front of him: Joe Flacco and Kenny Pickett.

But this is Cleveland, and it’s only a matter of time before the Browns go full Browns, which they did the day after drafting Gabriel when they drafted Sanders. Suddenly, there was a new plan, and Gabriel’s place in it was hard to track.

It didn’t matter that he had nothing to do with where either player was selected. Fans viewed him as the quarterback standing in Sanders’ way.

Gabriel nevertheless won the backup job behind Flacco. By the fifth game of the season, he became the starter.

He went 1-5 in six starts. He was leading at halftime of the Ravens game when he left with a concussion. He threw seven touchdown passes against only two interceptions, but he completed only 59.5 percent of his passes and struggled driving the ball down the field and creating explosive plays. Regardless of how he sees the game, he lacks the physical tools to be a difference-maker at the position.

As a cheap backup, Gabriel is serviceable in small doses. He isn’t a disaster, as he was painted at times last season. He generally protects the football and can operate an offense effectively. He just doesn’t do much to elevate it.

Gabriel hasn’t started a game since the concussion.

Sanders replaced him, struggled badly that evening, then won in Las Vegas the following week while Gabriel remained in the concussion protocol. The Browns initially indicated Gabriel would return as the starter when healthy. Sanders kept the job instead.

The concussion may have changed the direction of Gabriel’s career, showing how quickly opportunities can appear and disappear for young quarterbacks without the protection of a massive contract or premium draft status.

By the time Gabriel returned this summer, the coaching staff had been fired. Todd Monken inherited him rather than chose him. Watson returned from two Achilles surgeries. Sanders entered camp with a chance to start. The Browns drafted Green, whose 6-foot-6 frame and rare athleticism make him a fascinating developmental project.

Every other quarterback represented something larger.

Watson represented the Browns’ lingering desperation to salvage their franchise-altering gamble. Sanders represented celebrity, fan support and the possibility of something more. Green represented physical traits you can’t teach.

Gabriel represented last year.

He wasn’t included in the real starting competition. By the final preseason game, he was playing merely to retain his place in the organization. Then he produced his best performance as a Brown.

Gabriel was accurate. He created downfield plays. He threw three touchdowns in the first half and forced the Browns to reconsider how easily they could move on from him.

Monken made clear afterward that the performance changed nothing at the top of the depth chart. Watson remained the starter. Sanders remained the backup. All Gabriel did was complicate the bottom.

Then came the back injury and the injured-reserve designation. Whether by misfortune, convenient roster management or some combination of the two, the Browns opted to kick the football down the road at least a month before they have to make any decisions.

Gabriel pays a price for the arrangement. He cannot practice or play for at least four weeks. Green will receive the developmental work as the third quarterback. While Gabriel rehabilitates, the Browns will learn more about everyone else in the room.

By October, circumstances may decide his future again. Watson could struggle or get hurt. Sanders could play. Green could develop. Another team could need a quarterback. The Browns might activate Gabriel, trade him or leave him waiting.

That is the strange part of his story. Gabriel has started six NFL games, handled every demotion professionally and performed well when his roster spot appeared to depend on it. Yet the Browns still haven’t reached a firm conclusion about him.

They don’t believe in him enough to play him. They don’t doubt him enough to release him.

So they placed him in the spot that truly fits his Cleveland career — neither part of the present nor free to pursue a future elsewhere.

Still here. Still waiting.

Good enough to keep.

Not quite good enough to be chosen.

text:
The Philadelphia Eagles' initial 53-man roster included four tight ends, but it remains a position in question as we head toward the start of the regular season.

Of the quartet, only Dallas Goedert has caught more than 19 passes in a season. Johnny Mundt is a blocking TE and E.J. Jenkins has just one catch over 10 career games. Second-round pick Eli Stowers struggled mightily throughout training camp and the preseason and figures to be at least a year away from significant contributions.

With Goedert’s injury history -- he hasn't played a full slate of regular-season games since his rookie season in 2018 -- pass-catching depth from the TE position is becoming a popular topic in Philly. Recently, it’s turned to the question of whether general manager Howie Roseman would consider a reunion with Zach Ertz.

Asked on Monday if he’s had any conversation or interest in bringing back Ertz, who is roughly nine months removed from an ACL tear, Roseman mostly deflected.

“First, I'd say what an unbelievable player, what an unbelievable person, tremendous respect for him,” the GM said, via the team’s official transcript. “At the same time, love what we have going in our tight end room, too. I would say, have talked to Zach over a period of time, obviously rehabbing his ACL and the relationship, just like a lot of our former players who've been here. But like anything else, wouldn't get into any conversations about anything other than from a big picture perspective. In my opinion, one of the greatest tight ends to play the game and just tremendous respect for him, and also excited about the tight ends that we have here.”

Ertz spent his first eight and a half seasons in Philly before a 2021 trade to Arizona, where he participated in three campaigns. Ertz then moved in 2024 to Washington, where he still played a significant role last year -- catching 50 passes for 504 yards and four TDs -- before a Week 14 knee injury wiped out the end of his season. In a pass-challenged Commanders offense, Ertz still finished third in yards and second in catches last season, despite missing four games.

A savvy veteran, Ertz still owned the ability to make himself available to the QB last year. A week before his season-ending injury, the 35-year-old earned 106 yards on 10 catches against the Denver Broncos.

Roseman hasn’t shied away from reunions in the past -- Nick Foles and DeSean Jackson to name two. The first question is if Ertz is fully healthy. Next is if the TE would want to take on a platoon-type role in the Eagles' offense. Then there is the matter of if Philly would prioritize bringing in another TE, which would be the ultimate indicator they don’t believe Stowers will be a factor this season.

title: NFL execs pick snubs in ESPN's 2026 top 100 player rankings
authors: Jeremy Fowler, DJ Bien-Aime, Courtney Cronin, ESPN Staff, Sarah Barshop, NFL Nation, Seth Walder, Ben Solak, Tyler Fulghum, NFL Nation reporters

The NFL Rank project celebrates 100 players expected to have a terrific season.
ESPN's NFL experts rated players based on performance expectations for the 2026 season.
See the full NFL Rank list Baker Mayfield, QB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers Sixteen quarterbacks made this year's top 100, and Mayfield was not one.
Brian Branch, S, Detroit Lions Often an underappreciated position, five safeties were featured in this year's NFL Rank.
But according to NFL Rank, he's not a top-five guard.
text:
The NFL Rank project celebrates 100 players expected to have a terrific season. One problem: More than 100 qualify.

ESPN's NFL experts rated players based on performance expectations for the 2026 season. Though the players who made the cut are deserving, at least nine marquee players could be classified as snubs -- the most important part of any list, right?

This project arrives about a month after we finalized our annual positional top 10s project, in which NFL executives, coaches and scouts rank the top players at each position. A review of both rankings shows plenty of similarities in order -- but also a bunch of differences. So, we asked league personnel evaluators to peek at our rankings and nominate players who deserved to be included -- but weren't.

Note: Commanders offensive tackle Laremy Tunsil was not considered for this exercise due to his recent triceps injury -- again, this is predicting 2026 play. Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who came out of retirement Sunday, was also not considered.

See the full NFL Rank list

Baker Mayfield, QB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Sixteen quarterbacks made this year's top 100, and Mayfield was not one.

Mayfield ranks third in passing yards (12,237) and second in touchdown passes (95) since 2023. He has had some success in Tampa Bay, so much so that he turned down a two-year extension of over $100 million in hopes of more long-term security with his team. Mayfield is poised for another big year, which should help his standing on the list.

"When he's healthy, he's a top-10 quarterback," an NFL personnel evaluator said. "I don't think he was healthy last year. He should have a big season."

Denzel Ward, CB, Cleveland Browns

Ward is, quite comfortably, a top-seven cornerback. This list pushes him out of the top 10.

"I think durability and the fact he plays in Cleveland keeps him out of the top cornerback discussion, but he's so good," an AFC executive said. "One of the smoothest athletes in all of football."

Ward typically misses a few games per season because of injury, but his production is undeniable. He has 18 interceptions and 74 pass deflections over eight seasons.

Malik Nabers, WR, New York Giants

Recovery from a torn ACL affects Nabers' standing. He was limited to 18 catches for 271 yards in four games last season. But when he's healthy, the 23-year-old is easily a top-10 receiver. The top-100 list featured 12 receivers, with Nabers noticeably absent.

Nabers is one of 10 players all time to record 1,200-plus receiving yards as a rookie (2024).

"He completely changes the [Giants'] offense if he's healthy this year," an NFC executive said. "It might take him some time, but he moves differently than most receivers when he's full tilt."

Kenneth Walker III, RB, Kansas City Chiefs

Walker is squarely in his prime (25 years old) without much wear and tear (821 carries in four seasons). He's coming off a dominant three-game playoff stretch, including 313 rushing yards with four touchdowns and a Super Bowl MVP award. And Walker tied for third last season with 10 rushes of at least 20 yards. The other three backs with at least that many -- Jahmyr Gibbs, Derrick Henry and De'Von Achane -- ranked in the top 65 of this list.

"If Andy Reid commits to running the ball, [Walker] is in a position to be a true bell cow who can use his vision to dictate the line of scrimmage," an AFC scout said.

Brian Branch, S, Detroit Lions

Often an underappreciated position, five safeties were featured in this year's NFL Rank. Left off the ballot was Branch, who has established himself as a premier player over the past two seasons with a 1.9% pass breakup percentage that ranks third among safeties. In 2025, Branch was one of two defensive backs with at least five passes defended, five tackles for loss and 2.5 sacks.

His Achilles tear late last season doesn't help his cause. But the 24-year-old's skill set is undeniable.

"Really versatile, can put him in the slot or in open space, physical," an AFC personnel evaluator said. "Definitely a top-100 player."

Milton Williams, DT, New England Patriots

The game is loaded with star defensive tackles -- many of whom make more than $30 million per year. Williams makes $26 million a year, which is a relative bargain for his ability to change games.

Nine defensive tackles made the top 100 here, and Williams should have been in that group. New England's run defense was drastically improved with Williams in the lineup. And he had 3.5 sacks and eight tackles for loss over 12 games in 2025.

"He's a player that's gotten better every year, and he was clearly comfortable being a focal point for the defense," an NFC scout said.

Peter Skoronski, G, Tennessee Titans

Skoronski is the NFL's highest-paid guard at $25 million annually. But according to NFL Rank, he's not a top-five guard. Chicago's Joe Thuney, Denver's Quinn Meinerz, Indianapolis' Quenton Nelson, Atlanta's Chris Lindstrom and Dallas' Tyler Smith round out the top 100 at that position.

Skoronski has played his way into this conversation and should be on the list next year. He ranked fourth among guards with a 96.0% pass block win rate in 2025.

"He wasn't a finished product when he came into the league, but he's probably Tennessee's best player on offense, a guy you can build around up front," an NFC exec said. "He's gotten more powerful."

Kansas City's Trey Smith was another notable snub at guard.

Zack Baun, LB, Philadelphia Eagles

Baun became an All-Pro and consensus top-five linebacker over the past two seasons in Philadelphia. San Francisco's Fred Warner was the only off-ball linebacker to crack the top 75, and only four made the top 100. Baun has 273 tackles over the past two seasons, along with seven sacks and three interceptions.

"He's got range. He can play the run close to the box or can cover in space, has great awareness," an NFC executive said. "One of the best at his position."

Tucker Kraft, TE, Green Bay Packers

Several young tight ends deserve consideration, from Detroit's Sam LaPorta to Indianapolis' Tyler Warren. Let's go with Kraft here because of his upside after ACL surgery.

He's a vertical threat who can also block. And by Week 1, he might be the NFL's first $20 million-per-year tight end; the Packers and Kraft are discussing a contract extension.

title: Fantasy football injury report: 16 players who could change your 2026 draft - AS USA
description:
The 2026 NFL preseason is officially over, final roster cuts have been made, and fantasy football draft season has reached its busiest point.
NFL fantasy football: Latest injury report Christian McCaffrey, 49ers RB Injury: “Tightness” Fantasy concern: Medium/High McCaffrey remains one of the most important injury situations in fantasy football, but his outlook is more encouraging than it was a week ago.
Malik Nabers, Giants WR Injury: ACL recovery Fantasy concern: High Nabers remains one of the most difficult players to value in 2026 fantasy drafts.
