text:
A new study led by Boston-area researchers has set my media feeds abuzz with the finding that nearly 1 in 4 NFL players in their sample had CTE at time of death. CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is a degenerative brain disease. It is caused by repeated concussions and smaller non-concussive hits.

As shocking as the 25% statistic is to many, the authors have suggested that this estimate is on the “low end,” with maximum possible prevalence around 98%. Although they take care to note that the findings of this study “cannot necessarily be generalized to the American football community,” and reporters dutifully report on this caution, the announcement of this new evidence has been treated in the media as a landmark event for the whole of football. In a statement reported by ESPN, the NFL Players Association remarked that “the findings should serve as a call to action across the entire football ecosystem.”

As a historian of science who has studied the history of traumatic brain injury in football, I have an objection to this coverage. It’s not that I am surprised by the statistic — I’m not. Nor do I object to the notion that it should serve as a call to action for the whole of football.

Rather, I object to an assumption baked into the coverage of the new study: namely, that this new statistic changes everything.

The statistic re-quantifies but does not reveal a problem, and although it is appropriate for scientists to be cautious about extrapolating particular data to make scientific claims about prevalence in other populations, we do not have to wait for that level of scientific evidence before taking action to make other sports, and the college and youth levels of football, safer for brains. As I documented in the American Journal of Public Health in 2014, with an argument that I have elaborated with colleagues here and abroad in the decade since, people have long been aware that getting hit in the head — especially multiple times, and even when those hits are sub-concussive — is bad for the brain.

In the early years of college football, before there were children’s leagues and before there were pros, Harvard College team doctors highlighted the risk of concussion in a report published in the prominent Boston Medical and Surgical Journal. It was accepted in medical worlds of the time that concussion had lasting and serious consequences. There was ample evidence that football caused concussion and that concussion had serious consequences.

Those who loved the game set about designing technical reforms that they promised would make it safe enough. But those reforms took shape at the same time that many preferred to ignore, forget, or doubt the evidence-based conclusion that shaking up the brain was unsafe.

Throughout the history of the game, as concerned parties sought evidence, some of football’s most powerful protectors obfuscated the problem. Walter Camp, known in his time as the father of football for his influence on organizing, game rules, and advocacy, covered up reports of concussion as early as 1894. In his archived papers, you can find the original results of a survey in which player accounts of head injury are crossed out in thick black crayon, and missing entirely from the glowing accounts of the game and its virtues that Camp published and circulated.

With ongoing advocacy and reform, football not only persisted in colleges, but spread across the population and deepened its social, political, economic, and emotional stakes, carrying along with it the problem of traumatic brain injury. Evidence was dismissed in favor of preserving the game. No matter that collegiate sports authorities acknowledged, in a 1933 NCAA Medical Handbook for Schools and Colleges, that concussion caused “punch drunk,” or what we would now call CTE. In a statement that turned out to be prescient, the Harvard team doctors of 1906 had forecast that football would continue so long as people “fear unpopularity more than they dare to be right.”

To be sure, more granular and robust understanding of the extent and severity of hits to the head is crucial work that can guide and refine policy, practice, and personal judgments. But this shocking new statistic is not the first time this kind of evidence has been offered. Earlier studies have estimated similar prevalence of CTE among professional football players. Nor are we at a total loss of what to do. With existing estimates of risk in youth populations, experts have already laid out steps that can be taken to mitigate harm.

As we develop our next moves, we — the corporate football agents, players, families, researchers, health officials, fans — must remember that interventions of the past that promised to reduce risks have also masked the ongoing problem, cast parents (especially mothers) as responsible for risk inherent in their children’s available recreation, and in some cases worsened the problem now showing up as CTE statistics. Demanding more evidence has become a strategy for delaying action. It’s also worth asking whether, with clear eyes on the past, we still want to cheer for violent games that cause lifelong damage for entertainment.

This moment troubles me not only as a historian, but also as a longtime mentor for college-age student-athletes. For 10 years I served as a residential adviser to undergraduates and had long talks with students who sustained concussion after concussion but were expected to keep their head in the game and return to play once they received green lights from the athletic staff, even when none of the conditions that had caused their prior injuries had been changed. Few are privileged to have a view like this into the private struggle and worry born by students, because struggle and worry are stigmatized in sports until they become stories of overcoming.

I’m also moved now as a mother of young children increasingly curious about contact sports. Three years ago, I was struck all too painfully by an interactive article featuring interviews with parents of student athletes. The video essay followed the release of another study by Boston-based collaborators, this one centering contact-sport athletes who died young, which found signs of CTE in 40% of these youth. It is incredibly difficult to watch videos of parents who lost a child and know these parents have been left to do the work of explaining to themselves and the world why they had let their children play games that were popular, available, and nonetheless led them to be hit in the head again and again as a matter of course.

If the game of football is to continue, the best responses will not stop at court settlements and grief or technical fixes. They will integrate improved technical protections with regulatory modifications, enforcement of rules and polices, public education, consideration of social equity, and improved diagnostics and treatment for the injuries that will surely continue to occur. They will also, crucially, integrate awareness of how this problem we are talking about today has been repeatedly forgotten over time.

Emily Harrison is a historian of science and public health at Wellesley College.

title: 4 takeaways from Seattle Seahawks' initial 53-man roster
description:
The Seattle Seahawks set their initial 53-man roster on Sunday.
Pritchett, Neal and Smith each made Seattle’s initial 53-man roster, while Igbinoghene and Diggs were both released.

And as he explained, that means assembling the initial 53-man roster with an eye toward protecting as many top-70 players from waiver claims as possible.
That allows the Seahawks to use a few of the initial 53-man roster spots to protect younger players from being claimed off waivers.
text:
The Seattle Seahawks set their initial 53-man roster on Sunday. What stood out from cutdown day? Here are four takeaways.

More clarity on injury timelines

The Seahawks kept running back Zach Charbonnet on the physically unable to perform list as he continues to recover from February ACL surgery. That means he’s required to miss the first four games of the season.

There was speculation that Charbonnet had an outside chance of returning within the first few weeks of the season, but general manager John Schneider said Sunday the plan was always for him to open on the PUP list.

Meanwhile, it’s a good sign that standout safety Nick Emmanwori (ankle), wide receiver Tory Horton (undisclosed injury), running back Emanuel Wilson (undisclosed injury) and rookie cornerback Julian Neal (quad) are beginning the season on the active roster instead of injured reserve. An IR stint would have required them to miss the first four games, so that means they’re each on track to return sooner than later.

Schneider was coy when asked whether Emmanwori has a chance to play in the Sept. 9 season opener after undergoing ankle surgery in July.

“We’ll see how that goes,” Schneider said. “We’ll see what kind of progress he continues to make.”

Foster’s rapid rise earns him a spot

Second-year wideout Montorie Foster Jr. was the surprise story of the summer for the Seahawks. And in the wake of Jake Bobo’s season-ending injury, Foster’s rapid climb up the depth chart earned him the fifth and final receiver spot on Seattle’s initial 53-man roster.

It’s truly stunning how far Foster has come. As an undrafted rookie out of Michigan State, Foster hurt his knee early in 2025 training camp and was waived by Seattle with an injury designation. He returned home to the Cleveland area, got his real estate license and spent much of last fall working as a high school substitute teacher while waiting for his next crack at the NFL.

Foster finally got another chance after signing with Seattle’s practice squad last December. He stayed on through the Seahawks’ Super Bowl run, spent the offseason with the team and then emerged as a surprise standout in training camp.

Foster’s playmaking then carried over to the preseason, where he hauled in seven catches for 73 yards and a touchdown. He also made two tackles in kick coverage and delivered a key block on Jacardia Wright’s 69-yard TD run against Tennessee. And if not for a pair of overthrows by Drew Lock, Foster might have had two more TD receptions.

“It’s hard to remember a player at the receiver position that’s improved as quickly as he has,” said Schneider, who added that Foster appears to have learned a thing or two from Seahawks star wideout and reigning NFL receiving leader Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

“I told Jax I felt like he just took his film and just completely studied it, or just followed him around for all spring or something. And then his special team stuff’s been really nice too, so he’s done a great job.”

Stockpiling at cornerback

Three-time Pro Bowler Devon Witherspoon and Josh Jobe are entrenched as the Seahawks’ top two cornerbacks. But after that, it’s anyone’s guess how the rest of the cornerback room shakes out.

Heading into training camp, third-year pro Nehemiah Pritchett, free agent addition Noah Igbinoghene and Neal figured to be the top contenders to replace Riq Woolen in the CB3 role. But with Neal missing most of camp with a quad injury, Schneider began searching for additional depth.

The Seahawks signed former first-round draft pick Terrion Arnold, who faces eight felony charges and was placed on the NFL commissioner’s exempt list Sunday as his legal proceedings unfold. They also signed former two-time Pro Bowl cornerback Trevon Diggs, who is aiming to resurrect a once-promising career that’s been derailed by knee injuries.

And then on Sunday, the Seahawks swung a trade with the Los Angeles Chargers to acquire undrafted rookie cornerback Avery Smith, who reportedly was a standout in camp.

Pritchett, Neal and Smith each made Seattle’s initial 53-man roster, while Igbinoghene and Diggs were both released. But Schneider indicated that was strategic roster maneuvering. As vested veterans, Igbinoghene and Diggs aren’t subject to waivers, which means they can re-sign with the Seahawks’ practice squad and then be added to the 53-man roster later on.

When asked about the slew of cornerback additions, Schneider said it’s a position where depth is particularly vital.

“That position, you can never have enough guys all the way through,” Schneider said. “We’ve been in spots before where we’ve been stuck and we’re signing a guy to the practice squad (and then) elevating.

“We want to be able to have guys that are in the system for a long time that the coaches feel comfortable about playing in games. … You always (want to) have a guy in the chamber ready to go.”

Plenty more roster shuffling to come

While the initial 53-man roster draws significant attention, the reality is that it’s simply the first iteration in a season-long churn of signings, practice squad elevations and other transactions. And moreover, it’s an incomplete look at the full picture.

Schneider has stressed his goal is to compile the best possible 70-man roster – a reference to the 53-man active roster and the 17-man practice squad. And as he explained, that means assembling the initial 53-man roster with an eye toward protecting as many top-70 players from waiver claims as possible.

Keep in mind, if a player with fewer than four seasons of accrued service time is cut, he’s subject to waivers and can be claimed by other teams. But if a player with four-plus seasons of service time is cut, he immediately becomes a free agent and can sign with any team or practice squad.

That’s why the Seahawks released veterans like Diggs, Igbinoghene, safety D’Anthony Bell and wide receiver Cody White. Since they aren’t subject to waivers, they can re-sign with Seattle’s practice squad and be added to the 53-man roster later on. That allows the Seahawks to use a few of the initial 53-man roster spots to protect younger players from being claimed off waivers.

“Having veterans on the practice squad has enabled us to not expose certain players to the waiver wire,” Schneider said. “It’s a strategy for the initial 53 cut, and then as well as what we’re gonna look like in the middle of October, and trying to be as strong as we possibly can and as deep as we possibly can with a combination of older and younger players down the stretch.”

Schneider said there will be “a lot of moving parts” with the roster in the coming days and weeks. That continues in earnest on Monday, when teams can begin signing players to their practice squads after the 10 a.m. waiver-claim deadline.

The NFL season begins this week, but America's favorite sport has been on our minds for other reasons recently. New research released in the journal BMJ reveals that 1 in 4 former NFL players in this sample had CTE, a neurodegenerative brain disease caused by repetitive head injuries.

text:
Aaron Donald is back with the Rams, but Los Angeles still has to decide how quickly it wants to put him back on the field.

Pro Football Talk reported Sunday that a Week 1 debut against the 49ers in Australia remains “possible,” with Donald’s availability depending on how his ramp-up progresses after two years away from football.

Had he returned earlier in August, the Rams reportedly believed they could have built him toward 30-40 snaps in the opener.

PFT also raised the possibility of Los Angeles using an injury designation to create a longer runway.

After the initial 53-man roster is established, teams can place an injured player on reserve/IR and later designate him to return.

The catch is substantial: Donald would need a legitimate qualifying injury, would have to miss at least four games and would use one of the Rams’ limited return designations.

Los Angeles has already used the special cutdown-day provision on offensive linemen Justin Dedich and Keagen Trost, who were placed on injured reserve before the 53-man deadline.

NFL rules allow only two players placed on an applicable reserve list during final cuts to retain return eligibility.

But if Donald simply needs more time to regain football conditioning, the Rams have a far easier option.

They can keep him on the 53-man roster, allow him to practice and simply list him inactive on game day for as long as they believe necessary.

There is no four-game minimum attached to that approach, meaning Donald could miss Week 1, Week 2 or however much time Sean McVay believes he needs before returning.

That flexibility could prove especially valuable for a 35-year-old defensive tackle who has not played an NFL snap since January 2024.

The Rams have already gone all in defensively, pairing Donald with Myles Garrett after their blockbuster offseason move.

PFT’s injury-list scenario offers one possible path.

The simplest one, though, may be giving Donald all the practice he needs without forcing an artificial timetable for his return.

text:
Guard Cordell Volson joined the Titans in March, and before training camp began, it appeared he had the edge on his competition for Tennessee’s starting RG job. A month later, Volson is no longer in the club’s plans, as NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport says the Titans have released the 28-year-old blocker.

The move comes on the heels of a recent report suggesting fifth-round rookie Fernando Carmona had gained ground on Volson and 2025 draftee Jackson Slater, who is the only member of the team who took snaps at right guard last season. Carmona is believed to have won the job.

Slater has reportedly shown improvement in his second offseason in the pros, so the Titans will move on from Volson, taking on $2MM of dead money (the amount of the guarantee on his one-year contract) in the process.

Today’s release represents another tough break for Volson, who entered the league as a fourth-round pick of the Bengals in 2022. The North Dakota State product won the Bengals’ starting left guard job as a rookie and held it for his first three seasons. He rarely looked the part of a high-end starter during that time, though, and was even demoted in favor of Cody Ford towards the tail end of the ’24 slate.

Volson lost any chance he had to improve his platform-year stock when he suffered a shoulder injury last August. The 6-foot-6, 325-pounder missed the entire season as a result.

Prior to Volson’s injury, the Bengals had reduced his 2025 salary, trimming it from $3.66MM to $1.5MM. Volson, 28, ended up collecting that on IR. Downward momentum notwithstanding, he still found a better guarantee ($2MM) in free agency. Volson will now return to the open market, but despite having made 48 starts in 50 career appearances, he is unlikely to do as well on his next contract.

We're under two weeks away from the start of the 2026 NFL season, when the Seahawks and Patriots meet in a Super Bowl rematch Sept. 9. And with the preseason play wrapped up, front offices and coaching staffs have been busy around the league getting the rosters ready to go.

The deadline for each team to finalize its 53-man roster was Sunday at 6 p.m. ET. Teams can still make moves, of course, before the opener, but getting down to 53 players by the deadline meant a lot of cuts and trades. Of note, the Cowboys released second-year running back Jaydon Blue, while the Colts retained quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr.

Swapping Ewers for McCord is still risky; McCord is yet to play an NFL game while Ewers has three starts under his belt. But McCord was one of the top performers of the preseason and is young enough to qualify as a developmental passer for a young Miami team. text:
Tyrel Dodson just had the best season of his NFL career.

Now the former Buffalo Bills linebacker is looking for a job.

The Miami Dolphins are releasing Dodson despite the 28-year-old starting 16 games last season and recording career highs of 129 tackles and five sacks along with an interception and fumble recovery.

The move comes one year after Miami re-signed Dodson to a two-year, $8.25 million contract.

Dodson began his NFL career with Buffalo, signing with the Bills as an undrafted free agent out of Texas A&M in 2019.

Dodson spent five years with the Bills, appearing in 59 games with 15 starts. He competed with Terrel Bernard for the starting middle linebacker job in 2023 before Bernard won the role, but Dodson eventually started 10 games after Matt Milano suffered a season-ending leg injury.

Dodson finished that season with 74 tackles, 2.5 sacks and a forced fumble. Pro Football Focus named him the Bills' most improved player and gave him a 90.2 grade, best among NFL linebackers.

Dodson left Buffalo in free agency and signed with Seattle in 2024. The Seahawks surprisingly released him midway through that season despite Dodson starting all nine games and leading the team with 71 tackles.

Miami claimed him off waivers the next day.

Dodson made an immediate impact for the Dolphins, recording three interceptions in eight games to finish the 2024 season. He had 15 tackles and an interception against Cleveland in Week 17 and was named AFC Defensive Player of the Week.

That performance helped earn Dodson another contract with Miami, and he followed it with his most productive NFL season in 2025. He finished second on the Dolphins in tackles and third in sacks.

Dodson has now been released twice in less than two years despite being a productive starter both times.

title: Titans cut quarterback Will Levis, Giants keep Odell Beckham Jr. as NFL teams trim their rosters
description:

text:
Quarterback Will Levis was waived by the Tennessee Titans on Sunday, while Odell Beckham Jr. made the New York Giants.

More than 1,100 players were cut as NFL teams trimmed their rosters.

A second-round pick in 2023 who started 21 games for the Titans, Levis was stuck behind Cam Ward and Mitch Trubisky. He was 5-16 for Tennessee in two seasons and didn't play in 2025 following shoulder surgery.

“I think he’s been awesome,” Titans coach Robert Saleh said of Levis following Saturday's game. “I thought he did a really nice job today. I thought he had a really good two-minute drive at the end of the half. Very good awareness with the time.”

Levis said he believes he can be a starting quarterback in the NFL.

“I feel like you’ve got to have that confidence in yourself regardless of your position,” Levis said after going 14 for 22 for 143 yards against the Bears in a 24-15 loss to close out the preseason. “I saw a quote, I forget who it was, but it’s, ‘Everyone in the league here is a starter.’ You’ve got to have that mentality. You could be in at the press of a button and just be ready to play. That’s one thing that I feel like I gained a lot in my time away, is gaining back some of the confidence that I lost throughout the last year that I played and I’m going to maintain that mindset the rest of my career.”

Teams had to be down to 53 players from 90 before 6 p.m. EDT.

Beckham, a three-time Pro Bowl receiver, is back with the Giants after missing the 2025 season. He started his career in New York and last played for the Giants in 2018.

The Vikings kept J.J. McCarthy, a first-round pick in 2024. Anthony Richardson, a first-round pick in 2023, remains with the Colts. Both quarterbacks were on the bubble.

The Browns kept four QBs after placing Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve with a back injury. Shedeur Sanders will back up Deshaun Watson and rookie Taylen Green is No. 3 on the depth chart. Gabriel, who started six games as a rookie last season, can return in Week 5.

Atlanta also went with four QBs, keeping Tua Tagovailoa, Michael Penix Jr., Cooper Rush and Jack Strand.

Tampa Bay cut quarterbacks Jake Browning and Connor Bazelak, leaving undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels to back up Baker Mayfield.

Numerous players traded on cutdown weekend

Several teams made trades ahead of the cutdown deadline.

Offensive tackle Broderick Jones, a 2023 first-round pick, changed teams. So did quarterback Quinn Ewers and defensive lineman CJ Okoye. Quarterback Kyle McCord, tight ends Hunter Long and Mark Redman, offensive lineman Luke Meredith, cornerback Avery Smith, tackles Walter Rouse and Nate Thomas, defensive back Clark Phillips III, defensive linemen TeRah Edwards and Gervon Dexter, and centers Sedrick Van Pran-Granger and Jarrett Patterson were also traded.

A day after trading Ewers to Jacksonville, the Dolphins landed a new backup quarterback by acquiring McCord from Green Bay for a 2028 sixth-round pick. The Dolphins had acquired a 2028 sixth-round pick from the Jaguars for Ewers.

McCord threw four touchdown passes in a 42-38 victory over Arizona on Friday, including two in the final 3 1/2 minutes. But the Packers signed Tyrod Taylor in May to back up Jordan Love.

McCord will back up Malik Willis, who signed a three-year, $67.5 million contract in March after playing behind Love in Green Bay the past two seasons.

The Cardinals acquired Long and a 2028 seventh-round selection from Jacksonville for a sixth-round selection in 2028. Long has 20 receptions for 153 yards in 46 games.

The Colts got Van Pran-Granger and a 2027 seventh-round pick from Buffalo for a 2027 sixth-round selection. Van Pran-Granger appeared in 18 games, including one start with the Bills in two seasons.

The trade is an indication starter Connor McGovern will be ready to go after missing much of the past month with an undisclosed lower-body injury. Lloyd Cushenberry had replaced McGovern when he was sidelined.

The Bears acquired a 2027 fifth-round pick and Phillips from Atlanta for Dexter.

The 49ers added a backup center in Patterson from Houston for a 2027 seventh-round pick, a person familiar with the deal said on condition of anonymity because it hadn’t been announced. Patterson started 21 games over the last three seasons after being a sixth-round pick by the Texans in 2023. He will back up Jake Brendel in San Francisco. The Niners had signed Brett Toth to fill that role in the offseason, but he has been out since early August with a concussion.

The Packers continued to boost their tight end depth by acquiring Redman from the Rams for a 2028 seventh-round pick. The move comes three days after Green Bay signed veteran tight end Jonnu Smith.

The Vikings sent Rouse and a 2027 seventh-round pick to the Patriots in exchange for a sixth-round pick in the 2027.

The Texans got Thomas from the Cowboys for a 2027 late-round draft pick.

The Chargers sent Smith to Seattle for a 2027 sixth-round pick and Edwards to Carolina for a 2028 sixth-rounder.

The Jets got Meredith and a 2029 seventh-round pick from the Raiders for a 2027 sixth-rounder. Meredith, who can play guard and center, gives New York depth on its offensive line and reunites him with quarterback Geno Smith and left guard Dylan Parham, who played together last season in Las Vegas.

Saturday's trades

A day earlier, the Steelers sent Jones to Dallas for draft picks. Jones who was picked 14th overall by Pittsburgh three years ago, gives the Cowboys depth at offensive tackle.

Ewers, a seventh-round pick by Miami last year, will replace Nick Mullens as Trevor Lawrence’s backup.

Okoye went from the Ravens to the Giants, reuniting with Harbaugh.

Other notable cuts

The Saints cut Northern Irish kicker Charlie Smyth, who finished last season on the roster. Tanner Brown also was cut, so Daniel Carlson will be the kicker for New Orleans.

Veteran safety Geno Stone, who signed a one-year contract with the Bills, was released.

The Bears released defensive lineman Marcus Davenport, who has 25 sacks in 77 career games.

Edge rusher Sam Williams and former Texas running back Jaydon Blue were cut by Dallas.

The Cardinals cut linebacker BJ Ojulari and veteran cornerbacks Sean Murphy-Bunting and Starling Thomas V.

Practice squad is a lifeline for some

Many of the players who were cut will rejoin their teams on the practice squad. Others will go to new teams. Some will reach the end of their NFL career.

title: Raiders 53-man roster breakdown: Two injury developments shape the initial team
description:

text:
The Las Vegas Raiders’ initial 53-man roster is set. Within it are three quarterbacks, a few surprises, a trade and some injury news — good and bad.

To start with the positive, running back Ashton Jeanty avoided injured reserve and will start the season on the active roster. Jeanty suffered an ankle injury during practice last week, causing him to miss the preseason finale against the 49ers and sparking concern over his regular-season availability. But his lack of designation shows that the Raiders believe he’ll be ready to return within the first month of the year.

The negative is that rookie edge Keyron Crawford is out for the year with an ankle injury. The third-round pick had to be carted off during the 49ers game on Thursday, and the team placed him on IR with no designation to return on Sunday, effectively ending his season before it began.

The Raiders certainly have some remaining question marks at several positions, and by virtue of finishing with the worst record in the NFL last season, they have the top priority on the league’s waiver wire. All players with fewer than four accrued NFL seasons are subject to a Raiders claim first. There’s certainly lots of talent out there, so it’s likely the Raiders will still look a little bit different for Week 1 than they do now.

Regardless, let’s dig into the roster as it currently stands:

Offense (24)

Quarterback (3): Kirk Cousins, Fernando Mendoza, Aidan O’Connell

Waived: Jacob Clark

After the preseason finale, Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak said he felt the team had three quarterbacks “that are ready to play.” Ultimately, he kept all of them.

Cousins and Mendoza were locked in as the current and future answers at the position. But O’Connell, who serves somewhat as an in-between, gets to stick around as well. The fourth-year pro might have had some value on the trade market, but the Raiders could see more value in having him as an insurance option for Cousins if Mendoza isn’t ready to play just yet.

Running Back (3): Ashton Jeanty, Mike Washington Jr., Dylan Laube

Released: Dare Ogunbowale

Waived: Roman Hemby

Keeping just three backs on the roster given Jeanty’s injury is a bit perplexing. The team had a veteran in Ogunbowale who looked solid in the preseason, but let him go. If Jeanty can’t play Week 1, the Raiders would have just Washington, a fourth-round rookie, and Laube, who has nine career rushing yards over two seasons. That makes the position seem like one Las Vegas will be looking for on waivers.

Fullback (1): Connor Heyward

Waived: Patrick Gurd

As evidenced by Kubiak’s usage of the position in Seattle and throughout this training camp and preseason, the fullback will be an important part of the Raiders’ offense. Heyward is a versatile weapon there, as he’s capable of lining up in the backfield and on the line of scrimmage as a tight end.

Wide Receiver (6): Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor, Jack Bech, Malik Benson, Dareke Young, Dont’e Thornton Jr.

Waived: Shedrick Jackson, E.J. Williams Jr.

Waived/Injured: Chase Roberts

Released: Deven Thompkins, Brandon Johnson, Phillip Dorsett II

Kubiak called out his receiver group after the second preseason game, saying that the team was “still looking” for someone who is accountable and can help on Sundays. There are still questions of whether that player exists in this final group. The top three of Tucker, Nailor and Bech provide a variety of skill sets that should mesh well within Kubiak’s offense. But whether their talents are great enough for them to excel remains to be seen.

Tight End (3): Brock Bowers, Michael Mayer, Ian Thomas

Injured Reserve: Carter Runyon

Released: Albert Okwuegbunam Jr., Chris Myarick

Tight end is the most solid position on the roster. Much of that is because of Bowers, arguably the most talented tight end league-wide, but also because Mayer has found success in Kubiak’s heavy sets, and Thomas continues to provide value as a blocker. Though for the Raiders to have success this year, they’ll have to keep Bowers healthy; he figures to be the engine that keeps the offense moving.

Offensive Line (9): Kolton Miller, DJ Glaze, Tyler Linderbaum, Jackson Powers-Johnson, Spencer Burford, Caleb Rogers, Charles Grant, Trey Zuhn III, Atonio Mafi

Traded: Jordan Meredith

Waived: Will Putnam, Dalton Wagner, Braeden Daniels, Isaiah Jatta, Kamar Missouri, Niklas Henning

Meredith was shipped off to the New York Jets on Sunday, pairing him with former Raiders quarterback Geno Smith and guard Dylan Parham. The move didn’t come as much of a shock as it saved the Raiders money, and Meredith had fallen out of favor by the end of training camp. But keeping Mafi, a Pete Carroll holdover with Chip Kelly ties, is a head-scratcher after he struggled in the preseason. He could be a potential cut to make room for waiver claims.

Defense (26)

Defensive Tackle (6): Tonka Hemingway, Adam Butler, Jonah Laulu, Thomas Booker IV, Folorunso Fatukasi, JJ Pegues

Waived: Brandon Cleveland, Treven Ma’ae, Gary Smith III

Rookies Smith and Cleveland had some success in the preseason but couldn’t crack the veteran group of six that will man the interior of new defensive coordinator Rob Leonard’s front. Still, the position has to be a point of concern after Vegas struggled to stop the run in each of its three exhibition games. Having Maxx Crosby back on the field will help, but improvements need to be made if the Raiders want to be competitive.

Edge Rusher (4): Maxx Crosby, Kwity Paye, Malcolm Koonce, Patrick Johnson

IR: Keyron Crawford

Waived: Cian Slone, Jahfari Harvey

Crawford’s designation could have opened an avenue for the Raiders to keep Johnson and Slone on the roster — two unheralded offseason additions who stood out during practice and in the preseason. But the team instead kept depth elsewhere and gave the veteran Johnson the nod over the undrafted rookie Slone. Las Vegas will want Slone back on its practice squad, but it might be difficult to sneak him through waivers.

Crosby didn’t play at all in the preseason, but wreaked havoc in practice. He hasn’t looked slowed by injury at all despite offseason drama concerning his knee. Ensuring he remains healthy will be key for the Raiders defense, as they struggled to get a pass rush or a run stop without him during the exhibitions.

Linebacker (4): Quay Walker, Nakobe Dean, Tommy Eichenberg, Cody Lindenberg

Waived: Xavian Sorey Jr.

Released: Segun Olubi, Cameron McGrone, Buddy Johnson

Walker and Dean look like a dynamic tandem that will pull Leonard’s defense together. The defensive coordinator described Walker as an “Avatar” because of his size and ability to play different roles, which Leonard has been taking full advantage of. And Dean will be the quintessential Mike, commanding the defense as the green dot. However, the Raiders will be asking a lot of Eichenberg and Lindenberg if either starter goes down.

Cornerback (5): Eric Stokes, Darien Porter, Jermod McCoy, Hezekiah Masses, Decamerion Richardson

Waived: Greedy Vance, Caleb Offord, Devyn Perkins

Las Vegas opted to keep depth on the perimeter over the slot by keeping Richardson instead of Vance. Porter has staked his claim as the starter opposite Stokes, though rookies McCoy and Masses should continue to challenge him for that role throughout the season. While there isn’t a lot of experience among the trio, the Raiders are excited about their promise, and each should see significant playing time this year.

Safety/Nickel (6): Jeremy Chinn, Taron Johnson, Treydan Stukes, Isaiah Pola-Mao, Dalton Johnson, Tristin McCollum

Waived: Devin Lafayette

The Raiders opted to keep Pola-Mao around despite the veteran ceding his starting role to rookie Stukes. They held onto even more depth at safety by giving McCollum one of the last roster spots.

Stukes should play back deep alongside Chinn to start the year. But Las Vegas loves his versatility, so seeing him play in the slot instead of Taron Johnson at some point wouldn’t be a surprise. His development will be key for unlocking the multiple defense Leonard wants to deploy.

Specialists (3)

Punter: AJ Cole

Kicker: Matt Gay

Long snapper: Alex Ward

Waived: K Kansei Matsuzawa, LS Tyler Duzansky

Both rookies Matsuzawa and Duzansky lost out on their competitions. It’s possible that the Raiders keep Matsuzawa on the practice squad as their International Pathway Program player. But with his struggles in the preseason, they’ll also be looking at other options.

text:
John Sigler

Saints Wire

Updated Aug. 30, 2026, 7:15 p.m. CT

It's finally here. The New Orleans Saints have reduced their roster from 91 players to just 53 names by the NFL roster cuts deadline at 5 p.m. CT on Sunday, Aug. 30. It was a difficult process with dozens of guys getting unfortunate calls into the office on what should be their day off. Some of them could land with new teams. Others might re-sign with the Saints' practice squad or return to the 53-man roster once other procedural moves are completed. But for many of them, this is the end of the line for their NFL career.

We kept up with analysis and reactions on every report and roster move right here. The Saints weren't just going to be releasing players from their contracts. They also called other teams and fielding trade offers while preparing to scour the waiver wire for potential claims. It's important to remember that the initial 53-man roster on Aug. 30 won't be the same group available for their first regular season game on Sept. 13 as injured players recover and new additions settle in. There are going to be a ton of moving parts. You can find the initial 53-man roster right here.

Saints confirm final roster moves to reach 53-man limit

In addition to all of the previously-reported moves listed below, the following playere were waived or released at the deadline:

DL Myles Cole. Cole had a productive summer and may have made the 53-man roster if not for some veterans hanging on. He's a good pick to sign with the practice squad if another team doesn't snap him up first.

EDGE Fadil Diggs. Last year's seventh-round draft pick made some strides in run defense this offseason, and his willingness to play special teams was another point in his favor. The Saints just had too many pas rushers ahead of him. At the end of the day getting to the QB is what matters most here.

WR Trey Palmer. Palmer was one of several players who picked up an injury at the worst time, missing the last week of practice and final preseason game, which opened the door for Kevin Austin Jr. to run away with the WR5 job. Palmer could make sense for the practice squad if he clears waivers.

OL Torricelli Simpkins III. Simpkins made the team last year, but no such luck this time around. He worked solely at center after previously working at guard, but the Saints may value his versatility and experirenceenough to bring him back on the practice squad.

LB Jackson Sirmon. Sirmon could return on the practice squad to keep the Saints' numbers up while Jaylan Ford is sidelined by an injury; Chris Rumph II is also managing an ankle issue that's forced him to miss most of training camp. Sirmon played a ton of special teams snaps but was picked on in coverage during the preseason.

K Tanner Brown. Brown had just as many ups and downs as Charlie Smyth, which explains why neither of them won the job. He has proven he can make kicks from distance in the pros but Brown must nail down his accuracy inside 40 yards. Those kicks need to be automatic in the NFL.

Saints place two players on IR with designation to return

As we expected, WR Jordyn Tyson will be sidelined for at least four games while recovering from his hamstring injury, but he'll be joined by LB Jaylan Ford, who was injured in the final preseason game. The actual time lost remains to bee seen but both guys must miss at least four weeks on injured reserve.

Additionally, the Saints put five other players on injured reserve with season-ending injuries, most of whom were nicked up in the preseason finale:

EDGE Michael Heldman. Heldman was injured in Dallas and isn't going to get to play again as a rookie. The Saints made a big investment in him as an undrafted free agent so expect them to hang onto hm while he recovers.

CB Dalys Beanum. Beanum was limited for a few days midway through August before the Saints shut him down, and he hasn't practiced at all since Aug. 20. He won't get to play this season after making a positive early impresssion.

CB David Long Jr. Long was brought in for the final week of preseason and had some struggles before going down with an injury. It isn't immediately clear what has sidelined him.

RB Devin Neal. This is a disappointing end to Neal's sophomore season, but it might be for the beset. His rookie year was derailed by hamstring issues and they lingered into training camp; now he can effectively take a redshirt and try to return in 2027. There may be more opportunities waiting for him with Alvin Kamara and Kendre Milller both playing in a contract year. Read more here.

OT Barry Wesley. Wesley was actually injured last week and didn't participate in any of the Saints' final three training camp practices. Whatever he's dealing with, he's been shut down for the year.

Saints waiving rookie RB CJ Donaldson

RB CJ Donaldson, an undrafted free agent from Ohio State, is also being waived per Mike Triplett for NewOrleans.Football. Donaldson runs hard but has some movement skills for a larger rusher given his background as a wide receiver recruit in high school. He’s a practice squad candidate if he clears waivers.

In surprise move, Saints cut cornerback Isaac Yiadom

Wow. Yiadom made the cut in 13 of 14 projections from around the team beat this week, but the Saints are going in a different direction, per Nick Underhill for NewOrleans.Football. He just lost a step in his age-30 season and was too ineffective over the summer. Yiadom is an obvious candidate for the practice squad, or to return later once the Saints have processed other moves and sent some guys to injured reserve. But we should expect them to explore other options at cornerback in the days ahead. Read more here.

Saints release veteran cornerback Michael Davis

CB Michael Davis is being released, per NewOrleans.Football's Nick Underhill. The 133-game pro has played in enough seasons to count as a vested veteran (many of them with Brandon Staley's Los Angeles Chargers teams) and will not test the waiver wire. He appeared in 11 games with the Saints last year, almost exclusively playing on special teams, and could take one of those six places on the practice squad reserved for vets like him.

Saints waive a draft pick, seventh-round CB TJ Hall Jr.

CB TJ Hall Jr. is being waived but should re-sign with the Saints' practice squad, per Nick Underhill for NewOrleans.Football. The seventh rounder out of Iowa is a good scheme fit in Brandon Staley's zone defense but struggled in one-on-one coverage during the preseason. He's one of the youngest players on the team (turning 22 back in April) and could benefit from more experience. Read more here.

Saints waive backup offensive linemen Easton Kilty, Alan Herron

The Saints waived two of their backups on the offensive line: Easton Kilty, a guard (via NewOrleans.Football's Nick Underhill), and Alan Herron (per Mike Triplett at NOF), who had been their third-string left tackle throughout training camp and preseason. Kilty worked at both guard spots and initially landed with the Saints last year as a rookie free agent. He's a practice squad candidate if he clears waivers. That's also the case for Herron, who ranked second in the UDFA class with $272,500 in guarantees this spring.

Saints release former 49ers running back Zamir White

The Saints released former San Francisco 49ers RB Zamir White just one week after trading for him, per Mike Triplett for NewOrleans.Football. It wasn't much of a trade -- the Saints dealt veteran linebacker Deion Jones, who wasn't going to make their team, to San Francisco for a running back the 49ers weren't going to keep either -- but it was still a way for White to introduce himself to his new team. He ran hard in the final preseason game and had some possitive moments on special teams, and in pass protection. He won't test waivers and could be one of the six vested veterans the Saints can keep on their practice squad depending on the severity of injuries for Alvin Kamara and Devin Neal. Read more here.

The 49ers are releasing Jones, too, making this essentially a net neutral deal. Read more here.

Saints waive fan-favorite rookie WR Brock Rechsteiner

This was expected, but it's still a setback for WR Brock Rechsteiner, per Luke Johnson for NOLA.com. The rookie from Jacksonville State earned a longer look for himself with a strong tryout early this summer and did what he could to make the team, standing out with strong blocking and an appreciable attitude at practices. He also won over a lot of Saints fans for his background in pro wrestling (his father is the legendary Scott Steiner, a WWE Hall of Famer) and the German suplex he demonstrated during a fight at joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys. He's a candidate to return on the practice squad after missing six games with a suspension for PEDs. Read more here.

Saints waive rookie defensive lineman Jay'Viar Suggs

Another rookie free agent, DL Jay'Viar Suggs, has been waived despite a strong finish to his preseason. NewOrleans.Football's Nick Underhill had it first. Suggs signed with the Saints out of Wisconsin (he also played college football at LSU and Grand Valley State) but had a tough time climbing the depth chart. He's a practice squad candidate unless another team makes him a better offer.

Saints waive rookie tight end Cody Hardy

TE Cody Hardy didn't draw many targets in practice, but his physical style of play translated from NC State and helped him stand out at times (including a chippy period against the Dallas Cowboys a few weeks ago). He's being waived, via Nick Underhill for NewOrleans.Football, but the commitment the Saints made to him earlier this spring (guaranteeing him $170,000, fourth-most among undrafted free agents) suggest they'll try to bring him back on the practice squad if he isn't claimed on waivers.

Saints release veteran safety Terrell Burgess

S Terrell Burgess is being released, via NFL Network's Mike Garafolo, but as a vested veteran he won't test the waiver wire. He can either sign with a new team or choose to return on the practice squad. He played well in the preseason but as is the case for some other backups, numbers weren't on his side. Maybe he's worth stashing while the Saints sort through their injuries ahead of the season opener.

Saints release former starting kicker Charlie Smyth

K Charlie Smyth is on the outs, per Mike Triplett for NewOrleans.Football. He could re-sign with the practice squad and not count against the 16-man limit thanks to an International Pathway Program exemption, but we'll see what he chooses to do next. Smyth has talent but he needs more development after picking up the game so late in life. Now we're waiting to see if it's Tanner Brown or Daniel Carlson winning the job. Read more here.

Saints waive former UFL wide receiver Jalen Moreno-Cropper

WR Jalen Moreno-Cropper is also being waived, via ESPN's Jeremy Fowler. Moreno-Cropper was a late arrival this offseason after playing with former Saints quarterback Hunter Dekkers on the UFL's Houston Gamblers. He tried out in the return game and did well on the third-string offense but struggled to set himself apart in a loaded position group.

Saints waive undrafted rookie OL Alex Wollschlaeger

RT Alex Wollschlaeger is being let go but has an opportunity to return on the practice squad if he clears waivers, per Matt Paras for the Times-Picayune | The Advocate. The rookie free agent from Kentucky (and before that, Bowling Green) practices as the third-team right tackle throughout the summer before an injury to Barry Wesley opened up reps on the second unit as well. He was guaranteed more money in his rookie contract ($277,500) than any other Saints undrafted free agent, so the team clearly values him.

Saints announce ten players have been waived before deadline

On Saturday evening, the New Orleans Saints confirmed each of the previously-reported waivers (Dekkers, Means, Mitchell-Paden, and Saunders) as well as a couple of additions. Read more here:

WR Ronnie Bell. Bell was on the practice squad last year and made some great plays in the preseason, flashing some much-needed physicality in the receiving corps. He's a good pick to return on this year's practice squad if he clears waivers.

S Elliott Davison. Another member of the practice squad last season, Davison was one of the team leaders in special teams snaps this summer and looked the part at free safety. Numbers just weren't on his side with so many veterans stacked ahead of him.

EDGE Garrett Nelson. The Saints claimed Nelson off of waivers from the Seahawks midway through training camp, and he led the defense in quarterback pressures through three preseason games. Don't be surprised if he returns on the practice squad after spending time in New Orleans last year, too.

DT Brien Taylor Jr. Taylor was one of several free agents the Saints brought in after Bryan Bresee's unfortunate injury at the start of training camp. He's proven he has the strength NFL teams look for, so this shouldn't be the end of the line for him at the pro level.

OL Xavier Truss. Here's another hit to our 53-man roster, but we did admit Truss was a long shot as the tenth offensive lineman in our model. The Saints claimed him off waivers last season and converted him to guard after he initially worked at right tackle with the Denver Broncos. It's worth stashing him on the practice squad if he clears the waiver wire this time.

EDGE Malakai Williams. Williams was another free agent pickup during training camp (brought in after Cameron Jordan was sidelined by a hamstring injury) but he struggled to get meaningful practice reps with guys like Anfernee Jennings and Tyree Wilson ahead of him on the depth chart.

Saints waive tight end Zaire Mitchell-Paden

TE Zaire Mitchell-Paden is the next player to be waived, per Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.Football. He was claimed off of waivers late last October and is a candidate to return to the practice squad if he clears the waiver wire this time around.

Saints waive WR Bub Means, 2024 draft pick

WR Bub Means has been waived, per Nick Underhill for NewOrleans.Football. This is the first surprise of the weekend (and the first hit to our own 53-man roster projection). Means was picked in the fifth round of the 2024 draft but struggled to stay healthy, and while he had a strong start to the preseason he faded as the summer wore on and wasn't targeted in team drills during the last couple of practices. He could be an option for the practice squad if he clears waivers. Read more here.

Backup cornerback Dalys Beanum waived/injured by Saints

CB Dalys Beanum is being waived with an injury designation, per KPRC 2 Houston's Aaron Wilson, which should allow him to revert to injured reserve and effectively take a redshirt this season. The Saints may also release him with an injury settlement if he gets another opinion. He would have the option to try out for other teams later this year, but not the Saints. Beanum hasn't practiced fully since Aug. 20 and didn't participate in either of the second two preseason games.

Saints waive backup quarterback Hunter Dekkers

QB Hunter Dekkers has also been waived, per Mike Triplett for NewOrleans.Football and confirmed by ESPN's Katherine Terrell. Dekkers was dealt a bad hand in the preseason -- he only got into a single preseason game while trying to run a two-minute offense without any prior snaps in team drills at training camp. The Saints have talked about a long-term vision for him in the past, and they waited for his stint in the UFL to wrap up this spring, so don't be surprised if he returns on the practice squad. Read more here.

Saints waive defensive lineman Kahlil Saunders

DT Kahlil Saunders is being waived, per NewOrleans.Football's Nick Underhill. Saunders, a rookie who played college football at Kentucky, was signed after an early training camp injury put Bryan Bresee out of action for the year. He's a candidate to return to the practice squad but the Saints may have other defensive linemen in mind for those spots.

New Orleans Saints trade rumors and reports

QB Spencer Rattler came up in trade conversations with the Jacksonville Jaguars, per NewOrleans.Football's Nick Underhill, but the Jags pivoted to a deal with the in-state rival Miami Dolphins instead. Assuming they only offered a sixth-round pick in the 2028 draft (which is what's going to Miami in exchange for former Texas Longhorns quarterback Quinn Ewers), it's a good thing the Saints said "no thanks." Read more here.

Chicago Bears DT Gervon Dexter Sr. was dealt to the Atlanta Falcons in exchange for veteran cornerback Clark Phillips III and a fifth-round draft pick, but the Saints were in on him too, per NFL insider Jordan Schultz. Dexter is a proven starter who could have helped New Orleans navigate life without Bryan Bresee. We'll see if they continue to ask about interior defensive linemen or if this was a unique opportunity to buy low on a talented player. Read more here.

Injured reserve and physically unable to perform list

WR Mason Tipton will transition from the training camp PUP list to the in-season PUP list, per NewOrleans.Football's Mike Triplett; the difference is he won't count against the 53-man roster limit until he's healthy enough to be activated. Tipton suffered a groin injury late last season that kept him out of spring training and the preseason this summer. We'll see if there's room for him on the depth chart once he's cleared to play. Read more here.

This has been confirmed by NOF's Nick Underhill.

Players who have been ruled out for the season on injured reserve include defensive lineman Bryan Bresee, offensive lineman Dillon Radunz, cornerback Rejzohn Wright, running back Ty Chandler, and tight end Moliki Matavao. Additionally, offensive lineman Nick Saldiveri was placed on the season-ending PUP reserve list earlier this summer. This was a contract year for the former fourth-round draft pick, so he's likely played his last down with the Saints,

title: TWENTYMAN: Breaking down the initial 53-man roster - Detroit Lions
description:
It's roster cut-down day, and Detroit has pared their roster down to an initial 53.
It's important to note this is an initial roster because more moves could be on the horizon throughout the week as players become available around the league.
The league also allows two injured players to be placed on injured reserve with a designation to return.
The Lions kept only eight defensive backs on the initial 53-man roster last season, so they are going into the regular season a little heavy here.
SPECIAL TEAMS (3) On the roster: Jake Bates, Jack Fox, Hogan Hatten Missing cut: None Twentyman: Nothing to see here.
text:
Every general manager and head coach around the NFL hates today. It's roster cut-down day, and Detroit has pared their roster down to an initial 53.

"It would be up there if not some of the hardest decisions that we've had to make," Lions head coach Dan Campbell said of roster cuts last week. "A lot of competition, a lot of good players. And we're going to have to let go of some guys that are going to be able to go to other rosters and make some waves. That could happen. That's real and that's hard to do."

It's important to note this is an initial roster because more moves could be on the horizon throughout the week as players become available around the league. The Lions hold the 17th waiver priority this season, a significant jump from 28th last year.

Detroit can begin building their 16-man practice squad starting Monday.

As a reminder, players who started camp on the non-football injury or physically unable to perform list may remain there without counting against the 53-man total.

The league also allows two injured players to be placed on injured reserve with a designation to return. Those two players miss at least the first four regular-season games, but they won't count against the 53.

Following is my breakdown of the initial roster:

QUARTERBACKS (2)

On the roster: Jared Goff, Josh Dobbs

Missing cut: Luke Altmyer

Reserve/Retired: Teddy Bridgewater

Twentyman: Credit Altmyer for making the backup competition much closer than most predicted when Dobbs signed after Bridgewater's retirement. Altmyer sees the field well and plays with a lot of confidence, but Dobbs' experience and familiarity with offensive coordinator Drew Petzing ultimately won out. Dobbs sealed the deal with his performance in the final preseason game in Indianapolis. Altmyer could be a candidate for the practice squad if he clears waivers.

RUNNING BACK (5)

On the roster: Jahmyr Gibbs, Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki, Jacob Saylors, Jabari Small

Missing cut: Trayveon Williams, Roydell Williams

Twentyman: Campbell said after the second preseason game against Washington he was expecting the decision for final spots to be 'very interesting.' Saylors runs hard and has earned the trust of the coaching staff not only with his play on offense but also his play on special teams. He led the preseason in total scrimmage yards. He could be in the mix to return kicks if active on gameday. Small makes it after a good camp as the Lions head into the regular season heavy at the position with the injury uncertainty surrounding Pacheco (knee/back).

TIGHT END (3)

On the roster: Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright, Jackson Meeks

Missing cut: Tyler Conklin, Thomas Gordon, Zach Horton

Twentyman: The Lions opted to go with second-year wide receiver turned tight end Meeks over the veteran Conklin. Meeks' ability to make plays on special teams surely helped his cause. It gives Petzing versatility in how he wants to deploy his tight ends in certain packages and special teams coordinator Dave Fipp gets a playmaker for his unit as well.

WIDE RECEIVER (4)

On the roster: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa, Tay Martin

Missing cut: Greg Dortch, Tom Kennedy, Dominic Lovett, Tarik Black, Malik Cunningham, Lucky Jackson

Reserve/Injured: Kendrick Law

Twentyman: There were probably some tough conversations regarding the initial composition of this room and ultimately the Lions went a little light to begin with just four. Maybe we see an addition to the group before Week 1. Martin earned a spot with his playmaking ability just about every day in camp both on offense and special teams.

OFFENSIVE LINE (9)

On the roster: Penei Sewell, Christian Mahogany, Juice Scruggs, Tate Ratledge, Blake Miller, Larry Borom, Miles Frazier, Ben Bartch, Seth McLaughlin

Missing cut: Devin Cochran, Colby Sorsdal, Mason Miller, Melvin Priestly, Michael Niese (waived/injured), Gus Hartwig

Reserve/Injured: Cade Mays

Reserve/Non-Football Injury: Giovanni Manu

Twentyman: Not a lot of mystery with the nine making it out of camp after the unfortunate wrist injury to Mays that will keep him out for awhile. Frazier's ability to play both guard and tackle gives Detroit some flexibility. Borom starts the year as the likely flex tackle. This is one of the youngest starting offensive lines in the NFL and the Lions will need them to hit the ground running Week 1 as they look to get back to being a top unit in the NFL.

DEFENSIVE LINE (11)

On the roster: Aidan Hutchinson, DJ Wonnum, Derrick Moore, Ahmed Hassanein, Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams, Tyler Lacy, Skyler Gill-Howard, Levi Onwuzurike, Eric O'Neill, Mekhi Wingo

Missing cut: Chris Smith, Myles Adams, Anthony Lucas, Ben Stille, Tyre West

Reserve/Injured: Payton Turner

Twentyman: I expect a couple of the players missing the cut to end up on the practice squad if they clear waivers. There are some promising youngsters and veterans the Lions trust to put in the lineup on game day, if needed. Sixth-round rookie Gill-Howard made a huge push to earn a roster spot with his play in practice and the preseason. He provides some juice as a pass rusher along the interior and it will be fun to watch his development as he continues getting stronger and fine tunes his technique and hands. Onwuzurike's ability to play along the interior and play the big end ultimately won him a roster spot. O'Neill really turned it on in camp and the preseason as the Lions have a ton of depth and versatility along the edge of their front heading into the season.

LINEBACKER (6)

On the roster: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Devin White, Malcolm Rodriguez, Trevor Nowaske, Jimmy Rolder

Missing cut: Joe Bachie, Erick Hunter, Troy Reeder, Amen Ogbongbemiga

Reserve/Injured: Damone Clark

Twentyman: Rolder missed most of training camp with a hamstring injury, but he is trending toward a return this week and avoids the injured list. Minus Rolder, it's a pretty veteran-heavy group led by the All-Pro Campbell. White has been a nice addition, and he and Campbell have looked good next to each other all camp. A couple of these linebackers missing the cut could potentially end up on the practice squad.

DEFENSIVE BACK (10)

On the roster: D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Ennis Rakestraw Jr., Keith Abney II, Roger McCreary, Chuck Clark, Avonte Maddox, Christian Izien, Thomas Harper, Khalil Dorsey

Missing cut: Nick Whiteside, Dan Jackson, Aamaris Brown, Bump Cooper Jr., Ekow Boye-Doe, Jason Taylor II, Eric Scott Jr.

Reserve/PUP: Kerby Joseph, Brian Branch

Twentyman: Joseph and Branch starting the season on PUP means we won't see them until Week 5 at Arizona, but remember, Detroit's bye is the following week in case they want to add a couple weeks to the recovery time for both. The Lions kept only eight defensive backs on the initial 53-man roster last season, so they are going into the regular season a little heavy here. Reed and Ya-Sin are expected to be the starting outside corners. Whiteside was likely a tough cut given his versatility and experience. What will the Lions do at the nickel? Has one player won the role? Could they use multiple players depending on matchup and situation?

SPECIAL TEAMS (3)

On the roster: Jake Bates, Jack Fox, Hogan Hatten

Missing cut: None

Twentyman: Nothing to see here. The Lions didn't bring in competition at any of these spots in camp, and all three head into their third season as a unit.

title: Titans To Waive QB Will Levis - Pro Football Rumors
description:
Drafted a few power structures ago in Tennessee, Will Levis will not make it to his contract year.
The Titans drafted Levis 33rd overall in 2023, doing so in Ran Carthon‘s first months on the GM job.
The Titans gave Levis the keys midway through his rookie season, when he replaced Ryan Tannehill.
The Ward pick essentially moved Levis out of the picture, as the Titans had signed Brandon Allen as a veteran backup.

text:
Drafted a few power structures ago in Tennessee, Will Levis will not make it to his contract year. The Titans are moving on from the former second-round quarterback, The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero reports.

This is a move the fourth-year QB sought, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler adds. Levis had been buried on Tennessee’s depth chart, with ex-Brian Daboll Bills charge Mitchell Trubisky coming in as the surefire Cam Ward backup. With just about everything in terms of the Titans’ football operations changing since Levis was drafted, it appeared the Kentucky product’s time had run out with the organization.

The Titans drafted Levis 33rd overall in 2023, doing so in Ran Carthon‘s first months on the GM job. As we covered in our Titans Offseason in Review piece, the team went through a spree of adjustments to this power structure over the next three years. Mike Vrabel was still the Tennessee HC when Levis was drafted; the team is two (three if Mike McCoy counts) HCs removed from Vrabel. Carthon has been replaced, and the Tennessee football-ops czar exiting the 2025 season — Chad Brinker — is no longer with the club. The Robert Saleh-Mike Borgonzi operation will move on from the Carthon draftee, years after it became clear he would not be the long-term QB answer.

Levis has not seen any game action since the 2024 season, when he struggled during a campaign that involved then-HC Brian Callahan benching him for Mason Rudolph. Levis came up in 2025 trade rumors but suffered a season-ending shoulder injury. The Titans had Levis splitting offseason reps with Ward, but the older QB’s injury crystalized what was already fairly clear: Ward had taken over as the team’s franchise-QB hopeful. This created more trade rumors ahead in 2026, but the Titans did not find a taker.

The Titans gave Levis the keys midway through his rookie season, when he replaced Ryan Tannehill. While some promise came out of that showing — to the point Carthon loaded up his roster with veteran contracts complementing the young QB’s rookie-scale pact — Levis regressed in 2024. Turnovers plagued the erratic passer, and Rudolph’s Nashville one-and-done involved starting assignments. The Ward pick essentially moved Levis out of the picture, as the Titans had signed Brandon Allen as a veteran backup.

With Levis seeing nearly his full contract guaranteed, the Titans will eat a few million in dead money from the salary and signing bonus proration. A team claiming Levis would move Tennessee off the hook for his remaining guaranteed salary, but it seems unlikely he will be claimed. A lower-cost free agency addition or even a practice squad signing would be the more logical path considering Levis’ pre-injury form and the health trouble he subsequently encountered.

title: Giants To Release QB Brandon Allen, Waive WR Jalin Hyatt; Odell Beckham Jr., Darius ...
description:
Odell Beckham Jr.‘s impressive stretch to close out Giants preseason work will lead to a legitimate opportunity.
Beckham and Slayton’s inclusions will help lead Jalin Hyatt off the roster.
Additionally, the Giants have cut quarterbacks Brandon Allen and Jake Haener, per NFL.com’s Mike Garafolo and ESPN.com’s Jordan Raanan.
The drumbeat for Beckham to return to the Giants’ active roster increased this week, and by Saturday it was looking good for the 33-year-old pass catcher.
It is notable, however, the Giants appear willing to pay down some of the Slayton cost in a trade.
text:
Odell Beckham Jr.‘s impressive stretch to close out Giants preseason work will lead to a legitimate opportunity. The injury-prone veteran has made the 53-man roster. It did not come at Darius Slayton‘s expense, either, with SNY’s Connor Hughes indicating the eighth-year Giant is still with the team.

Beckham and Slayton’s inclusions will help lead Jalin Hyatt off the roster. The team is waiving the former Biletnikoff winner, NFL insider Jordan Schultz tweets. The 2023 third-round pick was viewed as being on the wrong side of the bubble, and a preseason injury hurt his chances.

Additionally, the Giants have cut quarterbacks Brandon Allen and Jake Haener, per NFL.com’s Mike Garafolo and ESPN.com’s Jordan Raanan. Jaxson Dart and Jameis Winston occupy the top two spots on the Giants’ QB depth chart. One of the vets may well be kept on the practice squad as the emergency third arm.

The drumbeat for Beckham to return to the Giants’ active roster increased this week, and by Saturday it was looking good for the 33-year-old pass catcher. Beckham returned to New York on a one-year, $1.3MM deal — the veteran minimum for a player with OBJ’s service time — with no guaranteed money at signing. Beckham will see his $1.3MM salary lock in soon as a vested veteran. After making minimal impact with the Dolphins in 2024 and being out of football last season, this represents an impressive comeback for the former Giants superstar.

Four of Beckham’s five 1,000-yard seasons came with the Giants (2014-16, 2018), but injuries in Cleveland and Los Angeles derailed his career. Beckham’s injury trouble started in New York, as he missed most of the 2017 season, and his 2024 Dolphins campaign began late because of offseason knee surgery. The Giants drafted Slayton weeks after trading Beckham to the Browns. Slayton has no ties to John Harbaugh and was drafted before Joe Schoen’s arrival. A trade remains realistic, and the Giants have been shopping him before the roster-setting deadline (5pm CT).

Big Blue is naturally interested in a trade suitor taking on some of Slayton’s money. It is notable, however, the Giants appear willing to pay down some of the Slayton cost in a trade. His base salary sits at $12.25MM; $9.75MM of that total is already guaranteed thanks to the former Daniel Jones target creating a nice free agent market for himself last year.

Slayton, 29, would make sense as an in-season trade chip, as an acquiring team would have less salary to eat once the deadline nears. Slayton, who married world champion heptathlete Anna Hall this offseason in New York, does not seem long for the Big Apple. Then again, the eighth-year vet has been in trade rumors for a while now and has managed to keep coming back.

Hyatt never found his footing in New York. As a few of Josh Heupel’s Tennessee pass-game products have, Hyatt has not translated well to an NFL offense. He has 36 receptions for 470 yards and no touchdowns through three seasons. Hyatt missed training camp time due to injury but was not viewed as likely to make the team going into camp. The Giants will save more than $1.5MM by waiving Hyatt.

title: Carolina Panthers' 53-man NFL roster is set. Here's who made the team
description:

text:
The Carolina Panthers have officially announced their active roster for the 2026 season.

The team spent the hours after its preseason finale on Friday reducing its 91-player training camp roster to a 53-man roster by the NFL-mandated deadline of Sunday night.

The results of such reductions are below.

This is the “initial” 53-man roster. Other players could be waived or released if the Panthers choose to pick any players up off the waiver wire — the deadline to do so is 1 p.m. Monday, according to NFL Operations. With the regular-season opener not being played until Sept. 13, a little bit more roster fluctuation will be expected.

There were a few surprises and things worth noting on this “first 53.” Among them:

At quarterback, the Panthers didn’t risk losing Haynes King on the waiver wire, and instead kept the former Georgia Tech star as their third QB even though he only played in one preseason game before hurting his hamstring. Veteran Kyle Trask, meanwhile, was the odd man out.

Veteran tight end Darren Waller, a late signing who is still learning the Panthers’ playbook, made the squad.

Veteran running back AJ Dillon also made it, helped out by an injury in late August to Trevor Etienne, who’s going to miss at least the first four weeks of the season.

In the offensive line room, both Chandler Zavala and UDFA Albert Reese made the squad as backups, as well as veteran Stone Forsythe.

On the defensive line, former Duke standout Aaron Hall made the roster despite being an undrafted rookie after an excellent training camp.

Former starting inside linebacker Trevin Wallace was waived after Carolina traded for veteran linebacker Bobby Okereke on Saturday.

Wide receiver John Metchie was kept over veteran David Moore — a longtime Dave Canales favorite.

The 53-man roster

Running backs (3): Chuba Hubbard, Jonathon Brooks, AJ Dillon

Wide receivers (6): Tetairoa McMillan, Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette, Brycen Tremayne, Jimmy Horn Jr., John Metchie

Offensive linemen (10): Luke Fortner, Sam Hecht, Robert Hunt, Damien Lewis, Chandler Zavala, Brady Christensen, Stone Forsythe, Monroe Freeling, Albert Reese, Rasheed Walker

Defensive linemen (6): Derrick Brown, Bobby Brown, Cam Jackson, Lee Hunter, Aaron Hall, TeRah Edwards

Inside linebackers (3): Devin Lloyd, Claudin Cherelus, Jackson Kuwatch

Outside linebackers (5): Jaelan Phillips, Pat Jones, Princely Umanmielen, Thomas Incoom, Trevis Gipson

Safeties (4): Tre’von Moehrig, Lathan Ransom, Nick Scott, Zakee Wheatley

Specialists (3): Ryan Fitzgerald (K), JJ Jansen (LS), Sam Martin (P)

Injured reserve (designated to return): Running back Trevor Etienne (ankle) and linebacker Bam Martin-Scott (hamstring). These two players will have to miss the first four weeks of the season but are retained on the Panthers’ roster.

The team also placed right tackle Taylor Moton (blood clot) on the reserve/non-football illness list, and left tackle Ikem Ekwonu (knee) and defensive tackle Turk Wharton (neck) on the reserve/physically unable to perform list. These three will also miss the first four games of the season but are retained on the Panthers’ roster as well.

The Panthers had to waive 17 players and release 10 more to get their roster to where it needed to be. They also traded for TeRah Edwards, an obscure defensive lineman from the L.A. Chargers who has had a nice preseason and will provide D-line depth.

OL Jake Curhan

A note on Trask: He has a long history with head coach Dave Canales, given they intersected in Tampa Bay in 2023. But he was a late-camp addition, joining the team only after King suffered a hamstring injury Aug. 6. He is a candidate to make the practice squad, as are many of the players who were released and waived Sunday.

Recapping what Panthers did Saturday

What the Panthers did Saturday could be described in three short sentences. They waived seven players. They released one. And they agreed to terms with another.

But let’s go a bit deeper.

The Panthers opted to waive these seven players:

Defensive tackle Kyon Barrs

Wide receiver Elijah Cooks

Running back Miles Davis

Defensive tackle Tywone Malone

Tight end Caden Prieskorn

Wide receiver Roc Taylor

Offensive lineman Ryan Hayes*

*Hayes was waived with an injury designation after getting hurt in the Houston Texans’ joint practice Wednesday. That means that if Hayes clears waivers, he will revert to the Panthers’ injured reserve, and then the team will need to negotiate an injury settlement with him before he can become a free agent.

The Panthers also opted to release wide receiver Dan Chisena with an injury settlement. The veteran wideout and special teams player was on the Panthers’ injured reserve prior to getting released, meaning that he was already not counting against the team’s 91-man training camp roster.

And finally — and perhaps most importantly — the team reportedly agreed to terms with inside linebacker Bobby Okereke. The 30-year-old, 6-foot-2, 235-pound defensive leader will bring some veteran wisdom to a room that, besides free-agent acquisition Devin Lloyd, was in search of some. Okereke, a former third-round pick in the 2019 NFL Draft, is coming off a season in which he played all 17 games and notched 143 tackles and two interceptions … which prompts the question: Has he been flung into the starting LB2 competition with Claudin Cherelus? That competition also included Trevin Wallace at one point, but he was waived Sunday.

One other fun fact about Okereke: He and Panthers linebackers coach Pete Hansen go way back. Hansen coached the position at Stanford, in fact, while Okereke was there and was the steward of Okereke’s All-Pac-12 years in 2017 and 2018. Said Hansen of Okereke in 2019 via GoStanford.com: “Bobby Okereke is an all-down linebacker. He is long, he is fast, he has good hip flexibility, and he can flip his hips and cover in space. He can tackle in space, too. He has extremely long arms so he can keep himself clean off blockers. He will fit in really well with the Colts.”

text:
The Arizona Cardinals announced their final 53-man roster on Sunday, Aug. 30, trimming down from the 90 players included on their preseason roster shortly after the NFL’s 3 p.m. deadline.

The roster release was most notable for the injury status of James Conner, who was placed on injured reserve with a designation to return. That means he must miss the first four weeks of the season and is not eligible to practice during that span.

Conner, who suffered a season-ending foot injury last September, returned to practice early in training camp but only participated in individual drills, never gearing up to a point where he was able to join full-team work.

Meanwhile, tight end Tip Reiman remained on the physically unable to perform list with a severe foot injury suffered last October. Earlier in the summer, there was optimism that Reiman could return in time for Week 1, but that will not be the case.

Like Conner, Reiman must miss the first four weeks of the season. The difference is that teams can activate only eight players from IR during the season. Reiman, on PUP, does not count toward that limit.

Elsewhere, the Cardinals remade their cornerbacks room, waiving Sean Murphy-Bunting and Starling Thomas V. Those two served as the Cardinals’ starting cornerbacks for much of the 2024 season, but both suffered torn ACLs ahead of the 2025 season. Despite returning to full health, neither could regain his starting spot this summer.

Murphy-Bunting’s release was especially surprising, as he had worked as the starting nickel cornerback for much of training camp. That move suggests that Garrett Williams — who was activated off PUP earlier this month — is nearing full strength ahead of Week 1. Kei’Trel Clark figures to serve as his backup in the slot.

Also at cornerback, the Cardinals released 2024 third-round pick Elijah Jones, in a widely-expected move. Edge rusher B.J. Ojulari — a 2023 second-round pick — was another former top pick with whom the Cardinals cut ties. Neither player had managed to establish themselves with the organization, as both were marred by injuries and underperformance.

The work, though, isn’t done yet for general manager Monti Ossenfort. The Cardinals have 16 spots on their practice squad to fill, either by re-signing players they waived or adding external players once others clear waivers.

Plus, the Cardinals hold the No. 3 waiver claim, by virtue of their 3-14 record last season. They could use that priority to add a player along the defensive front, where their limited depth is especially glaring.

Until then, here is a look at the roster.
