text:
A former Clemson running back is being waived ahead of this evening’s deadline for NFL roster cuts.

The Dallas Cowboys are waiving Phil Mafah, according to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler.

Today at 6 p.m. marks the NFL’s cutdown deadline, where teams have to reduce their rosters from 90 to 53 players.

After being drafted by the Cowboys in the seventh round of the 2025 NFL Draft (No. 239 overall pick), Mafah was placed on injured reserve last August due to a shoulder injury.

After being activated from IR, Mafah made his NFL debut in the final week of the 2025 NFL regular season and scored his first career NFL touchdown on a 1-yard rush in the fourth quarter of the Cowboys’ 34-17 loss to the New York Giants. Mafah finished that game with five carries for 18 yards and his score.

Mafah finished the 2026 NFL preseason with 13 carries for 61 rushing yards and one rushing touchdown.

A punishing workhorse running back, Mafah earned third-team All-ACC honors as a graduate senior in 2024, when he rushed 216 times for 1,115 yards with eight touchdowns and caught 21 passes for 103 yards over 14 games (all starts).

Mafah was hampered all year by a preseason shoulder injury but still recorded the 24th 1,000-yard rushing season in Clemson history, and his 1,115 yards ranked 14th in a season in school history. He posted 981 rushing yards and eight touchdowns over the Tigers’ first nine games of the season before being severely limited down the stretch.

A former four-star prospect from Grayson High School (Loganville, Ga.), Mafah finished his Clemson career with 561 carries for 2,887 yards and 28 touchdowns, as well as 58 receptions for 309 yards over 50 games (21 starts) from 2021-24.

He finished his career ranked ninth in Clemson history in career rushing yards and tied for 10th in career rushing touchdowns.

Unlike wide receiver Jordyn Tyson and linebacker Jaylan Ford, Neal was not given a return designation, officially ending his second NFL season before it began.

Neal had been dealing with a hamstring injury throughout August and aggravated it during the Saints' preseason loss to the Los Angeles Rams. It's another blow to a New Orleans running back room that has dealt with several injuries throughout the summer.

The Saints selected Neal in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL Draft out of Kansas. he appeared in 16 games as a rookie and had been competing for a larger role entering his second season. He rushed for 206 yards and two touchdowns on 3.6 yards per carry in 2025. Now, New Orleans will have to move forward without one of its young backfield options.

We're under two weeks away from the start of the 2026 NFL season, when the Seahawks and Patriots meet in a Super Bowl rematch Sept. 9. And with the preseason play wrapped up, front offices and coaching staffs have been busy around the league getting the rosters ready to go.

The deadline for each team to finalize its 53-man roster was Sunday at 6 p.m. ET. Teams can still make moves, of course, before the opener, but getting down to 53 players by the deadline meant a lot of cuts and trades. Of note, the Cowboys released second-year running back Jaydon Blue, while the Colts retained quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr.

AFC East

Miami Dolphins

Biggest move: Trading away Quinn Ewers and trading for Kyle McCord. The Dolphins' backup quarterback situation was untenable after a cumulatively underwhelming preseason from Cam Miller, Mark Gronowski and Ewers. Swapping Ewers for McCord is still risky; McCord is yet to play an NFL game while Ewers has three starts under his belt. But McCord was one of the top performers of the preseason and is young enough to qualify as a developmental passer for a young Miami team. On the other side of the ball, the Dolphins released linebacker Tyrel Dodson, clearing a starting job for second-round pick Jacob Rodriguez. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques

Biggest move: Based on the start of training camp, it would be waiving running back Jaydon Blue, a fifth-round pick in 2025. Biggest move: The Eagles opted to keep four quarterbacks -- Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Andy Dalton and Cole Payton -- on the roster, at least for now. HOUSTON -- Tank Dell's comeback from a major knee injury will have to wait at least four more weeks.

The Houston Texans wideout was placed on injured reserve Sunday as the team made its 53-man roster cuts, and Dell won't be eligible to return to action until Week 5.

Dell missed all of 2025 after suffering multiple torn ligaments and a dislocated kneecap in the Texans' Week 16 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in 2024. He was hurt when wideout Jared Wayne collided with his knee after he caught a touchdown pass from C.J. Stroud.

Dell landing on injured reserve isn't a surprise.

While he didn't start training camp on the physically unable to perform list, indicating he was ready to practice, most times, he took part in only individual drills. There were two days when he participated in team drills and only one was with pads -- the ultimate barometer to show whether a player returning from an injury is ready for physical contact. He did catch a pass over the middle from backup quarterback Davis Mills during the only team session he was involved in Aug. 10, but that morning was the last time he engaged in 11-on-11s.

Dell didn't practice in either of the Texans' joint sessions against the Carolina Panthers and the Las Vegas Raiders, either.

Throughout camp, Houston coach DeMeco Ryans explained how Dell's comeback still had steps to clear. Ryans was asked Aug. 17 whether Dell would be ready for the regular season, and the coach preached patience, saying Houston had a plan for its 2023 third-round pick.

"Tank Dell is on his own plan," Ryans said. "So however that looks, whatever it entails, it'll be all geared toward what's best for Tank Dell."

Dell is the second Texans receiver to land on injured reserve; Jayden Higgins suffered a season-ending torn ACL during joint practices with the Raiders.

Teams can still make moves, of course, before the opener, but getting down to 53 players by the deadline meant a lot of cuts and trades. text:
PHILADELPHIA -- The Eagles put outside linebacker Jonathan Greenard on the initial 53-man roster, a positive sign as he continues to recover from a pec injury.

Greenard was placed on the physically unable to perform list in late July after suffering what the team described as a pec strain while lifting weights before camp. If he was placed on regular-season PUP, he would have been sidelined for at least four games.

The Eagles said earlier in the offseason that this was not a long-term injury. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, though, cast some doubt on whether Greenard would practice with the team before the start of the regular season, saying "that remains to be seen." He has since reiterated his concern about Greenard not being ready for the start of the season.

Philadelphia acquired Greenard, 29, in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings during draft weekend in April and agreed to a lucrative new deal with the star linebacker.

The Eagles sent two third-round draft picks -- the No. 98 pick in this year's draft and a third-rounder next year -- to the Vikings for Greenard, who then agreed to a four-year, $100 million extension that also includes $50 million in guaranteed money.

Greenard is expected to assume a starting role for the Super Bowl-hopeful Eagles, leading a group that also includes Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith Jr., A.J. Epenesa and Arnold Ebiketie. Hunt, in particular, has enjoyed a strong summer.

Greenard had three sacks in 12 games last season after a pair of double-digit sack campaigns the previous two years in Minnesota.

text:
The return of James Conner will take a bit longer.

Among the moves the Cardinals made on Sunday to get to their initial 53-man roster was placing the veteran running back on Injured Reserve/designated to return, meaning Conner will miss at least the first four games of the season as he tries to come back from his serious ankle injury from a season ago.

The Cardinals also released 2023 second-round pick linebacker BJ Ojulari, who struggled to come back from a serious training camp knee injury suffered in 2024. Eku Leota, who had a good camp, made the team.

Veteran cornerback Sean Murphy-Bunting was also released, a sign that slot starter Garrett Williams is nearing his return to play. Williams was activated recently from the PUP list after coming back from an Achilles injury.

The Cardinals keep three quarterbacks for the first time in a few years, with Jacoby Brissett, Gardner Minshew II and Carson Beck.

For now, the Cardinals have kept seven wide receivers, including return man Devin Duvernay and the trio of Jalen Brooks, Simi Fehoko and rookie Reggie Virgil. Rookie safety Wydett Williams Jr. also makes it through, ending any discussion about him potentially going back to play in college.

The 53 on the roster Sunday are unlikely to be the 53 on the roster come Sept. 13 when the team opens its season in Los Angeles against the Chargers. In fact, the 53 on the roster are unlikely to be the same 53 by the time they get back to practice on Tuesday, after potential waiver claims or other roster machinations.

The Cardinals are third overall in the waiver claim order (behind the Raiders and Jets) and are expected to add a player or two thought that process.

Meanwhile, players subject to waivers would clear by Monday afternoon, allowing teams to build their 16-man practice squad by bringing back some of the players released on Sunday.

The Cardinals return to the practice field on Monday.

description:
Here is a list of the most notable cuts across the league from the initial 53-man rosters.
QB Will Levis, Tennessee Titans A quarterback who once had first-round pick projections, Levis’ fall to the second round of the 2023 NFL Draft is well-remembered.
He started 21 games across his first two NFL seasons, but struggled with injuries and turnovers.
Levis had surgery on his throwing shoulder that caused him to miss all of the 2025 season and, this summer, was competing with recently signed free agent Mitchell Trubisky for the backup role.

text:
NFL teams worked on a tighter deadline this year to make their final roster decisions.

To accommodate the logistics of the Week 1 matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams in Australia, the league moved up the deadline to trim rosters from the Tuesday after the third preseason game, as it has been since 2021, to 6 p.m. ET Sunday.

Here is a list of the most notable cuts across the league from the initial 53-man rosters. The players are listed alphabetically.

DT Uar Bernard, Philadelphia Eagles

One of the feel-good stories of the 2026 draft, the Eagles selected Bernard in the seventh round even though he had never played organized football. From Nigeria, Bernard is part of the NFL’s International Player Pathway Program. His size and athleticism made him an intriguing prospect, but there was a learning curve the team had to navigate throughout offseason workouts.

QB Shane Buechele, Buffalo Bills

After going undrafted in 2021 and backing up Patrick Mahomes for the Kansas City Chiefs in 2022, Buechele finally made his NFL debut last season.

The Chiefs signed Buechele to their active roster after injuries to Mahomes and Gardner Minshew in 2025. He served as the backup to new starter Chris Oladokun and, on Jan. 4, made his debut against the Las Vegas Raiders, completing 7 of 14 passes for 88 yards. He was released the next day, and the Bills signed him to their practice squad.

WR Mecole Hardman, Buffalo Bills

A second-round pick in 2019, Hardman earned a Pro Bowl nod in his rookie season. He went on to win three Super Bowls with the Chiefs and made the game-winning catch in overtime to seal Kansas City’s win over the San Francisco 49ers in Super Bowl 58.

After a brief stint with the Green Bay Packers, the Bills signed Hardman to their practice squad in 2025, but his impact was limited due to a calf injury.

TE Justin Joly, Denver Broncos

The 152nd pick of the 2026 draft, Joly was the highest-selected player to be cut as of midday Sunday. In the Broncos’ preseason win against the Minnesota Vikings on Friday, Joly scored an 88-yard touchdown and led all Broncos receivers with 95 total yards.

QB Will Levis, Tennessee Titans

A quarterback who once had first-round pick projections, Levis’ fall to the second round of the 2023 NFL Draft is well-remembered. He started 21 games across his first two NFL seasons, but struggled with injuries and turnovers.

His long-term outlook with the franchise looked unclear, particularly after the Titans used the No. 1 pick in the 2025 draft on quarterback Cam Ward. Levis had surgery on his throwing shoulder that caused him to miss all of the 2025 season and, this summer, was competing with recently signed free agent Mitchell Trubisky for the backup role.

OL Evan Neal, New York Giants

The No. 7 pick in 2022, Neal was released after four seasons with the Giants. In 2023, he caught attention for comments he made about displeased Giants fans, for which he later apologized. He has started 27 games, all at right tackle, and re-signed with the team in March, signaling a fresh slate under the new coaching staff. But a lack of production and injury issues over the past two years persisted.

DT Mazi Smith, New York Jets

Smith was once at the top of Bruce Feldman’s Freaks List, and in 2023, the Dallas Cowboys made him a first-round pick. But Smith wasn’t able to make a consistent impact in his three seasons in Dallas.

His former club dealt him to the New York Jets, along with two draft picks, in November 2025 as part of the blockbuster trade that sent four-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Quinnen Williams to Dallas. Smith appeared in three games for the Jets as a backup, and his roster spot didn’t appear safe with five defensive tackles solidifying themselves for the Jets this summer.

OT Jedrick Wills, Chicago Bears

A top-10 pick in the 2020 draft out of Alabama, Wills was a solid starter in Cleveland for his first three seasons. But injuries limited his impact in 2023 and 2024 and, as a free agent last year, Wills did not sign with a team, later saying he took the season off to recover. This summer, Wills, 27, was competing for the starting left tackle job in Chicago.

QB Bailey Zappe, New York Jets

Zappe has made nine starts across four seasons in the NFL. Six of those starts came with the New England Patriots during the 2023 season, when he got the call after Mac Jones struggled. But Zappe also struggled, going 2-4 with six touchdowns and nine interceptions.

The 2022 fourth-round pick out of Western Kentucky holds FBS records for the most passing yards in a season (5,967 in 2021) and the most passing touchdowns in a season (62 in 2021). He spent stints with the Kansas City Chiefs and Cleveland Browns before signing with the Jets in January.

text:
Spencer Shrader, who was named AFC Special Teams Player of the Month last September before sustaining a season-ending knee injury in October, will return as the Colts' kicker this season.

Shrader emerged from a tightly contested preseason competition with Blake Grupe, who joined the Colts last December and connected on all 11 of his field goals over the final five games of the 2025 season. The Colts on Sunday waived Grupe, who very well could quickly wind up on another team's roster as their kicker this week.

The 27-year-old Shrader connected on a 60-yard field goal in the Colts' preseason finale against the Detroit Lions on Saturday. He made all five of his field goal attempts over the Colts' three preseason games, with those kicks going through the upright from 46, 48, 57, 60 and 61 yards.

Shrader sustained season-ending ACL and MCL injuries when Las Vegas Raiders safety Tristin McCollum ran into his plant leg on a PAT during Week 5 of the 2025 season. He began training camp with some issues pushing kicks to the left, but he resolved those and resumed kicking at a consistently high level right around the Colts' preseason opener against the New England Patriots.

Prior to his injury last season, Shrader connected on 13 of 14 field goal tries – including a walk-off game-winner against the Denver Broncos in Week 2 – and made all 14 of his PATs.

Shrader made his NFL debut in Week 1 of the 2024 season with the Colts and bounced between the New York Jets and Kansas City Chiefs later that season. In his career, Shrader has connected on 18 of 19 field goals and all 23 of his extra points.

title: Packers RB Josh Jacobs placed on commissioner exempt list - ESPN
authors: Rob Demovsky, Adam Schefter, Michael F. Florio, Mike Reiss, Lindsey Thiry, Josh Weinfuss, Turron Davenport, Kevin Seifert, Todd Archer, Seth Walder
description:
Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs was placed on the commissioner exempt list Sunday.
It means Jacobs will not be on the Packers' 53-man roster and cannot practice or attend games.
In a statement, Jacobs' attorneys David Z. Chesnoff, Richard A. Schonfeld and Clarence F. Duchac III said: "Josh Jacobs has been placed on the Commissioner's Exempt List, which is an administrative procedure used by the NFL while a matter is being reviewed.
Josh respects the NFL process, the Packers, and his Coaches and Teammates.
Because of the uncertainty around Jacobs, the Packers acquired running back Kaleb Johnson in a trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
text:
Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs was placed on the commissioner exempt list Sunday.

The move comes three days after Jacobs was formally charged with two misdemeanors stemming from an alleged incident with a woman in May.

It means Jacobs will not be on the Packers' 53-man roster and cannot practice or attend games. He will be paid and, with the team's permission, is allowed to be at the facility for meetings, individual workouts, medical treatments and other non-football activities.

The NFL has said it is still reviewing Jacobs' case. His initial court appearance is Nov. 17, but the league does not have to wait for the legal process to be completed before issuing discipline. Jacobs was charged with misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property.

In a statement, Jacobs' attorneys David Z. Chesnoff, Richard A. Schonfeld and Clarence F. Duchac III said: "Josh Jacobs has been placed on the Commissioner's Exempt List, which is an administrative procedure used by the NFL while a matter is being reviewed. It is not a final determination. Josh respects the NFL process, the Packers, and his Coaches and Teammates. He looks forward to his return to the team and the NFL."

According to article 46, section 5 of the collective bargaining agreement, time spent on the commissioner exempt list is credited toward any suspension that is later imposed provided that the player "return and shall have no further right to any salary for the games for which he was paid while on the commissioner exempt list that were credited to the suspension (i.e., for a number of games no greater than the length of the suspension)."

The Packers also will be starting the season without pass rusher Micah Parsons, who will officially start the season on the physically unable to perform list. He'll miss at least the first four games because of the designation. Parsons, who is rehabbing from a torn ACL/meniscus injury suffered last year, has said that a return by Week 6 when the Packers play the Dallas Cowboys, his former team, is "realistic."

Because of the uncertainty around Jacobs, the Packers acquired running back Kaleb Johnson in a trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers.

The Steelers drafted Johnson at No. 83 last year, but the Iowa product rushed for only 69 yards on 28 carries in 10 games as a rookie.

Behind Jacobs, the Packers have MarShawn Lloyd and Chris Brooks. The Packers are optimistic that Lloyd can finally contribute after injuries ruined his first two NFL seasons. The 2024 third-round pick has played in just one career game. Brooks has been a third-down blocking back and is also expected to make the team. With the trade for Johnson, Pierre Strong Jr. will not make the Packers' 53-man roster despite a strong preseason.

Johnson never found his footing in Pittsburgh. His most notable moment was a special teams gaffe when he let a live ball bounce past him on a kickoff. Instead of recovering the ball, which landed in the landing zone, Johnson let the ball bounce into the end zone, where Seattle recovered it for a touchdown in the Seahawks' Week 2 win.

From there, Johnson lost his spot as a returner, and he played just 62 snaps the rest of the season.

Despite a fresh start with a new coaching staff, Johnson didn't make much headway in the offseason. Not only did he have Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle solidly ahead of him on the depth chart, but former undrafted free agent Lew Nichols often got snaps ahead of Johnson in camp too. The Steelers also added running back Travis Homer, a special teams ace, to the depth chart in the offseason.

Also Sunday, the Packers acquired tight end Mark Redman from the Los Angeles Rams in exchange for a 2028 seventh-round pick. Green Bay has been searching for depth behind starter Tucker Kraft, who is coming off ACL surgery. With Luke Musgrave on the PUP list with a neck injury, the team also signed veteran Jonnu Smith last week.

ESPN's Brooke Pryor contributed to this report.

The Las Vegas Raiders head into their Week 1 game against the Miami Dolphins on Sept. 13 with a question mark surrounding Ashton Jeanty. Before the preseason finale against the San Francisco 49ers, Jeanty suffered an ankle injury.

Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak is expecting Jeanty to play, but he did leave room for the second-year running back to miss the game if his ankle isn't 100 percent ready to go.

Advertisement

"Still on the mend, still working to get him back," Kubiak told reporters on Aug. 28. "We got another week to assess how he's going to look going into this first game, but we're counting on him."

For now, if Jeanty does miss the game, the Raiders would be counting on Mike Washington Jr. to carry the load. However, one veteran running back issued a message to the Silver and Black that he'd be willing to help.

While speaking to 8 News Now's Madyson Marie, former Los Angeles Chargers running back Austin Ekeler expressed interest in playing for the Raiders.

"I'm unemployed right now," Ekeler said in an Aug. 28 video. "Being in my hometown anyway would be a dream for my family. I know that. Is the situation right? We'll have to see. How is Jeanty feeling? Do they need another guy?"

Advertisement

After leaving Los Angeles, Ekeler spent the last two seasons with the Washington Commanders, and the production wasn't the best. Ekeler had 91 carries for 410 yards and scored four touchdowns in 14 games for the Commanders, per StatMuse.

What Austin Ekeler Could Bring to the Raiders

Nonetheless, the 31-year-old noted the role he would be open to filling with the Raiders, should Las Vegas be interested in bringing him back to the AFC West.

"If I'm on a team, I'm going to be your third-down back," Ekeler added. "I'm going to be your two-minute guy. I'm going to be protecting your quarterback in passing situations. That's where I'm best.

Advertisement

"I'm best in passing situations. I can still run the ball. I can return kicks, absolutely. But my biggest strength is that. So if that presents itself, sure. If not, it's all good."

Klint Kubiak on Las Vegas' Running Back Situation

The Raiders look to have an impressive running game heading into the season with Jeanty and Washington. Kubiak spoke about the duo that can take pressure off the quarterback and boost the passing game. Furthermore, it doesn't sound like he's looking to sign a veteran free agent.

"I think that they're both going to prepare to play a lot of football," Kubiak told reporters. "As these games unfold, you react to the game. I think we got two guys that we're really excited about. We got some younger guys that we're really excited about too."

Advertisement

If the Raiders do decide to give Jeanty a rest for Week 1 and lean on Washington, the rookie running back might be ready for that task.

Last season, while playing for the Arkansas Razorbacks, Washington played 571 total snaps, earning a 78.3 overall PFF grade. Moreover, the 23-year-old carried the ball 167 times for 1,066 rushing yards and eight touchdowns.

He also averaged 6.4 yards per attempt and forced 34 missed tackles as a runner. Meanwhile, in the passing game, Washington caught 28 passes on 36 targets for 226 receiving yards and one touchdown.

text:
BEREA, Ohio -- The Cleveland Browns on Sunday trimmed their roster from four quarterbacks to three ahead of the NFL's cut-down deadline at 6 p.m. ET Sunday but did so without cutting or trading a passer.

Instead, Cleveland placed Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve and designated him to return with a back injury. The Browns will carry Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders and rookie Taylen Green as the quarterbacks on their initial 53-man roster.

Gabriel injured his back in Cleveland's preseason-closing win against the New England Patriots on Thursday night, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter. Gabriel had pain Saturday and underwent an MRI. He will be eligible to return after the first four games of the regular season.

The No. 94 pick in the 2025 draft, Gabriel started and played the first half of the preseason finale, throwing three touchdown passes. First-year coach Todd Monken was complimentary of Gabriel, who also started six games as a rookie.

"He's a prideful guy, he's had a lot of success in his career and all he does is prepare," Monken said. "That's all he does. Comes to work every day, prepares like a pro. You can see he can really operate. I mean, he gets it. He gets what we want to do. He has a certain confidence about him when he takes the field. And I'm fired up. ... It's like having a coach."

Green, a sixth-round pick, played in the second half of Thursday's game, his first action in the preseason. He completed 5 of 7 passes for 27 yards and ran for a game-high 66 yards on eight carries. The Browns sat Watson, who was previously named the Week 1 starter, and his backup, Sanders, after they received extensive work in training camp and the first two preseason games.

As part of moves to trim the roster to 53, the Browns placed rookie tight end Joe Royer on the reserve/non-football illness list. Royer, a fifth-round pick, missed all of training camp because of personal reasons. He will be eligible to return after the first four games of the season.

When Monken was asked Saturday whether he expected Royer to play in 2026, Monken said, "I'm not going to comment on that."

title: Fantasy Football Deep Dive on Christian Watson: The Packers' Clear WR1
authors: Adam Pfeifer, Dwain McFarland, Kendall Valenzuela, Sam Wallace
description:
All offseason, the fantasy football community has been debating whether Jayden Reed or Matthew Golden will emerge as the Green Bay Packers' WR2.
It’s Christian Watson season, y’all.
If you look at the games where he ran at least 70% of the routes, Watson averaged closer to 15 PPR PPG.
Join Our Newsletter Trusted by 400,000+ fantasy football players.
Christian Watson: WR1 If you are looking for the next breakout fantasy wideout, Watson checks seemingly every box.
text:
All offseason, the fantasy football community has been debating whether Jayden Reed or Matthew Golden will emerge as the Green Bay Packers' WR2. Both are intriguing, late-round upside swings, though there remains some uncertainty about their week-to-week role. There is no doubt, however, who the alpha in this offense will be.

It’s Christian Watson season, y’all.

For much of his career, Watson has flashed so much upside. Tons of touchdowns and fantasy points in certain stretches have unfortunately been paired with missed time due to injury. That was once again the case this past season when Watson returned halfway through the year following a late 2024 ACL tear. But Watson is now fully healthy, and following a four-year, $110.5 million contract extension, he is set to play the largest role of his career, not just for the Green Bay offense—but for fantasy teams as well.

A Sign Of What’s To Come

A 2024 late-season ACL tear sidelined Watson for the first seven games of last season, presenting serious risk as a fantasy option. But when he made his debut in Week 8, Watson wasted no time showing his immense upside. From Weeks 8-18, Watson ran 72% of the routes, while posting a 23% TPRR and 20% target share. During that stretch, Watson was the WR22 in fantasy points per game (13.2), but the underlying metrics prove that, with added volume, he can do so much more.

Watson Weeks 8-18:

17.5 Yd/Rec (2nd)

2.54 YPRR (8th)

11 plays of 20-plus yards (10th)

6 TDs (5th)

Despite ranking just 33rd in targets during that stretch (55), Watson ranked 14th in receiving yards (608), showcasing his huge play potential. Watson was fantasy’s WR21 on a PPG basis upon his return, while his 0.57 fantasy points per route were good for fifth-best among all wideouts. But keep in mind that Watson wasn’t always a full-time player during that stretch. He dealt with shoulder issues down the stretch, limiting him to just 56.3% of the routes from Weeks 15-17. If you look at the games where he ran at least 70% of the routes, Watson averaged closer to 15 PPR PPG.

Watson was once again mostly used down the field, ranking sixth in the league in aDOT from Week 8 on (18.0), while running go routes just under 22% of the time. Watson’s skill set is always going to lend itself to explosive plays deep down the field. But he can also do more than that.

And for the first time in his career, he’ll be asked to prove it.

By registering or logging in, you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Christian Watson: WR1

If you are looking for the next breakout fantasy wideout, Watson checks seemingly every box. Talented player? Check. Fantasy-friendly offense? Yep. Vacated targets and routes? You bet. Good quarterback? I’d say so.

It’s time to roll.

The departure of both Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks is going to have a massive impact. Though Watson has demonstrated serious potential throughout his career, it has unfortunately been on limited volume. Since entering the NFL in 2022, Watson has averaged just 4.73 targets per game, while never eclipsing a 20% target share. The Fantasy Life projections have Watson penciled in for closer to seven targets per game this season, as Green Bay’s usual wide receiver rotation will be much, much tighter this year. Doubs led the Packers with a 77% route rate last season, while Wicks was just over 50%. But overall, five Green Bay receivers ran at least half of the routes. That is going to be very condensed this upcoming season, while Doubs’ absence in particular could really benefit Watson.

We love touchdowns in fantasy football, right? I thought so. Watson has scored 20 touchdowns on 133 career receptions (15%) and could be in line for the most red zone work of his career. Both Watson and Doubs entered the league in 2022. Since then, Watson ranks 20th among receivers in end zone targets (33), with Doubs right behind him (29). And once Watson made his debut this past season, he and Doubs actually tied for the team lead in end zone target share (33%). Doubs also accounted for 32% of the Packers' targets from inside the 10-yard line, the eighth-highest rate in football. So Watson has essentially been splitting end zone looks with Doubs, yet still has scored plenty of touchdowns. And now Doubs is gone?

Sign me up.

Overall, Watson’s role seems ready to expand. We already know that while Reed and Golden compete for snaps in two-wide sets, Watson will be a staple. Doubs led the team in routes from 12 personnel during the second half of last season, but Watson was right behind him. With both Doubs and Wicks gone, Watson will always be on the field in 12 personnel, a grouping Matt LaFleur deployed 20 plays per game a year ago, the sixth-most in football. It also looks like Watson’s usage is set to change in 2026. Watson appears to be playing more of the ‘Z’ receiver role this season, which means more movement and designed looks. Dwain McFarland highlighted Watson’s encouraging preseason usage in his Week 2 Preseason Takeaways article (an absolute must-read), pointing out that he was used quite a bit in motion and play-action passes, two fantasy cheat codes for wide receivers.

More creative usage would be a welcome sight for Watson, who ranks just 64th among receivers in routes from motion since 2022 (108). LaFleur’s offense should lean on motion, helping Watson get more free releases and layup looks. Since 2020, Green Bay’s ranks in shift-motion:

2020: 50% (5th)

2021: 54% (5th)

2022: 57% (8th)

2023: 61% (5th)

2024: 70% (3rd)

2025: 59% (8th)

We mentioned how the lack of volume has held Watson (and most Green Bay pass-catchers) back in fantasy over the years. Playing in a WR rotation already hurts your target and route upside, but it’s even more difficult in a run-first offense. Over the past three years, the Packers have sported the league’s fourth-lowest neutral script pass rate (53%), while Jordan Love ranks 17th in dropbacks per game during that span (33.3). Given Love’s efficiency, it would be fun to see what this offense could look like if he threw the football more.

But what if that’s this season?

This time last year, the Packers looked like one of the best defenses in all of football. And that carried over into the season. But everything changed in Week 15. Green Bay lost Micah Parsons to a torn ACL, and from that point on, this once vaunted defense suddenly became one to attack.

During the final four weeks of the year (including the playoffs), Green Bay’s defense fell apart. With Parsons off the field, the Packers posted a 3.7% sack rate, compared to 7.3% with Parsons on the field. And with Parsons sidelined for the final four weeks of the season, Green Bay allowed over 28 points per game. That resulted in the Packers' pass rate when leading by four-plus points climbing to 62%, the fifth-highest rate in football. For reference, from Weeks 1-15 with Parsons healthy, that pass rate was down at 52% (18th).

Entering the 2026 campaign, it appears the earliest possible date we could see Parsons return is Week 6, which means Green Bay’s passing rate might climb quite a bit during the first half of the season. And an uptick in potential targets for Watson is exciting. Again, we project Watson to average 6.7 targets per game this upcoming season. There have been 20 regular season games in Watson’s career where he’s seen at least six targets. In those games, Watson has averaged 66 receiving yards and 14.9 PPR PPG. For reference, 14.9 PR PPG would have been good for WR10 last season, albeit in a down year for the wide receiver position. That still would have been good for WR17 in 2024.

Should You Draft Christian Watson?

If he can stay healthy (yes, that is a concern), Watson legitimately has top-15 upside this season. Yet he’s still being drafted as the WR29 over on Underdog, and I’ve done drafts on other platforms where Watson has been a bench receiver.

Yes, please.

I understand some skeptics point to Watson’s injury track record, which is rather lengthy. ACL tear, ankle sprain, hamstring strains, knee bruise, etc. Some may see that resume and think “injury prone.” But every player in the NFL is injury prone.

Until they’re not.

My excitement in Watson’s talent and opportunity outweighs any potential injury concerns. And far too many times in fantasy, our “glass half empty” mindset wins. “What if Watson gets hurt?”

But what if he doesn’t? That’s something I’m excited to find out.

ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Denver Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper was placed on the NFL's commissioner exempt list Sunday, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter.

It means Cooper, who is scheduled to be in Douglas County (Colo.) court Monday for arraignment on domestic violence charges, can neither practice nor play in games for the Broncos while he is on the list. The Broncos have elected to allow Cooper to participate throughout training camp practices and the preseason games, saying the team was "staying the course with the league protocol, with the club protocol, relative to what we've been advised to do."

The affidavit that was included in the police investigation into Cooper's first arrest June 4 included a report from the medical exam of Cooper's girlfriend. Payton has consistently deferred to the NFL's investigation and the legal process when he has discussed the team's approach with the sixth-year linebacker. Payton said the Broncos set guidelines for Cooper after the arrest, and that has included therapy.

Cooper was a seventh-round pick in the 2021 draft and has 31.5 sacks in 81 career games with the Broncos, including eight sacks last season. He has started every game in each of the past three seasons.

The Atlanta Falcons will try to shore up their defensive line with the acquisition of Gervon Dexter Sr. from the Chicago Bears on cut-down day.

The Falcons traded cornerback Clark Phillips III and a fifth-round draft pick to the Bears on Sunday morning for Dexter, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and Jeremy Fowler.

Dexter, 24, was a starter the last two seasons in Chicago, accumulating 11 sacks combined during that period. He was a second-round pick by the Bears in 2023.

New Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham was the assistant GM of the Bears when they selected Dexter, who is now in the final season of his rookie contract.

The Falcons struggled against the run last season and have made it a priority to improve the interior of their defensive line. They traded for Maason Smith and signed Da'Shawn Hand and Chris Williams in the offseason.

But Hand, who was expected to be an impact player, suffered a leg injury early in training camp and has not yet returned to practice. The 6-foot-6, 326-pound Dexter brings a big, physical presence to the position.

Dexter suffered a hamstring injury during Tuesday's practice, according to Bears coach Ben Johnson. He did not travel with the team to Tennessee for Chicago's joint practice and preseason finale Saturday night against the Titans.

Phillips, 24, was a fourth-round pick by the Falcons in 2023. He started seven games in 2023 and 2024 as mostly an outside corner, but missed most of last season with a triceps injury.

Chicago used ample resources to shore up its interior depth this offseason by signing free agents Neville Gallimore, Kentavius Street and James Lynch. The Bears' sole defensive line addition in the draft came in the sixth round, when they selected defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg from Georgia Tech.

The rookie earned high praise from coaches over the last six weeks as he worked his way into regular first-team reps.

"He's a beast," Johnson said of van den Berg. "This guy ... he's an incredible athlete. He's still learning the game of football to a degree, and yet it's amazing what he brings to the table."

text:
INDIANAPOLIS – Running back Isiah Pacheco's status for the start of the regular season is up in the air because of a back injury. If Pacheco can't play Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said he's "comfortable" with Jacob Saylors opening the year as Jahmyr Gibbs' backup.

"I am," Campbell said. "I’m comfortable with those guys. And I just like the thought of having a guy in our system, think that's important. Knows our terminology, knows our guys, knows the protections. Just kind of knows it all, man. Understands our quarterback and how he thinks. I just think that's important."

Saylors ran for 100 yards on 17 carries Saturday, Aug. 29, as the Lions closed the preseason with a 25-16 win over the Indianapolis Colts.

He had three runs of 16-plus yards Saturday and averaged 6 yards per carry for the preseason.

The Lions signed Pacheco to be Gibbs' primary backup after trading David Montogmery to Houston in the offseason, but Pacheco missed most of training camp with knee and back injuries.

Campbell said last week Pacheco's sprained knee had healed but the running back was "touch and go" with his back injury.

Gibbs is expected to shoulder the bulk of the work in the Lions backfield this fall, but he's never had more than 250 carries in a season.

Along with Saylors, the Lions are expected to keep Sione Vaki as a backup on their initial 53-man roster, and have Trayveon Williams and Jabari Small vying for roster spots. Small, who spent part of last season on the Lions' practice squad, left Saturday's game with an injury while Williams ran for 57 yards on nine carries.

Vaki did not play Saturday for precautionary reasons after missing the first two games of the preseason with a broken nose and back spasms.

"Small would kind of fall into that bucket just like Saylors would," Campbell said. "They’ve kind of got a feel of what we're doing and they've shown a little bit of stuff here that's good and they know our system. It doesn't mean we wouldn't go outside and see if something else is there, but I like those guys, and I like Saylors."

Saylors played primarily on special teams for the Lions last season after playing the 2024-25 spring seasons with the St. Louis Battlehawks of the UFL. He had two carries for 11 yards for the Lions last fall.

"He’s made plays out of the backfield.," Lions quarterback Josh Dobbs said. "He runs hard, he made plays. He’s hard to tackle. He’s very fast so I’m excited to see how we use him this year for sure."

Head Coach of Tampa Bay, Todd Bowles, recently commented on his two WRs, giving some insight into their availability for the Bucs' Week 1 matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Jalen McMillan

16 player squads

Practice squads were limited to 10 players in 2019, but that was set to change with the new CBA signed in 2020. The number was going to 12 players for 2 years, and then was going to be increased to 14 players in 2022. That all changed when the uncertainty of COVID-19 hit, and the league increased practice squads to 16 players, which will once again be the limit in 2026.

International Player Pathway Program

Teams participating in the International Player Pathway(IPP) program can have 91-man rosters during the offseason. They can also have a 17th practice squad member for the season, but if signed to the practice squad, that player can’t be signed to the regular season roster; however, starting in 2024 he can be elevated for up to three games. If the player is kept on the 53-man roster, he is subject to waiver rules.

The Washington Commanders currently have DE T.J. Maguranyanga on the roster, and he is eligible to be signed to their practice squad as the 17th member if he is waived and clears waivers. He is unlikely to be part of the 53-man roster.

Practice squad players moving up to the main roster

Like the last three seasons, teams have more flexibility with using practice squad players on game day. PS players can be activated on game day before the team announces their inactives (90 minutes before game time). Teams are allowed to elevate players from their practice squad to the game day roster without having to cut a member of the 53-man team. Accordingly, clubs can increase from the standard 53 to 55 players while game day active squads expand from a previous 46 to 47 players (or 48 if a team carries eight offensive linemen). Any practice squad player can be elevated and automatically reverts back to the practice squad after a game.

Each practice squad player is now able to be elevated up to three times per season. To be activated a fourth time requires the player to be signed to the regular roster. During the playoffs, practice squad players have unlimited elevations. This makes it easier for teams to have players they know and trust on game day, and also not have to subject them to waivers when they are signed to the main roster and cut to get back to the practice squad as was true in the past.

Veteran players

Another change is the eligibility requirements for veteran players. Previously teams could have up to 4 players who had two years of NFL experience. Now teams can have 6 veterans with no limit on the amount of accrued seasons they have in the league. A player must have been on full-play status for at least six regular-season games in a given season to gain an accrued season. This includes being on the active/inactive list, injured reserve or reserve PUP.

Weekly payment

Practice squad players make $13,750 per week or $247,500 for 18 weeks. Veteran players with over two years of experience make a minimum of $18,350 per week or $330,300 for 18 weeks, and a maximum of $22,8590 per week or $411,300 for 18 weeks.

Signing with the practice squad

Teams must complete their roster cuts by Sunday August 30th at 6 p.m. ET, meaning that almost 1,200 players will be released or placed on an injury list.

Teams have until Monday at noon to claim unvested players that have been waived.

Vested veterans (players with a minimum of 4 accrued seasons) become free agents immediately and are able to sign with any team.

Starting at 12:00 p.m. ET on August 31st, teams can begin signing players to their practice squads.

Practice squad basics

Practice squad players practice with the team. They do not play in games, unless they are elevated (see above)

Practice squad players are paid per week and can be released at any point during the season.

Practice squad players are free to sign with other NFL teams, but they have to be signed to the 53-man active roster of the acquiring team. A practice squad player cannot be signed to another practice squad unless he is first released or waived.

A practice squad player cannot sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game, or 10 days if his team is currently on a bye week.

If a practice squad player is signed to the active roster, he will receive a minimum of three weekly paychecks, even if he is released before spending three weeks with the new team.

In order to be signed to a practice squad after being released, a player who is not a vested veteran must first clear waivers, and is subject to waiver claims by other teams.

Waiver wire

The Washington Commanders had the No. 7 overall pick in this year’s draft, which means they have six teams in front of them that could potentially claim a player Washington wants. There should be plenty of players available, and Washington will be on the look out for some offensive line help next week.

The waiver order goes by original draft order not counting trades.

Teams maintain their places on the waiver priority list through Week 3 of the regular season.

After Week 3 the waiver priority order is determined by reverse order of wins.

Teams don’t lose their spot on the priority list like in fantasy football.

Teams can put in as many waiver claims as they want, and will be awarded the player(s) if they are the highest-ranked claiming team. Any player added through waivers will need a corresponding roster move to make room for him on the roster.

The claiming team picks up the player’s contract, not including any signing bonuses that his original team already paid.

Vested veterans (on an NFL roster for at least 6 games per season, for at least 4 seasons) aren’t subject to waivers until after the trade deadline, which will be after Week 9 this season.

Players who are waived/injured, and not claimed on waivers, return to their team and are placed on injured reserve unless an injury settlement is made.

text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers concluded their 2026 preseason slate on Friday evening with a 19-0 loss in Jacksonville. That means the next time they take the field it will count as the regular season begins.

That won't happen immediately. Since paring its preseason down to three weeks in 2021, the NFL has had an extra week in the schedule between the final exhibition contest and the first set of regular-season games. The Buccaneers and all other NFL squads will use the next week to get their 53-man rosters and 16-man practice squads in shape before Week One begins. Once that happens, the Buccaneers will be ticketed for an opener in Cincinnati on Sunday, September 13 to take on Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, Dexter Lawrence and the Bengals. Kickoff is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET at Paycor Stadium.

The Buccaneers will be looking for a 1-0 start to their regular season for the sixth year in a row, but it will be against a Cincinnati team that boasts a high-powered offense and is hoping for much better defensive results after the offseason trade for Lawrence and the free agency additions of safety Bryan Cook and edge rusher Boye Mafe. Since going to the Super Bowl in the 2021 season and the AFC Championship game in 2022, the Bengals have missed the playoffs for three straight years, but that has largely been due to injuries to Burrow and a cratering defense.

When healthy, Burrow is clearly one of the most productive quarterbacks in the NFL. He played all 17 games in 2024 and led the NFL with 4,918 passing yards and 43 touchdown passes. He is surrounded with elite playmaking talent in Chase (6,837 receiving yards and 54 touchdowns in five seasons), fellow wideout Tee Higgins and running back Chase Brown. The Buccaneers will hope that their efforts to significantly amplify their edge rush rotation have paid off, giving them a chance to disrupt Burrow's timing.

After the additions of Lawrence and Mafe, the Bengals appear to have a more dangerous defensive front of their own, also now featuring defensive tackle Jonathan Allen and second-round edge rusher Cashius Howell. The Bucs will counter with an offensive line that, after a severely injury-plagued 2025 season, is back to the starting five that produced very impressive results in 2024, anchored by All-Pro left tackle Tristan Wirfs. The Bucs will also be unveiling a new offensive coordinated by Zac Robinson and now featuring a stacked receiver room and a new running back tandem with Kenny Gainwell joining Bucky Irving.

The Buccaneers won four straight NFC South titles from 2021-24, and that was after capturing the Super Bowl LV title in 2020, but they missed the playoffs last season on a tiebreaker. The team is aiming to get back into title contention in 2025, and it starts in Cincinnati.

text:
NEW YORK — Aaron Boone was peeved by his team’s performance in a matinee loss in Saturday’s doubleheader at Yankee Stadium. Then George Lombard Jr., the shortstop who had played every inning of his brief New York Yankees career, twisted his right knee early in the second game.

“Good enough to stay in right now,” Boone, the Yankees’ manager, told Ken Rosenthal on Fox as the top of the third inning began, but he didn’t sound hopeful. The next pitch sailed over the right field fence for a Boston Red Sox homer. The day was becoming a disaster.

But while Lombard was visiting New York-Presbyterian Hospital in the middle innings, the Yankees (77-59) recovered to wallop the Red Sox, 9-2, and earn a split. They now lead Boston (74-62) by three games for the top American League wild-card spot.

Lombard might not play on Sunday, when the winner will clinch the season series and a potential tiebreaker between the teams. But the Yankees believe Lombard will avoid the injured list, even without definitive word on his test results.

“They’re still waiting to make sure and clarify, but it looks like a day-to-day situation,” Boone said postgame.

Lombard was batting against Brayan Bello in the second when he twisted his knee while rotating his hips on a fastball that veered inside. The ball did not hit Lombard, but he asked for time after the awkward movement.

He grimaced and hopped out of the box on his left foot, then grabbed at his knee and flexed it with a trainer before staying in and singling to left on the next pitch.

“A little weird discomfort,” Boone described it after the game. “He was going to swing and then kind of really shut down. I think he caught his spike a little bit as he was kind of putting the brakes on. Just kind of tweaked it.”

Lombard played defense in the top of the third and batted again in the bottom of the inning, flying out to left. But Boone removed him before the top of the fourth, shifting José Caballero to shortstop and bringing in Amed Rosario to play third base.

“I heard that it’s not too bad,” Caballero said. “It’s great news because he’s been playing really well. So we need the whole group together and healthy.”

Lombard, 21, has become integral to the group since arriving on Aug. 4, after the Yankees refused to trade him at the deadline. He is hitting .253/.310/.367 with two home runs in 23 games, though he has committed seven errors.

His single was part of an unusual attack by the Yankees, who had 13 singles without an extra-base hit in Saturday’s second game. The last time they did that in a nine-inning game (per a Stathead search) was May 1, 1999, in Kansas City. Chuck Knoblauch had three hits that night; Luis García Jr. did it this time.

García, acquired from the Washington Nationals in a trade on Aug. 3, has 15 hits (including four homers) in his last 10 games. He is hitting .309 for the Yankees and will not be a free agent until after the 2027 season.

“You’re seeing a guy (at) 26 years old really come of age this year, and he hasn’t really missed the beat since coming over to us,” Boone said. “We’re thrilled to have him because he’s a dangerous, dangerous hitter.”

The Yankees haven’t had enough of those in their summer without Aaron Judge, who has not played since May 31 because of a stress fracture of his right rib. In 75 games without Judge before Saturday, the Yankees had a .220 average and a .290 on-base percentage, both MLB lows, and had outscored only the Seattle Mariners during that time.

The first game brought more futility, with the Yankees looking all but helpless in a 6-0 loss to Jake Bennett and three relievers. Their Game 2 outburst came mostly with an eighth-inning singles parade off Raymond Burgos, Boston’s extra man for the doubleheader.

The Yankees’ best news was probably the return of Max Fried, who missed two weeks with a recurrence of a left elbow bone bruise. Fried was on a pitch count and still hasn’t earned a victory since April, but he said he felt strong for 3 ⅔ innings, striking out four and allowing one run.

“I would say I was feeling really strong before this IL stint, and I was feeling good in the (Aug. 14) game, it was just one little pitch that irritated it,” Fried said. “So to be able to get through, feel really good and come out healthy, that’s all I can ask for.”

Lombard will be back at Yankee Stadium on Sunday with an update on his status. If he can say something similar after Saturday’s scare, that is all the Yankees can ask for, too.

title: Parents should think twice about letting their kids play tackle football - MS NOW
authors: Anthony L. Fisher, Jason Page, Keith Reed, Kevin B. Blackistone

text:
On Tuesday, yet another study linking the repetitive head trauma experienced by NFL players to chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, later in life was released.

The New York Times reported on research published in the British Medical Journal examining CTE among former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021. Of 878 former players who died during that period, 235 had their brains examined. Of those, 215 were diagnosed with CTE.

That’s 91.4%.

But researchers cannot say 91.4% of NFL players develop CTE because those brains weren’t a random sample. Even if every one of the other 643 players whose brains weren’t examined did not have CTE, those 215 confirmed cases still represent 24.5% of the entire group.

At least 1 in 4.

As usual, the NFL’s media partners at ESPN were largely silent. “Get Up” host Mike Greenberg spent 55 seconds reading the findings from a teleprompter. “First Take” similarly devoted 43 seconds to it. The network’s highest-paid star commentator, Pat McAfee, didn’t touch the story at all.

But this isn’t another column arguing that the NFL isn’t doing enough to protect its players, nor am I suggesting we abolish professional or college football. I think the NFL is doing about as much as it reasonably can to make an inherently violent sport safer when its athletes are bigger, stronger and faster than ever.

College and NFL players are adults. They know the risks. If they decide those risks are worth taking, that’s their choice.

My concern is with those who cannot meaningfully make that choice for themselves.

Children.

Roughly two million American kids under 18 play tackle football each year. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found an average of about 53,700 emergency-department visits annually for football-related traumatic brain injuries among children.

And those are just the injuries serious enough to reach an emergency room.

What about the concussion that never gets diagnosed? Or the kid who “gets his bell rung,” sits out a couple of plays and goes back into the game? More importantly, what about the hundreds of ordinary hits a child can absorb during a season that never produce concussion symptoms at all?

That’s increasingly where the CTE conversation is headed: not simply diagnosed concussions, but the cumulative effect of repetitive head impacts.

It’s one thing if an adult wants to roll the dice with his future health. And let’s be honest, it’s a gamble worth considering when you look at the money being handed out in college football and the NFL. We’re talking about life-changing and, in some cases, generational wealth.

An adult can weigh the potential reward against the potential consequences. A 12-year-old cannot.

More articles

A child — whose father hopes to live out his football dreams vicariously through his son — doesn’t possess that same depth of knowledge. He cannot meaningfully consent to the potential long-term consequences of repeatedly subjecting his developing brain to violent collisions.

Children need to be protected, even if they want to play.

So how do we do it without eliminating the game?

Perhaps tackle football shouldn’t begin until age 10 or 12. Flag football could replace it before then, eliminating years of unnecessary collisions. We could dramatically reduce or eliminate full-contact tackling in practice. We could ban high-impact collision drills. We could require independent medical professionals at games. We could also examine matching younger players by size and physical development, rather than simply age, so a 90-pound child isn’t routinely colliding with someone twice his size.

None of these ideas alone ultimately solve the problem, and there is no uniform national standard. Different leagues, organizations and states operate under different rules.

So football season begins again around the country. Games will be played. Teams will win and teams will lose. Millions of us will watch because football remains an incredible game.

I’m certainly going to watch.

But the more we learn about what repeated blows to the head can do to the human brain, the harder it becomes to pretend we don’t know there’s a cost.

Adults can decide whether that cost is worth paying.

Children cannot.

And if we aren’t willing to stop them from playing tackle football, we owe it to them to make sure they aren’t paying a price decades from now for a decision they weren’t old enough to understand.

text:
Dillon Gabriel's stellar performance in the Cleveland Browns' preseason finale was enough to earn him a spot on their 53-man roster.

The Browns will be keeping the second-year quarterback entering the regular season, ESPN reported Sunday.

However, ESPN also reported that the Browns have placed Gabriel on injured reserve, designated for return, due to a back injury. Gabriel reportedly suffered a back injury during the preseason finale and underwent an MRI. The injury was notable enough to land him on injured reserve.

Gabriel joins Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders as the other quarterbacks on Cleveland's roster.

Watson has already been named Cleveland's starting quarterback, and Sanders is expected to be the primary backup after competing with the veteran for the starting job. However, Gabriel could have a chance at starting at some point this season if the Browns' quarterback woes continue. Cleveland started three quarterbacks last season and has had seven different starting quarterbacks since the start of the 2024 campaign.

Gabriel was one of the three quarterbacks who started a game for the Browns in 2025. The 2025 third-round pick went 1-5 as a starter, though, as he largely struggled. He completed 59.5% of his passes for 937 yards, seven touchdowns and two interceptions to go with an 80.8 passer rating over the 10 games he appeared in.

Gabriel's final start came in Week 11, when he suffered a concussion against the Baltimore Ravens. While the injury wasn't season-ending, Sanders started the final seven games for the Browns, going 3-4.

With Sanders performing relatively well and Watson returning from an Achilles injury, it was believed that Gabriel was fighting for a roster spot during training camp and the preseason. He got the start in the Browns' preseason finale against the New England Patriots on Thursday, completing 12 of 15 passes for 186 yards and three touchdowns in the victory.

Jamel Dean, Jaquan Brisker, and Rayshawn Jenkins all provide options in a secondary that was challenged a year ago.

But where does the Steelers’ roster rank in the larger NFL landscape? According to CBS Sports, it’s in the bottom half of the league. Jordan Dajani and Tyler Sullivan ranked all 32 NFL rosters and had Pittsburgh at No. 19, with their main questions being at two positions.

At safety, the question is less about the players’ ability but more about their ability to stay on the field.

“There are some durability concerns with this group. Pittsburgh inked Jaquan Brisker to a one-year deal in free agency, and while he played in all 17 games for Chicago last season and broke up eight passes, he has a history of concussions,” Dajani and Sullivan wrote. “Meanwhile, DeShon Elliott was limited to five games last year due to injury. To compound the concern surrounding their injury history is the lack of depth behind them.”

Brisker has missed the entire preseason with an injury and his status is unclear as the regular season nears. Elliott is healthy after missing the second half of last season due to injury and will return to his starting role, but who will start beside him if Brisker remains out is unclear.

Jenkins has played well in preseason action as a late addition to the roster but is not guaranteed to make the team. Robert Spears-Jennings has impressed as well, but likely can’t be trusted as a starter as a seventh-round rookie.

Jalen Ramsey, who has battled injury himself since training camp, is another option at safety, but Pittsburgh would prefer to use him as a chess piece that moves around the defense.

The injury concerns are real at safety, but it isn’t the only reason Dajani and Sullivan docked Pittsburgh’s roster in their rankings. They also pointed to the quarterback position.

“Aaron Rodgers already announced this season as his last, and it stands to wonder what Pittsburgh will get out of the 42-year-old,” Dajani and Sullivan write. “While his 24-7 touchdown-to-interception ratio was inside the top 10 in 2025, Rodgers’ numbers beyond that were middling. He was 16th among 33 qualified QBs in completion percentage, 15th in passing yards and 27th in yards per attempt. Does that improve, decline, or stay the same in 2026?”

Pittsburgh’s best hope is that added weapons on offense and a new, offensive-minded head coach who has a history with Rodgers is enough to see an improved Rodgers in 2026. Given the weight of the position, and what we saw from Rodgers last season, it’s fair to negatively impact Pittsburgh’s ranking based on not having one of the league’s best signal callers.
